title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
lines: These questions are fast if you know the particle counts, the electron arrangements of the first 20 elements and the direction of each trend. Most "hard" items simply combine two trends, so learn each trend together with its reason.
## Protons, neutrons and electrons
- An atom has a tiny, dense nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons. Almost all the mass is in the nucleus.

- Nuclide notation puts the mass number A top left and the atomic number Z bottom left of the symbol, e.g. ²³₁₁Na. Z is the atomic number (protons), A is the mass number (protons + neutrons). Neutrons N = A − Z.
- In a neutral atom electrons = Z. For an ion, electrons = Z − charge: Na⁺ has 11 − 1 = 10 electrons; Cl⁻ has 17 + 1 = 18.
- Proton charge +1, electron −1, neutron 0. Proton and neutron masses are each about 1 u; an electron is about 1/1836 of that.
> Example: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in ³²S²⁻ (Z = 16)?
> Protons 16, neutrons 32 − 16 = 16, electrons 16 + 2 = 18.

- Species with 10 electrons: Ne, HF, H₂O, NH₃, CH₄, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺, F⁻, O²⁻, OH⁻, NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺. Species with 18 electrons: Ar, HCl, H₂S, PH₃, SiH₄, H₂O₂, N₂H₄, C₂H₆, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻, S²⁻, HS⁻. These lists appear often in "which pair has the same number of electrons" questions.
! Trap: OH⁻ has 9 protons and 10 electrons; NH₄⁺ has 11 protons and 10 electrons. Same electrons, different protons.
## Isotopes, nuclides and allotropes
- A nuclide is one kind of atom with a definite Z and N. Isotopes are nuclides of the same element with different neutron numbers: ¹H, ²H (D), ³H (T); ¹²C, ¹³C, ¹⁴C; ³⁵Cl, ³⁷Cl.
- Isotopes have almost identical chemical properties (same electron arrangement) but different masses and physical properties.
- Do not confuse: isotopes are atoms; allotropes are different forms of an element (O₂, O₃); isomers are compounds with the same formula.
- H₂, D₂ and HD are all molecules of the element hydrogen; they are not isotopes of each other (isotopes are atoms).
> Example: How many different HCl molecules (by mass) can form from ¹H, ²H, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl?
> Two H isotopes × two Cl isotopes = 4 molecules: masses 36, 37, 38 and 39. All four masses differ.
> Example: Find the mass of neutrons in 2 g of D₂O (²H₂¹⁶O).
> M(D₂O) = 20 g/mol, so 2 g is 0.1 mol. Each molecule has 1 + 1 + 8 = 10 neutrons, giving 1 mol of neutrons.
## Electron configuration

- Electrons fill shells (energy levels) n = 1, 2, 3... Maximum in a shell is 2n² (2, 8, 18). The outermost shell holds at most 8 electrons (2 if it is the first shell); the second-to-outermost at most 18.
- Shell notation for the first 20 elements: Na 2,8,1; Mg 2,8,2; Al 2,8,3; Si 2,8,4; P 2,8,5; S 2,8,6; Cl 2,8,7; Ar 2,8,8; K 2,8,8,1; Ca 2,8,8,2.
- Subshell notation: s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10. Order of filling: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p. So K is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s¹ and Fe (Z = 26) is [Ar]3d⁶4s².
- Simple transition cases: Cr (Z = 24) is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ and Cu (Z = 29) is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹, because half-filled and full d subshells are extra stable.
- Transition metal ions lose 4s electrons first: Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶; Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵ (half-filled, so Fe³⁺ is more stable than Fe²⁺).
- Hund's rule: electrons occupy separate orbitals of a subshell with parallel spins before pairing. Nitrogen 2p³ has three unpaired electrons.
> Example: Which element has an outer shell with twice as many electrons as its inner shell?
> If there are two shells, the inner shell holds 2, so the outer holds 4: 2,4 is carbon (Z = 6).
! Trap: 3d fills after 4s but is written before it, and 4s empties first when an ion forms.
## The periodic table: groups and periods
- Elements are arranged by increasing atomic number. Period number = number of occupied electron shells. Main-group number = outer-shell electrons.
- Period lengths: 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32. There are 18 columns: 7 main groups (A), 7 subgroups (B), group VIII (three columns) and group 0 (noble gases).
- Group 1 (alkali metals, except H), group 2 (alkaline earth metals), group 17 (halogens), group 18 (noble gases). Transition metals are all metals.
- Locating an element from Z: subtract noble-gas numbers 2, 10, 18, 36, 54, 86. Z = 35: 35 − 18 = 17, so period 4, group 17 (Br). Z = 20: period 4, group 2 (Ca).
- For main-group elements: highest positive oxidation state = group number (except O and F); lowest negative state = group number − 8. Chlorine: +7 and −1. The sum of their absolute values is 8.
> Example: Elements X and Y are in the same period. X's highest oxide is X₂O₅ and Y forms H₂Y. Which is further right?
> X₂O₅ means highest state +5, so group 15. H₂Y means −2, so group 16. Y is further right.
## Periodic trends: atomic radius
- Across a period (left to right), radius decreases: more protons pull the same number of shells closer.
- Down a group, radius increases: more shells.
- For ions with the same electron arrangement, more protons means a smaller ion: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺.
- A cation is smaller than its atom (Na⁺ < Na); an anion is larger (Cl⁻ > Cl).
! Memory trick: "more shells, bigger; same shells, more protons, smaller."
## Ionisation energy and electronegativity
- First ionisation energy is the energy to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom. It generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.
- Exceptions across period 2 and 3: group 2 > group 13 (Be > B, Mg > Al) because the s subshell is full; group 15 > group 16 (N > O, P > S) because the half-filled p subshell is stable.
- Large jumps in successive ionisation energies show when a new, inner shell is reached. A jump after the 2nd electron means 2 outer electrons (group 2).
- Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom attracts bonding electrons. It increases across a period and decreases down a group. F is the most electronegative (4.0), then O, then N and Cl.
> Example: Successive ionisation energies of X (kJ/mol): 578, 1817, 2745, 11577. Which group is X in?
> The big jump comes after the 3rd electron, so X has 3 outer electrons: group 13 (aluminium fits).
## Metallic and non-metallic character
- Metallic character (ease of losing electrons) decreases across a period and increases down a group. Non-metallic character does the reverse.

- Evidence of stronger metallic character: reacts more vigorously with water or acids to give H₂; its hydroxide is a stronger base (NaOH > Mg(OH)₂ > Al(OH)₃); it displaces a less active metal from its salt.

- Evidence of stronger non-metallic character: combines more easily with H₂ and the hydride is more stable (HF > HCl > HBr > HI); its highest-oxide acid is stronger (HClO₄ > H₂SO₄ > H₃PO₄ > H₂SiO₃); it displaces a weaker non-metal (Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂).
- The boundary between metals and non-metals runs diagonally from B to At; elements near it (Si, Ge) are semiconductors.

! Trap: only the highest-oxidation-state oxyacid shows non-metallic strength. HClO is a weak acid, but that does not make chlorine a weak non-metal. Also, the acidity of hydrides (HCl stronger than HF) does not follow non-metallic character.
> Example: X, Y, Z are Na, Mg, Al. Rank the basic strength of their hydroxides and their atomic radii.
> Base strength: NaOH > Mg(OH)₂ > Al(OH)₃ (Al(OH)₃ is amphoteric). Radius: Na > Mg > Al. Both fall across the period.
## Putting it together

- A typical "element inference" question gives clues such as: "W's outer electrons are three times its inner electrons" (2,6 is O); "X is the most active metal in period 3" (Na); "Y's oxide is amphoteric" (Al); "Z has the highest electronegativity" (F). Identify each element first, then apply the trends.
- Check the answer with two trends together: an element with large radius usually has low ionisation energy, low electronegativity and strong metallic character.

title: Chemical Bonding and Structure
lines: Bonding explains why salt melts at 801 °C while ice melts at 0 °C. Exam questions ask you to name the bond type, draw or judge an electron-dot structure, predict a shape, decide polarity, and link structure to melting point, hardness and conductivity.
## Ionic bonds
- An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal. Typical: NaCl, MgO, CaF₂, K₂S.
- Compounds containing NH₄⁺ (such as NH₄Cl) are ionic even though they contain no metal. AlCl₃ is covalent even though it contains a metal.
- Ionic compounds: high melting points, hard but brittle, conduct when molten or dissolved, not when solid.
- Lattice strength grows with ion charge and falls with ion size: MgO (2+, 2−) melts far higher than NaCl (1+, 1−); NaF > NaCl > NaBr in melting point.
> Example: Which has the higher melting point, CaO or KCl?
> CaO has ions of charge 2+ and 2−; KCl has 1+ and 1−. Higher charges and similar sizes give stronger attraction, so CaO melts higher (about 2600 °C against about 770 °C).
## Covalent bonds
- A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two atoms, usually non-metals. Single (H–H), double (O=O), triple (N≡N).
- Non-polar covalent bonds join identical atoms (H–H, Cl–Cl, C–C). Polar covalent bonds join different atoms (H–Cl, O–H); the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge.
- Bond strength: triple > double > single between the same atoms; shorter bonds are stronger. Bond strength decides the thermal stability of molecules: HF > HCl > HBr > HI.
- Covalent compounds: acids (HCl, H₂SO₄), non-metal oxides and hydrides, and most organic compounds.
- Coordinate (dative) bonds: both shared electrons come from one atom, as in NH₄⁺ (from NH₃'s lone pair to H⁺) and H₃O⁺. Once formed, the four N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ are identical.

! Trap: a compound that contains any ionic bond is ionic. NaOH contains an ionic bond and a polar O–H bond; Na₂O₂ contains ionic bonds and a non-polar O–O bond; NH₄Cl contains ionic, polar covalent and coordinate bonds.
## Metallic bonds
- In a metal, positive ions sit in a sea of delocalised electrons that are free to move. This explains conductivity of heat and electricity, malleability, ductility and lustre.
- Metallic bond strength rises with more valence electrons and smaller ions: Na < Mg < Al in melting point; Li > Na > K down group 1.
## Electron-dot (Lewis) structures
- Show outer-shell electrons as dots (or crosses) around each symbol. Most atoms reach 8 outer electrons (2 for H).
- For ions, put the ion in square brackets with its charge: [Na]⁺ and [:Cl:]⁻ with eight electrons around Cl. For MgCl₂ draw one Mg²⁺ between two separate Cl⁻ ions, never Cl⁻ merged together.
- Covalent examples: H₂O has two bond pairs and two lone pairs on O; NH₃ has three bond pairs and one lone pair; CO₂ is O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O; N₂ is N≡N with one lone pair on each N.
> Example: How many lone pairs and bonding pairs are in a CO₂ molecule?
> Each C=O double bond is 2 shared pairs, so 4 bonding pairs in total. Each O keeps 2 lone pairs, so 4 lone pairs in total. Carbon has none.
! Trap: in HClO the atom order is H–O–Cl, not H–Cl–O, because O needs two bonds. In CCl₄ remember the 3 lone pairs on each Cl; dropping them is the most common mistake in dot-structure options.

- Molecules where some atom does not reach 8: BF₃ (B has 6), BeCl₂ (Be has 4); PCl₅ and SF₆ exceed 8. Questions asking "which molecule has every atom with 8 outer electrons" usually reject these. CO₂, PCl₃, CCl₄ and N₂ pass; H₂O fails only because H has 2.
## Molecular shapes (VSEPR basics)
- Electron pairs (bonding and lone) around a central atom repel and spread as far apart as possible. Count pairs: bonding pairs + lone pairs, treating a double or triple bond as one region.
- 2 regions: linear, 180° (CO₂, BeCl₂, C₂H₂).
- 3 regions: trigonal planar, 120° (BF₃, SO₃, C₂H₄ around each carbon). With one lone pair: bent (SO₂).
- 4 regions: tetrahedral, 109°28′ (CH₄, CCl₄, NH₄⁺). One lone pair: trigonal pyramidal, about 107° (NH₃, H₃O⁺). Two lone pairs: bent, about 104.5° (H₂O).
- Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so angles shrink: CH₄ 109.5° > NH₃ 107° > H₂O 104.5°.
- Lone pairs on the central atom = (central atom's outer electrons − electrons used for bonding) / 2, where each bonded H or Cl uses 1 and each O (double bond) uses 2.
> Example: Predict the shape of SO₂.
> S has 6 outer electrons; each O takes 2, so 6 − 4 = 2 electrons remain, one lone pair. Regions: 2 bonds + 1 lone pair = 3, so the shape is bent (V-shaped), less than 120°.
> Example: Predict the shape of NH₃ and of BF₃.
> N: 5 − 3 = 2 electrons, one lone pair; 4 regions, so trigonal pyramidal. B: 3 − 3 = 0, no lone pair; 3 regions, so trigonal planar.
## Polarity of molecules
- A molecule is polar if its bond dipoles do not cancel. Symmetrical molecules with polar bonds can still be non-polar.
- Non-polar: H₂, O₂, N₂, CO₂, CH₄, CCl₄, BF₃, C₂H₄, benzene. Polar: HCl, H₂O, NH₃, SO₂, CH₃Cl, CHCl₃, ethanol.
- Quick rule for ABₙ: if the central atom has no lone pair and all outer atoms are the same, the molecule is non-polar.
- "Like dissolves like": polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents (NH₃ and HCl in water); non-polar in non-polar (I₂ in CCl₄, Br₂ in benzene).
! Trap: CO₂ has polar C=O bonds yet is non-polar; H₂O₂ is polar. Do not decide polarity from bond type alone.
## Intermolecular forces and hydrogen bonding

- Van der Waals forces act between all molecules; they are much weaker than chemical bonds. They grow with molar mass for similar molecules: F₂ < Cl₂ < Br₂ < I₂ in boiling point, and CH₄ < SiH₄ < GeH₄.
- Hydrogen bonds form when H bonded to N, O or F is attracted to a lone pair on another N, O or F. They are stronger than van der Waals forces but weaker than covalent bonds.

- Effects: H₂O, HF and NH₃ boil far higher than expected for their size (H₂O 100 °C vs H₂S −60 °C). Ice is less dense than water because hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open network. Ethanol and NH₃ mix very well with water.
- Melting and boiling of molecular substances break intermolecular forces only; covalent bonds inside the molecules stay intact. Stability (decomposition) depends on covalent bond strength.
> Example: Why does H₂O decompose only above 2000 °C but boil at 100 °C?
> Boiling separates molecules (hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces). Decomposition must break strong O–H covalent bonds.
! Trap: hydrogen bonds do not explain why HF is more stable than HCl; that is bond strength. Hydrogen bonds explain why HF boils higher than HCl.
## Crystal types and their properties
- Ionic crystals (NaCl, CsCl, MgO): ions held by ionic bonds; high melting point, brittle, conduct only when molten or dissolved. In NaCl each ion is surrounded by 6 of the other; in CsCl by 8.
- Molecular crystals (ice, dry ice, I₂, S₈, solid noble gases, most organic solids): molecules held by intermolecular forces; low melting points, soft, non-conducting.

- Covalent network (atomic) crystals (diamond, Si, SiO₂, SiC): a giant 3D network of covalent bonds; very high melting points, very hard, insoluble, usually non-conducting (Si is a semiconductor). In diamond each C bonds to 4 others; in SiO₂ each Si bonds to 4 O and each O to 2 Si, and there are no SiO₂ molecules.
- Metallic crystals: metal ions and delocalised electrons; conduct in both solid and liquid states, melting points vary widely (Hg liquid, W about 3400 °C).

- Graphite is a layered (mixed) crystal: strong covalent bonds within layers, weak forces between layers, delocalised electrons that conduct along layers. It is soft and slippery yet has a melting point higher than diamond's.
- Typical melting order: covalent network > ionic > molecular, with metals spread across the range.
> Example: Rank by melting point: SiO₂, NaCl, CO₂, Na.
> SiO₂ (network) > NaCl (ionic, 801 °C) > Na (metallic, 98 °C) > CO₂ (molecular, sublimes at −78 °C).
! Memory trick: "CO₂ is a gas, SiO₂ is sand." Same group, same formula type, completely different crystal type, which is a favourite comparison.

title: Matter, Chemical Language and Equations
lines: This topic is the vocabulary of the whole chemistry paper. Questions are usually quick: classify a substance, decide whether a change is physical or chemical, write a formula from valencies, or balance an equation. Learn the definitions precisely, because the exam likes options that are almost right.
## Classifying matter

- A pure substance has a fixed composition and fixed properties (sharp melting point, fixed boiling point). A mixture contains two or more substances that keep their own properties and can be present in any proportion.
- Pure substances split into elements (one kind of atom: Fe, O₂, O₃, P₄, C as diamond or graphite) and compounds (two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio: H₂O, NaCl, CO₂).

- Allotropes are different forms of the same element: O₂ and O₃, diamond, graphite and C₆₀, red and white phosphorus. A sample containing O₂ and O₃ together is a mixture even though it holds only one element.
- Isotopes (¹H, ²H) are not allotropes. Heavy water D₂O mixed with H₂O is still treated as one pure substance, water.
- Common mixtures: air, sea water, alloys (steel, brass), hydrochloric acid (HCl dissolved in water), ammonia water, bleach, glass, petroleum, any solution or colloid.
- Common pure substances that sound like mixtures: ice-water mixture (only H₂O), CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue vitriol, a single compound with fixed composition), dry ice (solid CO₂), liquid chlorine (Cl₂).
- Oxides contain exactly two elements, one of which is oxygen. KClO₃ contains oxygen but is not an oxide; it is a salt.

- Acidic oxides react with bases to give salt and water (CO₂, SO₂, SO₃, SiO₂). Basic oxides react with acids to give salt and water (Na₂O, CaO, CuO, Fe₂O₃). Al₂O₃ is amphoteric. CO and NO are neutral (non-salt-forming).

! Trap: a metal oxide is not always basic (Mn₂O₇ is acidic) and a non-metal oxide is not always acidic (CO and NO are neutral). Na₂O₂ is a peroxide, not a basic oxide, because it also releases O₂ with water.
> Example: Which is a pure substance: brass, liquid chlorine, hydrochloric acid, or air?
> Brass is an alloy, hydrochloric acid is HCl in water and air is a gas mixture. Liquid chlorine is just Cl₂, so it is pure (an element).
## Physical and chemical change
- A chemical change forms new substances: old bonds break and new bonds form. Signs include gas, precipitate, colour change, light and heat, but these signs alone do not prove a chemical change.
- A physical change makes no new substance: melting, boiling, dissolving sugar, cutting, distillation, evaporation, fractional distillation of liquid air or petroleum, adsorption by activated carbon.

- Chemical changes include burning, rusting, fermentation, cracking of petroleum, dry distillation (destructive distillation) of coal, the reaction of ozone forming from oxygen (3O₂ → 2O₃), and the colour change of anhydrous CuSO₄ turning blue with water.
- Nuclear changes (¹⁴C decay) are neither physical nor chemical in the exam sense; chemistry keeps the same atoms.
! Memory trick: distillation separates (physical); dry distillation decomposes (chemical). Fractional distillation is physical; cracking is chemical.
! Trap: dissolving NaCl in water breaks ionic bonds but forms no new substance, so it is a physical change. Light given off by a neon lamp is also physical.
## States of matter
- Solid: fixed shape and volume, particles vibrate about fixed positions. Liquid: fixed volume, takes the container's shape. Gas: fills the container, particles far apart, easily compressed.
- Changes of state: melting, freezing, vaporisation (evaporation and boiling), condensation, sublimation (solid to gas, e.g. iodine, dry ice) and deposition (gas to solid).
- Melting, vaporisation and sublimation absorb energy; freezing, condensation and deposition release energy.

- At constant temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules (Avogadro's law); the volume of a gas depends mainly on the number of particles and the spacing between them, not on the size of the particles.
## Formulas and valency

- Valency (combining power) is the number shown by an element when it forms a compound; in ionic compounds it equals the ion charge. Common values: H +1, Na +1, K +1, Ag +1, Mg +2, Ca +2, Ba +2, Zn +2, Al +3, O −2, Cl −1 (in chlorides), S −2 (in sulfides), Fe +2 or +3, Cu +1 or +2.
- Common radicals: OH⁻, NO₃⁻, HCO₃⁻, MnO₄⁻ (−1); CO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻, SO₃²⁻ (−2); PO₄³⁻ (−3); NH₄⁺ (+1).
- Cross-over rule: write the ions, then make the total charge zero. Al³⁺ with SO₄²⁻ needs 2 Al and 3 SO₄, giving Al₂(SO₄)₃.
- In every compound the sum of all oxidation numbers is zero; in an ion it equals the ion's charge.
> Example: What is the oxidation number of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇?
! Trap: always put brackets round a radical used more than once: Ca(OH)₂, not CaOH₂; (NH₄)₂SO₄, not NH₄₂SO₄.
## Naming simple compounds
- Binary compounds: metal first, non-metal with -ide: NaCl sodium chloride, MgO magnesium oxide, CaS calcium sulfide.
- Variable valency metals: FeCl₂ iron(II) chloride (ferrous), FeCl₃ iron(III) chloride (ferric), Cu₂O copper(I) oxide, CuO copper(II) oxide.
- Oxyanions: -ate has more oxygen than -ite: SO₄²⁻ sulfate, SO₃²⁻ sulfite; NO₃⁻ nitrate, NO₂⁻ nitrite. Chlorine series: ClO⁻ hypochlorite, ClO₂⁻ chlorite, ClO₃⁻ chlorate, ClO₄⁻ perchlorate.
- Prefixes for covalent compounds: CO carbon monoxide, CO₂ carbon dioxide, N₂O₄ dinitrogen tetroxide, P₂O₅ diphosphorus pentoxide (often called phosphorus pentoxide).
- Acids: HCl hydrochloric acid, HNO₃ nitric acid, H₂SO₄ sulfuric acid, H₂SO₃ sulfurous acid, H₂CO₃ carbonic acid, H₃PO₄ phosphoric acid, HClO hypochlorous acid.
- Common names worth knowing: NaOH caustic soda, Na₂CO₃ soda ash, NaHCO₃ baking soda, CaO quicklime, Ca(OH)₂ slaked lime, CaCO₃ limestone, CuSO₄·5H₂O blue vitriol.
## Balancing equations
- Mass is conserved: the number of each kind of atom is the same on both sides. Never change a formula to balance; change only the coefficients in front.
- Method: balance the element that appears in the fewest formulas first, leave H and O (or a free element) until last, and use fractions if needed, then multiply through.
> Example: Balance C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O.
> Carbon: 3CO₂. Hydrogen: 8 H gives 4H₂O. Oxygen on the right: 6 + 4 = 10 atoms, so 5O₂.
> C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.
> Example: Balance Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe + CO₂.
> Each CO takes one O atom to become CO₂. Fe₂O₃ has 3 O, so 3CO and 3CO₂, with 2Fe: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (at high temperature).
! Shortcut for hydrocarbons CₓHᵧ burning: O₂ needed = x + y/4 per molecule. For C₃H₈: 3 + 2 = 5.
## Reaction types
- Combination (synthesis): A + B → AB, e.g. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O; CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂.
- Decomposition: AB → A + B, e.g. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (high temperature); 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂ (MnO₂ catalyst, heat); 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂.

- Single displacement: element + compound → new element + new compound, e.g. Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu; Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂↑. A metal displaces a less active metal (activity series K > Ca > Na > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Sn > Pb > (H) > Cu > Hg > Ag > Pt > Au).
- Double displacement (metathesis): two compounds swap partners, e.g. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O; BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄↓ + 2NaCl. It needs a precipitate, gas or water (weak electrolyte) to go.

- A second way to classify: redox reactions (oxidation numbers change) and non-redox reactions. Every single displacement is redox; every double displacement is non-redox; combination and decomposition may be either.

! Trap: 3O₂ → 2O₃ involves no change in oxidation number, so it is not a redox reaction, yet it is a chemical change. CO + CuO → Cu + CO₂ is redox but not single displacement, because CO is a compound.
> Example: Which type is 2Na₂O₂ + 2CO₂ → 2Na₂CO₃ + O₂?
> Two compounds react, so it is none of the four basic types. Oxygen in Na₂O₂ is −1 and changes to −2 and 0, so it is a redox reaction.
## Colloids
- Dispersed systems are classified by particle size: solutions below 1 nm, colloids 1–100 nm, suspensions and emulsions above 100 nm. Particle size is the essential difference.
- The Tyndall effect (a bright path when a light beam passes through) identifies a colloid; a true solution shows no path.
- Colloid particles pass through filter paper but not through a semi-permeable membrane, so dialysis purifies a colloid.

- Other properties: electrophoresis (charged particles move in an electric field), coagulation when an electrolyte is added, heated or a colloid of opposite charge is mixed in. Examples: tofu making, river deltas, alum purifying water.

- Fe(OH)₃ colloid is made by dropping saturated FeCl₃ solution into boiling water and heating until red-brown: FeCl₃ + 3H₂O → Fe(OH)₃ (colloid) + 3HCl. Do not stir hard or boil too long, or a precipitate forms.
- Common colloids: fog, smoke, blood, milk, starch solution, egg-white solution, coloured glass.
! Trap: a colloid as a whole is electrically neutral; only the particles carry charge. Do not write ↓ after the Fe(OH)₃ colloid.

title: Reaction Rates and Equilibrium
lines: This topic has three parts: how fast a reaction goes (rate), how far it goes (equilibrium), and how much energy it releases or absorbs (ΔH). Many questions mix them, for example asking what a catalyst does to the rate, the yield and ΔH all at once. Keep the three ideas separate in your head.
## Reaction rate
- Rate is the change in concentration per unit time: v = Δc / Δt, in mol·L⁻¹·s⁻¹ or mol·L⁻¹·min⁻¹. It is always positive and is an average over the interval.
- For aA + bB → cC + dD, rates of different species are in the ratio of the coefficients: v(A) : v(B) : v(C) : v(D) = a : b : c : d.
> Example: In a 2 L flask, N₂ falls from 4 mol to 3 mol in 5 min in N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Find v(N₂) and v(NH₃).
> Δc(N₂) = 1 mol / 2 L = 0.5 mol/L. v(N₂) = 0.5 / 5 = 0.1 mol·L⁻¹·min⁻¹. v(NH₃) = 2 × 0.1 = 0.2 mol·L⁻¹·min⁻¹.

! Trap: use concentration change, not mole change; always divide by the volume first. To compare rates given for different species, convert all to the same species (divide each by its coefficient) and use the same unit.
## Factors affecting rate
- Nature of the reactants is the main factor (Na reacts with water much faster than Mg).

- Concentration: higher concentration, more collisions per second, faster. Solids and pure liquids have constant concentration, so adding more of them does not change the rate (but grinding a solid into powder increases its surface area and the rate).

- Pressure (gases only): compressing increases concentration and rate. Adding an inert gas at constant volume changes nothing, because concentrations stay the same; adding it at constant pressure expands the volume and slows the reaction.

- Temperature: higher temperature increases the rate of every reaction, exothermic or endothermic, mainly because more molecules have enough energy to react. A common rule of thumb is that the rate roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise.
- Catalysts: change the rate (usually increase it) without being used up.
- Other factors: light (H₂ + Cl₂), forming a galvanic cell (impure Zn reacts faster with acid; adding a little CuSO₄ speeds Zn + H₂SO₄).

> Example: Zn reacts with excess dilute H₂SO₄. Which change speeds the reaction without changing the total H₂: (A) add Na₂SO₄ solution (B) add a few drops of CuSO₄ solution (C) use zinc powder (D) add CH₃COONa?
> A dilutes the acid (slower). B forms a Zn–Cu cell (faster) but uses up some Zn, reducing H₂. D turns H⁺ into weak acetic acid (slower). C increases the surface area only, so C is correct.
## Activation energy and catalysts
- Activation energy Eₐ is the minimum energy colliding particles need to react. Effective collisions need enough energy and the right orientation.
- Raising the temperature increases the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Eₐ. Raising the concentration increases the number of molecules per volume, not the fraction.

- A catalyst provides a different pathway with lower Eₐ. It speeds forward and reverse reactions by the same factor, so it does not change the position of equilibrium, the yield or ΔH. It only makes equilibrium arrive sooner.
- On an energy profile, ΔH = energy of products − energy of reactants. Forward Eₐ − reverse Eₐ = ΔH.
> Example: A reaction has forward Eₐ = 120 kJ/mol and ΔH = −40 kJ/mol. Find the reverse Eₐ.
> Eₐ(reverse) = Eₐ(forward) − ΔH = 120 − (−40) = 160 kJ/mol.
! Trap: a catalyst does not raise the conversion of reactants at equilibrium, and it cannot make an impossible reaction happen. It does take part in the reaction and can be poisoned.
## Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
- A reversible reaction runs in both directions under the same conditions, shown with ⇌. Reactants are never fully converted.
- Equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse rates are equal (not zero). Concentrations then stay constant, but they are not necessarily equal to each other or in the coefficient ratio.

- Signs that a system is at equilibrium: concentration (or colour) of each species stays constant; for each species, the rate of formation equals the rate of consumption; for a gas reaction where the total moles change, total pressure at constant volume stays constant.

- A quantity that is constant anyway cannot prove equilibrium: total mass is always conserved; density at constant volume with all gases never changes; pressure does not change for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI (2 mol gas each side).

> Example: For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ in a rigid container, which shows equilibrium: (A) v(SO₂) used = 2v(O₂) used (B) total pressure stays constant (C) gas density stays constant (D) n(SO₂) : n(O₂) : n(SO₃) = 2 : 1 : 2?

> A compares two forward rates, so it is always true. C is constant because mass and volume are fixed. D can occur by chance. B: gas moles fall in the forward direction, so constant pressure means no net change. B is correct.
## Le Chatelier's principle
- If a condition of an equilibrium system changes, the position shifts in the direction that reduces (but does not cancel) the change.
- Concentration: adding a reactant or removing a product shifts right. Adding more of a solid does not shift the equilibrium.

- Pressure (by changing volume): increasing pressure shifts towards fewer gas moles. If both sides have the same gas moles (H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI), pressure has no effect on position, though concentrations and colour change.
- Temperature: raising the temperature shifts in the endothermic direction; lowering it shifts in the exothermic direction. Temperature is the only factor that changes K.
- Catalysts and inert gas at constant volume: no shift.
> Example: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH < 0, how do you increase the equilibrium yield of NH₃?
> High pressure (4 gas moles → 2), low temperature (forward exothermic), and removing NH₃ as it forms. A catalyst only increases the rate.
> Example: 2NO₂(g, brown) ⇌ N₂O₄(g, colourless), ΔH < 0. A syringe is suddenly compressed to half volume. What does the colour do?
> It first darkens (NO₂ concentration doubles at once), then fades somewhat as equilibrium shifts towards N₂O₄, but stays darker than at the start.
! Trap: "shifts right" does not always mean "higher conversion of every reactant". Adding more N₂ raises the conversion of H₂ but lowers the conversion of N₂ itself.
## Equilibrium constant expressions
- For aA(g) + bB(g) ⇌ cC(g) + dD(g): K = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / ([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ), using equilibrium concentrations.
- Leave out pure solids and pure liquids (and water as solvent): for CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), K = [CO₂]. For C(s) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂(g), steam is included because it is a gas.
- K depends only on temperature. For an exothermic forward reaction K falls as T rises; for an endothermic one K rises.
- Reversing an equation gives 1/K. Multiplying all coefficients by n gives Kⁿ. Adding equations multiplies their K values.
- Reaction quotient Q (same form, any concentrations): Q < K goes forward; Q = K at equilibrium; Q > K goes backward.
- Large K (above about 10⁵) means the reaction is nearly complete.
> Example: For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, 1 mol H₂ and 1 mol I₂ in a 1 L flask reach equilibrium with 0.5 mol H₂ left. Find K and the conversion of H₂.
> Change: H₂ −0.5, I₂ −0.5, HI +1.0. Equilibrium: [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.5, [HI] = 1.0 mol/L.
! Method: use an "initial, change, equilibrium" table in mol/L. The change row is always in the coefficient ratio; the other rows are not.
## Energy changes and ΔH
- Exothermic reactions release heat, ΔH < 0 (products lower in energy): combustion, neutralisation, most combinations, active metals with water or acid, CaO + H₂O.
- Endothermic reactions absorb heat, ΔH > 0: most decompositions (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂), C + CO₂ → 2CO, C + H₂O(g) → CO + H₂, Ba(OH)₂·8H₂O + 2NH₄Cl.
- ΔH from bond energies: ΔH = sum of bond energies broken (reactants) − sum of bond energies formed (products).

- Thermochemical equations show states and ΔH per the coefficients written: H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −286 kJ/mol. Doubling the coefficients doubles ΔH; reversing the equation changes its sign. Liquid water as product releases more heat than steam.
- Hess's law: ΔH depends only on the initial and final states, so equations can be added like algebra.

- The heat of neutralisation for a strong acid and strong base in dilute solution is about −57.3 kJ per mol of water formed. Weak acids or bases give less (ionisation absorbs heat); concentrated H₂SO₄ gives more (dilution releases heat).
> Example: Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 431. Find ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl.
> Broken: 436 + 243 = 679. Formed: 2 × 431 = 862. ΔH = 679 − 862 = −183 kJ/mol (exothermic).

! Trap: needing heat to start does not make a reaction endothermic. Coal must be lit, but burning it is exothermic. Also, the more stable substance has lower energy: graphite → diamond has ΔH > 0, so graphite is more stable.

title: Inorganic Elements and Compounds
lines: This is the largest chemistry topic, and most questions test whether you remember a reaction, a colour or a use. Learn each element as a chain from the element to its oxide, base or acid and salts. Equations below are balanced; write the conditions (heat, catalyst) as words when you revise.
## Sodium and its compounds
- Sodium is soft, silvery, less dense than water and stored under kerosene. It burns with a yellow flame.
- 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O (room temperature, white); 2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂ (heating, pale yellow).
- 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂↑: floats, melts into a ball, moves about, fizzes; the solution turns phenolphthalein red.
- Sodium peroxide: 2Na₂O₂ + 2H₂O → 4NaOH + O₂↑ and 2Na₂O₂ + 2CO₂ → 2Na₂CO₃ + O₂ (used for oxygen in submarines). In each, 2 mol Na₂O₂ transfers 2 mol electrons.
- Na₂CO₃ versus NaHCO₃: both are alkaline; NaHCO₃ decomposes on heating, 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂↑, while Na₂CO₃ does not. NaHCO₃ reacts faster with acid. Na₂CO₃ is more soluble.
- Conversions: Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → 2NaHCO₃; NaHCO₃ + NaOH → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O.
! Trap: sodium added to CuSO₄ solution does not displace copper. It reacts with water first, then NaOH gives blue Cu(OH)₂ precipitate.
> Example: Dropping HCl slowly into Na₂CO₃ solution: when does gas appear?
> First CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ → HCO₃⁻ (no gas). Only after all carbonate becomes hydrogencarbonate does HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂↑ begin. Adding the solution the other way round gives gas immediately.
## Magnesium and aluminium
- Mg burns with a dazzling white light: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO; it even burns in CO₂: 2Mg + CO₂ → 2MgO + C.
- Aluminium is protected by a thin, dense Al₂O₃ layer, so it resists corrosion. It is passivated by cold concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄.
- Al reacts with both acid and strong base: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂↑ and 2Al + 2NaOH + 2H₂O → 2NaAlO₂ + 3H₂↑. Equal masses of Al give equal H₂ with excess of either.
- Thermite reaction: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe (high temperature), used to weld rails.
## Amphoteric behaviour
- Al₂O₃ and Al(OH)₃ react with both acids and strong bases:
- Al(OH)₃ + 3HCl → AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; Al(OH)₃ + NaOH → NaAlO₂ + 2H₂O.
- Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O.
- Lab preparation of Al(OH)₃ uses aluminium salt plus ammonia water, because excess NH₃·H₂O does not dissolve the precipitate: Al³⁺ + 3NH₃·H₂O → Al(OH)₃↓ + 3NH₄⁺.
- Other substances that react with both acid and base: NaHCO₃, (NH₄)₂CO₃, amino acids, and Al itself (but Al is a metal, not an amphoteric compound).
> Example: NaOH solution is added drop by drop to AlCl₃ until in excess. What is seen?
> A white precipitate forms (Al³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Al(OH)₃↓), grows to a maximum, then dissolves as Al(OH)₃ + OH⁻ → AlO₂⁻ + 2H₂O. The mole ratio of NaOH used in the two stages is 3 : 1.
## Iron and its compounds
- Iron reacts with Cl₂ to give FeCl₃ (strong oxidant) but with S or HCl to give Fe(II): 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃; Fe + S → FeS; Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂↑.
- With steam at high temperature: 3Fe + 4H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂.
- Oxides: FeO black, Fe₂O₃ red-brown (rust, red pigment), Fe₃O₄ black and magnetic.
- Hydroxides: Fe(OH)₂ is white, quickly turning grey-green then red-brown in air: 4Fe(OH)₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃. Fe(OH)₃ is a red-brown precipitate.
- Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺: 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃. Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺: 2FeCl₃ + Fe → 3FeCl₂ (iron powder keeps Fe²⁺ solutions from oxidising); 2FeCl₃ + Cu → 2FeCl₂ + CuCl₂ (etching circuit boards).
- Fe²⁺ solutions are pale green; Fe³⁺ solutions are yellow to brown. KSCN turns Fe³⁺ blood-red.
! Trap: the reaction of FeCl₃ with Cu does not mean iron is less active than copper. It is Fe³⁺, a strong oxidant, that attacks Cu; the product is Fe²⁺, not Fe.
## Copper and its compounds
- Copper does not react with dilute HCl or dilute H₂SO₄. It reacts with oxidising acids:
- Cu + 2H₂SO₄(conc.) → CuSO₄ + SO₂↑ + 2H₂O (heat).
- Cu + 4HNO₃(conc.) → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂↑ + 2H₂O; 3Cu + 8HNO₃(dilute) → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO↑ + 4H₂O.
- Green patina: Cu₂(OH)₂CO₃ (basic copper carbonate). CuO black, Cu₂O red, Cu(OH)₂ blue precipitate, CuSO₄ white (anhydrous), CuSO₄·5H₂O blue.
> Example: In 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O, what fraction of HNO₃ acts as oxidising agent?
> Only the 2 N atoms that become NO are reduced, so 2 of 8, i.e. 1/4. The other 6 act as an acid (they stay as nitrate).
## Chlorine
- Cl₂ is a yellow-green, toxic, dense gas. It is a strong oxidising agent.
- 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl (white smoke); Cu + Cl₂ → CuCl₂ (brown-yellow smoke); H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl (pale flame, or explosion in light).

- With water: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. HClO is a weak acid, a strong oxidant and bleach, and decomposes in light: 2HClO → 2HCl + O₂↑. So fresh chlorine water bleaches; old chlorine water is just dilute HCl.
- With bases: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O (bleach); 2Cl₂ + 2Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + Ca(ClO)₂ + 2H₂O (bleaching powder, active part Ca(ClO)₂).
- Halogen displacement: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂ (I₂ turns starch blue); oxidising power Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.
! Trap: dry chlorine does not bleach dry coloured cloth; the bleaching agent is HClO, which needs water.
## Sulfur
- S + O₂ → SO₂ (blue-violet flame in O₂). SO₂ is a colourless, choking gas, an acidic oxide: SO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂SO₃.

- SO₂ bleaches by combining with coloured substances (reversible: heating restores the colour of decolourised magenta). It also acts as a reducing agent: SO₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O → H₂SO₄ + 2HCl, so mixing SO₂ and Cl₂ in equal moles removes bleaching power. SO₂ decolourises acidified KMnO₄ by reduction, not bleaching.
- 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (catalyst, heat). SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.

- Concentrated H₂SO₄: dehydrating (chars sugar), hygroscopic (drying agent for acidic and neutral gases), strong oxidant (reacts with Cu and C when hot: C + 2H₂SO₄ → CO₂↑ + 2SO₂↑ + 2H₂O). It passivates Fe and Al in the cold.
! Trap: concentrated H₂SO₄ cannot dry NH₃ (basic) or H₂S and HI (reducing). Dilution: always pour acid slowly into water while stirring.
## Nitrogen
- N₂ is very unreactive because of its N≡N triple bond. N₂ + O₂ → 2NO (lightning). 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ (red-brown). 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO.
- Ammonia: very soluble (fountain experiment), solution is weakly alkaline: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃·H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl (white smoke).
- Catalytic oxidation: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O (Pt catalyst, heat), the first step in making nitric acid.
- Ammonium salts decompose on heating (NH₄Cl → NH₃ + HCl, recombining when cool) and release NH₃ with bases.
- Nitric acid is a strong oxidant at any concentration; it does not release H₂ with metals. Concentrated HNO₃ decomposes in light (stored in brown bottles): 4HNO₃ → 4NO₂↑ + O₂↑ + 2H₂O.
## Carbon and silicon
- C: CO₂ is an acidic oxide; CO is toxic (binds haemoglobin) and a reducing agent. CO₂ + C → 2CO (high temperature).
- CO₂ into limewater: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O (cloudy); excess CO₂ clears it: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂.
- Silicon is a semiconductor (chips, solar cells). SiO₂ forms optical fibres, quartz and sand.
- SiO₂ is acidic but does not react with water. SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O (so NaOH bottles use rubber stoppers, not glass). SiO₂ + 4HF → SiF₄↑ + 2H₂O (HF etches glass).
- Silicic acid is weaker than carbonic acid: Na₂SiO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → H₂SiO₃↓ + Na₂CO₃.
- Silicate materials: glass, cement, ceramics.
## Acids, bases and salts in general
- Acid + metal (more active than H) → salt + H₂. Acid + basic oxide or base → salt + water. Acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂.
- A stronger acid makes a weaker acid from its salt: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑.
- Insoluble in water: most carbonates (except Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺), BaSO₄, AgCl, Mg(OH)₂, Al(OH)₃, Fe(OH)₃, Cu(OH)₂, CaCO₃. All nitrates and all Na⁺, K⁺ and NH₄⁺ salts are soluble.
## Everyday and environmental chemistry
- Acid rain (pH < 5.6) comes from SO₂ (coal burning) and NOₓ (car exhausts). Desulfurisation: add CaO to coal so 2CaO + 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2CaSO₄.
- Photochemical smog: NOₓ and hydrocarbons in sunlight. Ozone layer damage: CFCs (freons). Greenhouse effect: CO₂ and CH₄. Eutrophication: phosphates and nitrates in water. White pollution: plastics.

- Uses: NaHCO₃ in baking and antacids; Al(OH)₃ antacid; Fe₂O₃ red paint; NaClO and ClO₂ disinfectants; alum KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O purifies water (Al(OH)₃ colloid adsorbs dirt) but does not disinfect; N₂ as a protective gas; liquid NH₃ as a refrigerant.

title: Ionic Reactions and Tests for Ions
lines: Reactions in water are really reactions between ions. This topic asks you to write correct ionic equations, judge whether a group of ions can stay together in one solution, and pick the right test for an ion. Each skill rests on knowing which substances are strong electrolytes and which compounds are insoluble.
## Electrolytes and non-electrolytes
- An electrolyte is a compound that conducts electricity when molten or dissolved in water, because it forms mobile ions. Acids, bases, salts and metal oxides (when molten) are electrolytes.
- Non-electrolytes do not conduct in either state: sucrose, ethanol, most organic compounds, and non-metal oxides such as CO₂, SO₂ and NH₃.

- Strong electrolytes ionise completely in water: strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, H₂SO₄, HNO₃, HClO₄), strong bases (NaOH, KOH, Ba(OH)₂, Ca(OH)₂) and almost all salts, including insoluble ones like BaSO₄.
- Weak electrolytes ionise only partly: weak acids (CH₃COOH, H₂CO₃, H₂SO₃, H₂S, HClO, HF, H₃PO₄), weak bases (NH₃·H₂O, insoluble hydroxides) and water.
- Ionisation equations: NaHSO₄ → Na⁺ + H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ (in water); NaHCO₃ → Na⁺ + HCO₃⁻; CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺.

! Trap: CO₂ dissolved in water conducts, but the conducting species come from H₂CO₃; CO₂ itself is a non-electrolyte. Copper and salt water conduct but are not electrolytes, because electrolytes must be compounds, and salt water is a mixture.
! Trap: conductivity depends on ion concentration and charge, not on whether the electrolyte is strong. A very dilute HCl solution can conduct worse than a concentrated acetic acid solution.
> Example: Ba(OH)₂ solution is titrated with dilute H₂SO₄. How does the conductivity change?
> Ba²⁺ + 2OH⁻ + 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄↓ + 2H₂O removes almost all ions, so the bulb dims to nearly zero at the equivalence point, then brightens again as excess H₂SO₄ adds ions.
## Writing ionic equations
- Write: the balanced full equation. Split: only soluble strong electrolytes into ions. Cancel: spectator ions that appear unchanged on both sides. Check: atoms and charge both balance.
- Keep as formulas: precipitates, gases, water and other weak electrolytes, oxides, elements, and organic molecules.
- Ca(OH)₂: as clear limewater write Ca²⁺ + 2OH⁻; as lime milk (suspension) write Ca(OH)₂.
- Concentrated H₂SO₄ is written as a formula; concentrated HCl and HNO₃ are written as ions.
> Example: Write the ionic equation for marble dissolving in hydrochloric acid.
> CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑. CaCO₃ is insoluble and stays as a formula; Cl⁻ cancels.
> CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + H₂O + CO₂↑.
> Example: Ionic equation for acetic acid neutralising sodium hydroxide.
> CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O. Acetic acid is weak, so it is not written as H⁺.
## Common errors in ionic equations
- Breaking a weak electrolyte or a precipitate: writing H⁺ for CH₃COOH, or Ca²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ for CaCO₃.
- Unbalanced charge: Fe³⁺ + Cu → Fe²⁺ + Cu²⁺ looks balanced in atoms but has charge +3 on the left and +4 on the right. Correct: 2Fe³⁺ + Cu → 2Fe²⁺ + Cu²⁺.
- Wrong ratio: Ba²⁺ + OH⁻ + H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄↓ + H₂O is wrong; the formulas demand 2OH⁻ and 2H⁺ for each Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻.
- Impossible product: Fe + 2H⁺ → Fe²⁺ + H₂↑ is right; writing Fe³⁺ is wrong for non-oxidising acids. Cu + 2H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + H₂↑ does not happen at all.
- Ignoring amounts: with a small amount of CO₂, 2OH⁻ + CO₂ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O; with excess CO₂, OH⁻ + CO₂ → HCO₃⁻.

- With amount-dependent reactions, let the limiting reagent have coefficient 1. NaHCO₃ with a little Ca(OH)₂: Ca²⁺ + 2OH⁻ + 2HCO₃⁻ → CaCO₃↓ + CO₃²⁻ + 2H₂O. NaHCO₃ with excess Ca(OH)₂: HCO₃⁻ + Ca²⁺ + OH⁻ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O.
! Trap: ClO⁻ is strongly oxidising. SO₂ passed into Ca(ClO)₂ solution does not give CaSO₃; it is oxidised to sulfate (CaSO₄).
## Conditions for ionic reactions
- Double-displacement ionic reactions go when they form a precipitate, a gas or a weak electrolyte (including water), because these remove ions from solution.
- Redox reactions between ions also go: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂.
- Complex formation also removes ions: Fe³⁺ + 3SCN⁻ → Fe(SCN)₃ (blood-red).
- Two hydrolysing ions can drive each other to completion: Al³⁺ + 3HCO₃⁻ → Al(OH)₃↓ + 3CO₂↑ (foam fire extinguisher).
## Ion coexistence in solution
- Ions cannot coexist if they form a precipitate (Ba²⁺ with SO₄²⁻ or CO₃²⁻; Ag⁺ with Cl⁻; Ca²⁺ with CO₃²⁻; OH⁻ with Mg²⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe³⁺, Al³⁺).
- If they form a gas or weak electrolyte (H⁺ with CO₃²⁻, HCO₃⁻, SO₃²⁻, S²⁻, CH₃COO⁻, ClO⁻; OH⁻ with NH₄⁺; H⁺ with OH⁻).
- HCO₃⁻ and HSO₃⁻ cannot exist in either strongly acidic or strongly basic solution: HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O.
- If they react by redox: in acid, NO₃⁻ oxidises Fe²⁺, I⁻, SO₃²⁻ and S²⁻; MnO₄⁻ oxidises Fe²⁺, I⁻ and Cl⁻; Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻ and S²⁻; ClO⁻ oxidises Fe²⁺ and I⁻.
- If they form a complex: Fe³⁺ with SCN⁻.

- Hidden conditions: "colourless" rules out Cu²⁺ (blue), Fe³⁺ (yellow-brown), Fe²⁺ (pale green) and MnO₄⁻ (purple). "pH = 1" or "turns litmus red" means extra H⁺. "pH = 13" or "turns phenolphthalein red" means extra OH⁻. "Reacts with Al to give H₂" means acid or base (and in acid, no NO₃⁻, since HNO₃ gives no H₂).
> Example: Which group can coexist in a colourless solution at pH = 1: (A) Na⁺, K⁺, MnO₄⁻, SO₄²⁻ (B) NH₄⁺, Mg²⁺, NO₃⁻, Cl⁻ (C) Fe²⁺, H⁺, NO₃⁻, Cl⁻ (D) K⁺, Na⁺, CO₃²⁻, Cl⁻?
> A has purple MnO₄⁻, so it is not colourless. C: NO₃⁻ with H⁺ oxidises Fe²⁺ (and Fe²⁺ is coloured). D: CO₃²⁻ reacts with H⁺. B has no reacting pair, so B is correct.
! Trap: NO₃⁻ is harmless in neutral solution; it only becomes a strong oxidant together with H⁺. Watch for this pair in every coexistence question.
## Tests for anions
- Cl⁻: add dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃ solution; a white precipitate of AgCl that does not dissolve. HNO₃ removes CO₃²⁻ that would otherwise also give a white precipitate.
- SO₄²⁻: first add dilute HCl (no precipitate, no gas, which rules out Ag⁺, CO₃²⁻ and SO₃²⁻), then BaCl₂ solution; white BaSO₄ forms.
- CO₃²⁻: add dilute HCl; a colourless, odourless gas turns limewater cloudy. To tell CO₃²⁻ from HCO₃⁻, add CaCl₂ or BaCl₂ solution: only CO₃²⁻ gives a precipitate.
- SO₃²⁻ with acid gives SO₂, which also clouds limewater but has a choking smell and decolourises magenta (fuchsine) solution.
- Br⁻ and I⁻: AgNO₃ gives pale yellow AgBr and yellow AgI. Or add chlorine water, then CCl₄: the lower layer turns orange-red for Br₂ and purple for I₂.

! Trap: adding acidified Ba(NO₃)₂ to test for SO₄²⁻ is wrong, because HNO₃ oxidises SO₃²⁻ to SO₄²⁻ and gives a false positive. Adding BaCl₂ first and acid after is also wrong, because AgCl would look the same as BaSO₄.
## Tests for cations
- NH₄⁺: add NaOH solution and warm; a gas with a pungent smell turns moist red litmus blue (NH₃). Without warming, little NH₃ escapes from dilute solutions.
- Fe³⁺: KSCN solution turns blood-red. Or NaOH gives a red-brown Fe(OH)₃ precipitate.

- Fe²⁺: KSCN shows no colour; then add chlorine water (or H₂O₂) and the solution turns red (2Fe²⁺ + Cl₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻). Or NaOH gives a white precipitate that turns grey-green and finally red-brown. Fe²⁺ also decolourises acidified KMnO₄, which is the test when Fe³⁺ is also present. Another specific test is K₃[Fe(CN)₆], which gives a blue precipitate with Fe²⁺.
- Cu²⁺: blue solution; NaOH gives a blue Cu(OH)₂ precipitate.
- Al³⁺: NaOH gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess. Mg²⁺: white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess.
- Flame tests (clean Pt or iron wire, dipped in HCl and burnt until colourless first): Na⁺ yellow; K⁺ lilac, seen through blue cobalt glass to filter out sodium's yellow.
> Example: A solution may contain Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺ or both. Describe a two-step test.
> Take one portion and add KSCN: red means Fe³⁺ present. Take a second portion and add a few drops of acidified KMnO₄: if the purple colour fades, Fe²⁺ is present.
! Trap: for Fe²⁺, the order matters. Add KSCN first, then the oxidant. Adding chlorine water first cannot tell you whether the Fe³⁺ was there from the start.

title: Laboratory Work and Industrial Chemistry
lines: Practical questions test judgement: is this operation safe, is this apparatus right, does this method really separate or identify the substance? Industrial questions apply equilibrium and rate ideas to real plants. Read every option slowly, because one wrong word ("dilute" for "concentrated") makes it false.
## Lab safety
- Dilute concentrated H₂SO₄ by pouring the acid slowly into water while stirring, never water into acid (the heat makes water boil and spit).

- Acid on skin: rinse with plenty of water, then apply dilute NaHCO₃ solution. Alkali on skin: rinse with water, then dilute boric acid. Acid in eyes: rinse with water while blinking, never rub, see a doctor.
- Spilled burning alcohol or small fires on the bench: cover with a damp cloth or sand. Burning sodium or magnesium: sand only, never water or CO₂ extinguishers.

- Never light a flammable gas (H₂, CH₄, CO) before testing its purity, or it may explode. Heat a test tube evenly first, point its mouth away from people, and keep the solid-heating tube's mouth slightly lower so condensed water does not crack it.
- Toxic gases (Cl₂, SO₂, NO₂, H₂S) are made in a fume cupboard and their tail gas absorbed (NaOH solution for Cl₂, SO₂, NO₂). CO is burned or collected in a balloon.
- Sodium and potassium are stored under kerosene; white phosphorus under water; concentrated HNO₃ and AgNO₃ in brown bottles; NaOH solution in bottles with rubber stoppers.
- Safety symbols: corrosive (H₂SO₄, NaOH), flammable (ethanol), toxic (CO), explosive.
! Trap: when stopping a heated reaction that collects gas over water, take the delivery tube out of the water first, then remove the flame; otherwise water sucks back into the hot tube.
## Common apparatus
- Heated directly: test tube, evaporating dish, crucible. Heated on gauze: beaker, flask, conical flask. Never heated: measuring cylinder, volumetric flask, reagent bottle.

- Measuring: measuring cylinder (to 0.1 mL), burette and pipette (to 0.01 mL), balance (to 0.1 g on a school top-pan balance). A volumetric flask makes a solution of exact concentration at one volume only.

- Separation: funnel (filtration), separating funnel (extraction, separating immiscible liquids), distillation flask with thermometer bulb at the side-arm, Liebig condenser with cooling water entering at the bottom and leaving at the top.

- Making a solution of known concentration: calculate, weigh, dissolve in a beaker, cool, transfer with rinsing (two or three times) into the volumetric flask, add water until 1–2 cm below the mark, then use a dropper to the mark, invert to mix.
> Example: When making 250 mL of 0.1 mol/L NaCl, a student looks up at the mark while topping up. Is the concentration high or low?
> Looking up makes the liquid seem lower, so the student adds too much water. The volume is too large, so the concentration is low.
- Other errors: not rinsing the beaker loses solute (low); transferring a hot solution, then cooling, leaves a smaller volume (high); water already in the flask has no effect.
## Preparing and collecting gases

- Choose the generator from the reactant states: solid + solid with heat (test tube, mouth slightly down); solid + liquid without heat (flask or test tube with a funnel); solid or liquid + liquid with heat (round-bottom flask on gauze).

- Choose collection by solubility and density (compare M with 29 for air): over water for gases insoluble in water; upward air displacement (open end up, gas in at the bottom) for gases denser than air; downward air displacement for gases lighter than air.
- O₂: 2KMnO₄ → K₂MnO₄ + MnO₂ + O₂↑ (heat); 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂↑ (MnO₂, heat); 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂↑ (MnO₂, no heat). Collect over water or upward air displacement. Test: relights a glowing splint.
- H₂: Zn + H₂SO₄(dilute) → ZnSO₄ + H₂↑. Collect over water or downward air displacement. Test: burns with a squeaky pop.

- CO₂: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑. Collect by upward air displacement (it dissolves somewhat in water). Test: limewater turns cloudy. Do not use H₂SO₄ (CaSO₄ coats the marble and stops the reaction).

- NH₃: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2NH₃↑ + 2H₂O (heat, solid + solid). Dry with soda lime or CaO, never with concentrated H₂SO₄ or CaCl₂. Collect by downward air displacement; test with moist red litmus (turns blue) or a glass rod dipped in concentrated HCl (white smoke).

- Cl₂: MnO₂ + 4HCl(conc.) → MnCl₂ + Cl₂↑ + 2H₂O (heat). Pass through saturated NaCl solution (removes HCl), then concentrated H₂SO₄ (removes water). Collect by upward air displacement or over saturated NaCl solution; absorb excess with NaOH. Test: moist starch-KI paper turns blue.
> Example: Which pair of gases can both be dried with concentrated H₂SO₄ and collected by upward air displacement: (A) NH₃, O₂ (B) Cl₂, CO₂ (C) H₂, SO₂ (D) HCl, H₂S?
> NH₃ reacts with H₂SO₄; H₂ is lighter than air; H₂S is oxidised by concentrated H₂SO₄. Cl₂ (M = 71) and CO₂ (M = 44) are acidic or neutral, not reducing, and denser than air. B is correct.
! Order rule: wash gases through solutions first and dry last, otherwise the gas picks up water again.
## Separation and purification

- Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. "One sticks, two lower, three touches": paper sticks to the funnel, paper below the funnel rim, liquid below the paper rim, and the glass rod, beaker spout and funnel tip touch where they should.

- Evaporation and crystallisation: evaporate to obtain a solute whose solubility changes little with temperature (NaCl), stopping heating when most crystals have formed. Cooling crystallisation suits solutes whose solubility rises sharply with temperature (KNO₃); it also removes a little NaCl from KNO₃. Hydrated salts (CuSO₄·5H₂O) are obtained by evaporating, cooling and crystallising, not by evaporating to dryness.
- Distillation separates miscible liquids with different boiling points (ethanol from water, fresh water from sea water). Add boiling chips; thermometer bulb at the side-arm level.

- Extraction and separation: a solute moves from water into an immiscible solvent in which it dissolves better (I₂ from water into CCl₄ or benzene). CCl₄ is denser than water (lower layer); benzene is less dense (upper layer). Drain the lower layer through the tap and pour the upper layer from the top.

- Chemical purification: add a reagent that removes the impurity without adding a new one. CO₂ containing HCl: saturated NaHCO₃ solution. Cl₂ containing HCl: saturated NaCl solution. FeCl₂ containing FeCl₃: add iron powder and filter. FeCl₃ containing FeCl₂: pass Cl₂. Na₂CO₃ solid containing NaHCO₃: heat. CH₄ containing C₂H₄: bromine water.
> Example: Crude salt contains Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻. In what order do you add BaCl₂, NaOH, Na₂CO₃ and HCl?
> Na₂CO₃ must come after BaCl₂ so that it also removes the excess Ba²⁺. Then filter, and add HCl last to remove excess OH⁻ and CO₃²⁻. A valid order is BaCl₂, NaOH, Na₂CO₃, filter, HCl.
! Trap: ethanol cannot extract iodine from water because ethanol mixes with water.
## Identifying substances

- Use a reagent that gives a different observation for every substance. One reagent can tell apart many solutions if it gives distinct results: Ba(OH)₂ solution with warming distinguishes NH₄Cl (gas), Na₂SO₄ (white precipitate), (NH₄)₂SO₄ (gas and precipitate) and NaCl (no change).
- Gas tests: O₂ glowing splint; H₂ pop; CO₂ limewater; NH₃ red litmus; Cl₂ starch-KI paper; SO₂ decolourises magenta and the colour returns on heating.
- Water: anhydrous CuSO₄ turns from white to blue.
## Industrial processes

- Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH < 0. Conditions: about 400–500 °C (a compromise: lower temperature gives more NH₃ but too slowly, and suits the iron catalyst's activity), 10–30 MPa (high pressure raises yield and rate), iron catalyst, NH₃ liquefied and removed, unreacted gases recycled.

- Contact process for sulfuric acid: S or FeS₂ burnt to SO₂ (4FeS₂ + 11O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ + 8SO₂); 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, ΔH < 0, with V₂O₅ catalyst at about 400–500 °C and normal pressure (conversion is already high, so expensive high pressure is not worth it); SO₃ absorbed in 98 % concentrated H₂SO₄, not water, to avoid an acid mist.
- Nitric acid: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O (Pt); 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂; 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO.
- Chlor-alkali: electrolysis of brine with a cation-exchange membrane gives NaOH, Cl₂ and H₂.

- Metal extraction depends on activity: very active metals (K, Na, Mg, Al) by electrolysis of molten compounds; middle metals (Zn, Fe, Cu) by reduction with C, CO, H₂ or Al (blast furnace: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂; limestone removes SiO₂ as slag CaSiO₃); inactive metals (Hg, Ag) by heating their oxides: 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂.
> Example: Why is the Haber process run at about 450 °C even though a lower temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield?
> At low temperature the rate is too slow and the catalyst is not active enough. About 450 °C balances an acceptable yield with a fast enough rate.
! Memory trick: "Exothermic equilibrium in industry is always a compromise temperature; pressure goes high only when it pays." Haber uses high pressure; the contact process does not.

title: The Mole and Calculations
lines: This is the most calculation-heavy chemistry topic. The exam numbers are chosen to divide cleanly, so if your working gives an ugly decimal, check the molar mass or the ratio first. Every problem goes through one central quantity: the amount of substance n, in moles.
## Relative atomic and molecular mass
- Relative atomic mass Ar compares the mass of an atom with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. It has no unit. The listed value is a weighted average of the element's isotopes.
- Relative molecular (formula) mass Mr is the sum of the Ar values in the formula: Mr(H₂SO₄) = 2 + 32 + 64 = 98; Mr(CaCO₃) = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100; Mr(CuSO₄·5H₂O) = 160 + 90 = 250.
- Average Ar from isotopes: Ar = sum of (isotope mass × abundance).
> Example: Chlorine is 75 % ³⁵Cl and 25 % ³⁷Cl. Find Ar(Cl).
! Values to memorise: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Mg 24, Al 27, S 32, Cl 35.5, K 39, Ca 40, Fe 56, Cu 64, Zn 65, Ag 108, Ba 137.
## The mole and the Avogadro constant
- One mole is the amount of substance containing N_A particles, where N_A ≈ 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ (the Avogadro constant).
- n = N / N_A, where N is the number of particles. Always say which particle: 1 mol of O₂ contains 2 mol of O atoms and 16 mol of electrons.
- Molar mass M (g/mol) has the same number as Mr: M(H₂O) = 18 g/mol. Then n = m / M.
> Example: How many hydrogen atoms are in 9 g of water?
> n(H₂O) = 9 / 18 = 0.5 mol. Each molecule has 2 H, so n(H) = 1 mol, i.e. N_A ≈ 6.02 × 10²³ atoms.

! Trap: questions on N_A love hidden details: electrons in an ion (1 mol NH₄⁺ has 10 mol electrons), bonds in a structure (1 mol SiO₂ has 4 mol Si–O bonds; 1 mol diamond has 2 mol C–C bonds), and electrons transferred (1 mol Cl₂ with NaOH transfers only 1 mol electrons).
## Molar volume of gases
- At standard temperature and pressure (STP, 0 °C and 101 kPa), 1 mol of any gas occupies about 22.4 L. So n = V / 22.4 for a gas at STP.
- The 22.4 L/mol value applies only to gases, and only at STP. Water, SO₃, CCl₄, ethanol and HF are not gases at STP, so 22.4 L of them is not 1 mol.
- Density of a gas at STP: ρ = M / 22.4 g/L. Relative density of gas A to gas B = M_A / M_B.
> Example: 4.48 L of a gas at STP has a mass of 8.8 g. What is its molar mass?
> n = 4.48 / 22.4 = 0.2 mol. M = 8.8 / 0.2 = 44 g/mol (it could be CO₂ or N₂O or C₃H₈).
> Example: A gas has density 1.25 g/L at STP. Find M.
> M = 1.25 × 22.4 = 28 g/mol (N₂, CO or C₂H₄).
! Trap: "at room temperature and pressure" or "under normal conditions" (25 °C) means you cannot use 22.4 L/mol. A mass or particle number, however, does not depend on conditions.
## The ideal gas equation
- pV = nRT, with p in Pa, V in m³, T in K (T = t + 273) and R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹.
- Useful ratios: at the same T and p, V₁ / V₂ = n₁ / n₂ (Avogadro's law). At the same T and V, p₁ / p₂ = n₁ / n₂. At the same T and p, ρ₁ / ρ₂ = M₁ / M₂.
> Example: In a closed rigid container at constant temperature, 2 mol of gas has a pressure of 300 kPa. What is the pressure after 1 mol more gas is added?
> p is proportional to n: 300 × 3/2 = 450 kPa.
## Concentration of solutions
- Molar concentration c = n / V, with V in litres: c in mol/L. Also n = cV.
- Mass fraction w = mass of solute / mass of solution × 100 %.
- Conversion: c = 1000ρw / M, where ρ is the solution density in g/mL.
- The concentration of an ion = c(salt) × number of that ion in the formula: 0.1 mol/L Al₂(SO₄)₃ has c(SO₄²⁻) = 0.3 mol/L, whatever the volume.
> Example: Concentrated sulfuric acid has ρ = 1.84 g/mL and w = 98 %. Find c.
> Example: What mass of NaOH is needed for 250 mL of 0.4 mol/L solution?
! Trap: volume of solution, not volume of water. Dissolving 1 mol NaCl in 1 L of water does not give 1 mol/L, because the solution volume is not 1 L.
## Dilution and mixing
- Dilution keeps the amount of solute constant: c₁V₁ = c₂V₂.
- Mixing two solutions of the same solute: total n = c₁V₁ + c₂V₂; divide by the total volume (assume volumes add only if the question says so).
> Example: What volume of 5 mol/L HCl is needed to make 500 mL of 0.2 mol/L HCl?
> Example: 100 mL of 0.1 mol/L NaCl is mixed with 100 mL of 0.1 mol/L CaCl₂. Find c(Cl⁻), assuming volumes add.
## Stoichiometry
- The coefficients in a balanced equation give the mole ratio (and, for gases at the same T and p, the volume ratio). Mass ratios come from moles × M, never directly from coefficients.
- Method: convert what you know to moles, use the ratio, convert back to what you want.
> Example: What mass of CaCO₃ must be decomposed to give 5.6 L of CO₂ at STP?
> CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. n(CO₂) = 5.6 / 22.4 = 0.25 mol, so n(CaCO₃) = 0.25 mol and m = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g.
> Example: 2.7 g of Al reacts with excess HCl. What volume of H₂ forms at STP?
> 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂. n(Al) = 0.1 mol, so n(H₂) = 0.15 mol and V = 0.15 × 22.4 = 3.36 L.
! Shortcut: electrons lost by a metal equal 2 × n(H₂). 0.1 mol Al loses 0.3 mol electrons, so 0.15 mol H₂. This also works for metal mixtures.
## Limiting reagent
- When amounts of two reactants are given, find which runs out first. Divide each n by its coefficient; the smaller value belongs to the limiting reagent, and all products are calculated from it.
> Example: 4 g of H₂ and 16 g of O₂ react. What mass of water forms?
> 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. n(H₂) = 2 mol (2/2 = 1); n(O₂) = 0.5 mol (0.5/1 = 0.5). O₂ is limiting.
> n(H₂O) = 2 × 0.5 = 1 mol = 18 g. 1 mol H₂ (2 g) is left over.
! Trap: adding the masses (4 + 16 = 20 g) only works when nothing is in excess. Check the limiting reagent first.
## Yield and purity
- Percentage yield = actual mass of product / theoretical mass × 100 %.
- Purity = mass of pure substance / mass of impure sample × 100 %. Use only the pure mass in the equation.
- For a multi-step process, multiply the yields or use the conservation of a key element: e.g. FeS₂ → 2SO₂ → 2SO₃ → 2H₂SO₄, so 1 mol FeS₂ gives at most 2 mol H₂SO₄.
> Example: 20 g of limestone, 80 % CaCO₃, is heated completely. Find the mass of CO₂.
> Pure CaCO₃ = 16 g = 0.16 mol, so CO₂ = 0.16 × 44 = 7.04 g.
> Example: 0.5 mol of N₂ reacts with excess H₂ and 6.8 g of NH₃ forms. Find the yield.
> Theoretical n(NH₃) = 1 mol = 17 g. Yield = 6.8 / 17 × 100 % = 40 %.
## Quick no-calculator habits
- Look for numbers that are simple fractions of molar masses: 5.6 L is 1/4 mol, 11.2 L is 1/2 mol, 2.24 L is 1/10 mol at STP.
- Use conservation of atoms (e.g. all Na ends up in NaCl) to skip writing every equation.
- Use conservation of charge in solutions: total positive charge = total negative charge. For a solution of Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻: c(Na⁺) + 2c(Mg²⁺) = c(Cl⁻).
- Check units at the end: mL must become L before using c = n / V.

title: Organic Chemistry
lines: Organic questions reward pattern recognition: spot the functional group, and you know the reactions. Carbon forms four bonds, hydrogen one, oxygen two. Keep that count in mind when checking any formula.
## Alkanes
- General formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; saturated, single C–C bonds only. Methane CH₄ is tetrahedral (bond angle 109°28′).
- Stable: no reaction with acidified KMnO₄, bromine water, strong acids or bases.
- Combustion: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
- Substitution with Cl₂ in light: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, continuing to CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄. Each step replaces one H and gives one HCl. The products form a mixture.
- Boiling points rise with chain length; for the same formula, more branching means a lower boiling point. C1–C4 alkanes are gases at room temperature.
> Example: How many moles of Cl₂ are needed to convert 1 mol CH₄ completely into CCl₄?
> Each Cl atom that enters replaces one H, and each Cl₂ supplies one Cl to the product (the other forms HCl). Four H replaced, so 4 mol Cl₂.
## Alkenes and alkynes
- Alkenes CₙH₂ₙ contain C=C. Ethene C₂H₄ is planar (bond angles about 120°). Alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ contain C≡C; ethyne C₂H₂ is linear.
- Addition across the multiple bond: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br (bromine water or Br₂ in CCl₄ is decolourised).
- CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH (catalyst, heat, pressure); CH₂=CH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂Cl; CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃ (Ni catalyst).

- Alkenes and alkynes are oxidised by acidified KMnO₄ (purple colour fades); ethene is oxidised to CO₂, so KMnO₄ cannot be used to remove ethene from methane (it adds CO₂ impurity). Use bromine water instead.
- Ethene ripens fruit and is the measure of a country's petrochemical industry.
- Ethyne: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂↑. HC≡CH + 2Br₂ → CHBr₂CHBr₂.
! Trap: bromine water decolourised by benzene is extraction (physical), not addition. Only true addition counts as a reaction.
## Benzene
- C₆H₆: planar regular hexagon, all six C–C bonds identical, in between single and double. No ordinary C=C, so it does not decolourise bromine water by reaction or acidified KMnO₄.
- Substitution is easier than addition: C₆H₆ + Br₂ → C₆H₅Br + HBr (FeBr₃ catalyst, liquid bromine); nitration C₆H₆ + HNO₃ → C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O (concentrated H₂SO₄, 50–60 °C).
- Addition only under strong conditions: C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂ (cyclohexane, Ni, heat).
- Methylbenzene (toluene) is oxidised by KMnO₄ (the side chain), unlike benzene.
## Functional groups

- Alcohols –OH: ethanol C₂H₅OH. 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂↑ (gentler than water). Catalytic oxidation: 2CH₃CH₂OH + O₂ → 2CH₃CHO + 2H₂O (Cu or Ag catalyst, heat). Strong oxidants (acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, orange to green) take it to acetic acid.
- Aldehydes –CHO: ethanal CH₃CHO. Oxidised to acids; give a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent and a brick-red Cu₂O precipitate with fresh Cu(OH)₂ on heating. Reduced by H₂ back to alcohols.
- Carboxylic acids –COOH: acetic acid CH₃COOH, a weak acid stronger than carbonic acid: 2CH₃COOH + CaCO₃ → (CH₃COO)₂Ca + H₂O + CO₂↑ (removes scale).
- Esters –COO–: ethyl acetate CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, fruity smell, less dense than water, insoluble. Hydrolysis is reversible in acid and complete in base.
> Example: Which reagent tells ethanol, acetic acid and ethanal apart in one test?
> Fresh Cu(OH)₂ suspension: acetic acid dissolves it to a blue solution; ethanal gives a brick-red precipitate on heating; ethanol shows no change.
! Memory chain: alkene → alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid → ester. Each arrow is a named reaction: addition of water, oxidation, oxidation, esterification.
## Isomerism

- Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. Chain isomers differ in branching; position isomers differ in where the group sits; functional group isomers differ in the group (ethanol C₂H₅OH and dimethyl ether CH₃OCH₃).
- Count of alkane isomers: C₄H₁₀ has 2, C₅H₁₂ has 3, C₆H₁₄ has 5.
- Count monochloro products by counting the different kinds of H (symmetry). n-butane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ has 2 kinds of H, so 2 monochloro products.
- Cis-trans isomers need each C of C=C to carry two different groups (but-2-ene has them; propene does not).
> Example: How many isomers does C₅H₁₂ have and which has only one monochloro product?
> Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane: 3 isomers. In 2,2-dimethylpropane C(CH₃)₄ all 12 H are equivalent, so it gives only one monochloro product.
! Trap: CH₂Cl₂ has no isomers because methane is tetrahedral, not flat. This fact is evidence for the tetrahedral shape.
## Naming simple compounds
- Find the longest carbon chain (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex- for 1 to 6 carbons). Number from the end that gives the substituents (or the functional group) the smallest numbers.
- Write substituents in alphabetical order with numbers; use di-, tri- for repeats: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₃ is 2,3-dimethylbutane.
- For alkenes and alcohols the chain must contain the C=C or the C bearing –OH, numbered to give it the lowest number: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ is but-1-ene; CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ is propan-2-ol.
! Trap: a name like 2-ethylbutane is wrong; the longest chain actually has 5 carbons, giving 3-methylpentane.
## Reaction types
- Substitution: one atom or group replaces another (alkane halogenation, benzene bromination and nitration, esterification, ester hydrolysis).
- Addition: atoms add to both ends of a C=C or C≡C (hydrogenation, bromine addition, hydration).
- Elimination: a small molecule is removed to form a multiple bond: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O (concentrated H₂SO₄, 170 °C). At 140 °C the same mixture gives diethyl ether instead (a substitution).
- Esterification: CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O (concentrated H₂SO₄, heat). The acid loses –OH and the alcohol loses H (shown by ¹⁸O labelling: the ¹⁸O of the alcohol ends up in the ester).
- In the lab ester is collected over saturated Na₂CO₃ solution, which removes acid, dissolves alcohol and lowers the ester's solubility.
- Oxidation and reduction in organic chemistry: gaining O or losing H is oxidation; gaining H is reduction.
> Example: 6 g of acetic acid reacts with excess ethanol with a yield of 50 %. What mass of ethyl acetate forms?
> n(acid) = 6/60 = 0.1 mol, so theoretical ester = 0.1 mol × 88 = 8.8 g. At 50 %, 4.4 g.
## Polymerisation
- Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers: n CH₂=CH₂ → –[CH₂–CH₂]ₙ– (polyethene). Chloroethene gives PVC; propene gives polypropene; styrene gives polystyrene.
- To find the monomer of an addition polymer, take the two-carbon repeat unit and put back the double bond.
- Condensation polymerisation also releases small molecules (water); examples are polyesters and proteins (from amino acids).
## Basic biomolecules

- Sugars: glucose and fructose C₆H₁₂O₆ (isomers; glucose has an aldehyde group and gives a silver mirror). Sucrose and maltose C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. Starch and cellulose (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ are not isomers because n differs. Starch turns iodine blue; its hydrolysis finally gives glucose.
- Fats and oils are esters of glycerol with fatty acids. Oils (liquid) contain more C=C and can be hardened by adding H₂. Hydrolysis in NaOH is saponification and makes soap.

- Proteins are polymers of amino acids (–NH₂ and –COOH groups). They coagulate reversibly with light-metal salts like (NH₄)₂SO₄ (salting out) and irreversibly with heat, heavy-metal ions, strong acids or bases, ethanol or formaldehyde (denaturation). Concentrated HNO₃ turns some proteins yellow; burnt protein smells like burnt feathers.
! Trap: fats, sugars and proteins are not all polymers. Fats and glucose are small molecules; starch, cellulose and proteins are natural polymers.

title: Redox Reactions
lines: Redox questions look different on the surface but always ask one of four things: which element changes oxidation state, which substance is the oxidising or reducing agent, how many electrons move, or what happens at an electrode. Master oxidation numbers and the rest follows.
## Oxidation numbers

- Rules in order: an element alone is 0 (Fe, O₂, Cl₂). In compounds F is always −1; group 1 metals +1; group 2 metals +2; Al +3; H is +1 (but −1 in metal hydrides such as NaH); O is −2 (but −1 in peroxides such as H₂O₂ and Na₂O₂).
- The sum is 0 for a neutral compound and equals the charge for an ion.
> Example: Find the oxidation number of Mn in KMnO₄, of S in Na₂S₂O₃ and of N in NH₄⁺.
> KMnO₄: 1 + x − 8 = 0, so Mn = +7. Na₂S₂O₃: 2 + 2x − 6 = 0, so S = +2 (average). NH₄⁺: x + 4 = +1, so N = −3.
- Common ranges: N from −3 (NH₃) to +5 (HNO₃); S from −2 (H₂S) to +6 (H₂SO₄); Cl from −1 (HCl) to +7 (HClO₄); Mn from +2 (Mn²⁺) to +7 (MnO₄⁻).
## Oxidation and reduction
- Oxidation is loss of electrons, so the oxidation number rises. Reduction is gain of electrons, so it falls. Memory trick: OIL RIG (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain).
- A reaction is redox if any oxidation number changes. Oxidation and reduction always happen together, and electrons lost = electrons gained.

- The oxidising agent is reduced (it takes electrons); the reducing agent is oxidised (it gives electrons). The product of reduction is the reduced product; the product of oxidation is the oxidised product.
! Memory trick: "The agent does to others what is done to itself in reverse." An oxidising agent oxidises something else, and is itself reduced.
> Example: In MnO₂ + 4HCl(conc.) → MnCl₂ + Cl₂↑ + 2H₂O (heat), identify the agents and the moles of HCl oxidised per mole MnO₂.
> Mn goes from +4 to +2 (reduced), so MnO₂ is the oxidising agent. Cl goes from −1 to 0 in Cl₂, so HCl is the reducing agent.
> Only 2 of the 4 Cl atoms become Cl₂, so 2 mol HCl is oxidised; the other 2 mol acts as an acid in MnCl₂.
! Trap: in this reaction dilute HCl does not work; as the acid is used up and becomes dilute the reaction stops, so the Cl₂ formed is less than the HCl amount predicts.
## Strength of oxidising and reducing agents
- In a reaction that goes, oxidising agent > oxidised product in oxidising power, and reducing agent > reduced product in reducing power.
> Example: Given 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂ and Cl₂ + 2Fe²⁺ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻, order the oxidising agents.
> From the first: Fe³⁺ > I₂. From the second: Cl₂ > Fe³⁺. So Cl₂ > Fe³⁺ > I₂. Reducing power runs the other way: I⁻ > Fe²⁺ > Cl⁻.
- Common strong oxidising agents: F₂, Cl₂, O₂, concentrated H₂SO₄, HNO₃, KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇, Fe³⁺, HClO, H₂O₂, Na₂O₂. Common reducing agents: active metals, H₂, C, CO, H₂S, S²⁻, I⁻, SO₂, SO₃²⁻, Fe²⁺.
- An element in its highest state can only be oxidising (S in H₂SO₄, N in HNO₃); in its lowest state only reducing (S²⁻, I⁻); in a middle state it can be either (SO₂, Fe²⁺, H₂O₂, Cl₂).

- Priority rule: when one oxidising agent meets several reducing agents, the strongest reducing agent reacts first. Cl₂ added to FeBr₂ oxidises Fe²⁺ before Br⁻; Cl₂ added to FeI₂ oxidises I⁻ before Fe²⁺.
## Electron transfer and counting
- Electrons transferred = (change in oxidation number per atom) × (number of atoms that change).
> Example: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. How many electrons are transferred per mole of O₂ formed?
> O goes from −2 to 0: 2 electrons per O atom, 4 per O₂ molecule. So 4 mol electrons per mol O₂ (and 12 for the whole equation as written).
> Example: In Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O, how many electrons move per mole of Cl₂?
> One Cl goes 0 → −1, the other 0 → +1, so 1 mol electrons per mol Cl₂. Cl₂ is both oxidising and reducing agent (disproportionation).
- Comproportionation: two states meet in the middle, e.g. 2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S + 2H₂O. Oxidised product and reduced product are both S, in a ratio 2 : 1.
- A middle state never jumps over another: in KClO₃ + 6HCl → KCl + 3Cl₂ + 3H₂O, the +5 Cl goes to 0, not to −1, so only 5 electrons are transferred, and Cl₂ is both the oxidised and reduced product.
! Trap: in the last reaction the KCl chlorine comes from HCl, not from KClO₃. That is why the electrons transferred are 5, not 6.
## Balancing redox equations

- Step 1: mark the oxidation numbers that change. Step 2: find the electrons lost and gained per formula. Step 3: use the lowest common multiple to equalise electrons. Step 4: balance other atoms by inspection, then H and O (with H⁺/H₂O in acid or OH⁻/H₂O in base). Step 5: check charge for ionic equations.
> Example: Balance MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ + H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ + H₂O.
> Mn +7 → +2 gains 5; Fe +2 → +3 loses 1. So 1 MnO₄⁻ to 5 Fe²⁺.
> Oxygen: 4 O gives 4H₂O, needing 8H⁺. MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O.
> Charge check: left −1 + 10 + 8 = +17; right +2 + 15 = +17. Balanced.
> Example: Balance Cu + HNO₃(dilute) → Cu(NO₃)₂ + NO + H₂O.
> Cu loses 2; N (+5 → +2) gains 3. LCM 6: 3Cu and 2NO. Then 6 nitrate in 3Cu(NO₃)₂ plus 2 N in NO = 8HNO₃, giving 4H₂O.
> 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO↑ + 4H₂O.
! Shortcut for calculations: you rarely need the full equation. Electron conservation alone answers questions like "how much KMnO₄ oxidises 0.5 mol Fe²⁺?": 0.5 mol electrons, so 0.1 mol MnO₄⁻.
## Galvanic (primary) cells

- A galvanic cell turns chemical energy into electrical energy using a spontaneous redox reaction. It needs two different electrodes (or a metal and an inert conductor), an electrolyte and a closed circuit.
- The negative electrode (anode) is where oxidation happens; it is usually the more active metal. The positive electrode (cathode) is where reduction happens.
- Electrons flow through the external wire from negative to positive. In the solution, cations move to the positive electrode and anions to the negative electrode.
- Zn–Cu cell in dilute H₂SO₄: negative Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻; positive 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂↑ (bubbles appear on the copper).
- Hydrogen fuel cell (acidic): negative 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻; positive O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O. In alkaline electrolyte: negative 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻; positive O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻.
- Lead-acid battery discharge: Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O; both electrodes gain mass as PbSO₄ forms.
