- Corrosion: iron rusts faster when in contact with a less active metal (Fe is the negative electrode). Electrochemical corrosion in neutral or weakly acidic water is oxygen-absorbing: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Protection: connect a more active metal (Zn, sacrificial anode) or connect to the negative terminal of a power supply.
! Trap: in an Mg–Al cell with NaOH electrolyte, Al is the negative electrode, because only Al reacts with NaOH. In an Fe–Cu cell with concentrated HNO₃, Cu is negative because Fe is passivated.
> Example: In a Zn–Cu–H₂SO₄ cell, 6.5 g of Zn dissolves. What volume of H₂ forms at STP?
> n(Zn) = 0.1 mol, 0.2 mol electrons, so 0.1 mol H₂ = 2.24 L.
## Electrolysis basics
- Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction. The anode joins the positive terminal (oxidation); the cathode joins the negative terminal (reduction).
- At an inert cathode (graphite or Pt) the most easily reduced cation gains electrons: Ag⁺ > Cu²⁺ > H⁺ > Na⁺ (active metal ions are not reduced from solution; water's H⁺ is).

- At an inert anode the most easily oxidised anion loses electrons: S²⁻ > I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > OH⁻ > sulfate and nitrate (these are never oxidised; water is). An active metal anode (Cu, Fe) dissolves itself.
- Examples: CuCl₂(aq) → Cu + Cl₂; brine 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂↑ + Cl₂↑ (H₂ at cathode, Cl₂ at anode); CuSO₄(aq): 2CuSO₄ + 2H₂O → 2Cu + O₂↑ + 2H₂SO₄.

- Electroplating: object to be plated is the cathode, plating metal is the anode, and the electrolyte contains its ions; the electrolyte concentration stays constant. Copper refining: impure Cu anode, pure Cu cathode.
- Molten electrolysis extracts active metals: 2NaCl(l) → 2Na + Cl₂; 2Al₂O₃(l) → 4Al + 3O₂ (with cryolite). MgCl₂ (molten) gives Mg; AlCl₃ is not used because it is covalent.
> Example: Electrolysing CuSO₄ solution with inert electrodes deposits 6.4 g of copper. What volume of O₂ forms at STP?
> n(Cu) = 0.1 mol, 0.2 mol electrons. O₂ needs 4 electrons per molecule, so 0.05 mol = 1.12 L.

! Memory trick: "An Ox, Red Cat" (anode oxidation, reduction at cathode) works for both cell types. Only the signs differ: in a galvanic cell the anode is negative; in electrolysis the anode is positive.

title: Acids, Bases and Electrolyte Solutions
lines: This topic is about what really exists in a solution: which ions, how many, and how they react. pH questions on a no-calculator paper use powers of ten, so practise moving between [H⁺] and pH quickly. Assume 25 °C unless told otherwise.
## Acid-base theories
- Arrhenius: an acid gives H⁺ in water; a base gives OH⁻ in water. Simple, but limited to aqueous solutions.
- Brønsted-Lowry: an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor; a base is a proton acceptor. Every acid has a conjugate base that differs by one H⁺: CH₃COOH / CH₃COO⁻, NH₄⁺ / NH₃, H₂O / OH⁻, H₃O⁺ / H₂O.
- Water and HCO₃⁻ are amphiprotic: they can act as an acid or a base.
- Lewis (for awareness): an acid accepts an electron pair; a base donates one. BF₃ is a Lewis acid; NH₃ is a Lewis base.
- The stronger an acid, the weaker its conjugate base. HCl is strong, so Cl⁻ is an extremely weak base (it does not hydrolyse); CH₃COOH is weak, so CH₃COO⁻ is a noticeable base.
> Example: In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, identify the Brønsted acids.
> H₂O gives a proton to NH₃, so H₂O is an acid; in the reverse direction NH₄⁺ gives a proton to OH⁻, so NH₄⁺ is also an acid. The bases are NH₃ and OH⁻.
## Strong and weak electrolytes
- Strong acids and bases ionise completely (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, NaOH, KOH, Ba(OH)₂). Weak acids and bases ionise partly and reach an equilibrium (CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺; NH₃·H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻).
- Polyprotic weak acids ionise in steps, the first step much more than the second: H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, then HCO₃⁻ ⇌ H⁺ + CO₃²⁻.
- Ionisation of a weak electrolyte is endothermic, so warming increases it. Diluting a weak acid increases its degree of ionisation, but [H⁺] still falls.
- Adding a common ion suppresses ionisation: adding CH₃COONa to acetic acid lowers [H⁺].
- Order of some acid strengths: H₂SO₃ > CH₃COOH > H₂CO₃ > HClO > HCO₃⁻. A stronger acid can make a weaker one: CO₂ + H₂O + Ca(ClO)₂ → CaCO₃↓ + 2HClO.

! Trap: equal concentrations of HCl and CH₃COOH have different pH (HCl lower) but need the same amount of NaOH to neutralise. Equal pH solutions are the opposite: the acetic acid solution holds far more acid and neutralises more base, and releases more H₂ with excess zinc.
> Example: 10 mL of pH = 3 HCl and 10 mL of pH = 3 CH₃COOH are each diluted to 1000 mL. Which has the higher pH?
> HCl is fully ionised, so 100-fold dilution raises pH by exactly 2, to 5. Acetic acid ionises further as it is diluted, so its pH rises less (stays between 3 and 5). HCl ends with the higher pH.
## Water, Kw and pH
- Water ionises slightly: H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻. Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C. Kw increases with temperature (ionisation is endothermic). At 100 °C, Kw ≈ 1 × 10⁻¹², and neutral water has pH 6.
- pH = −lg[H⁺]. pOH = −lg[OH⁻]. At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14.
- Neutral means [H⁺] = [OH⁻], not necessarily pH 7.
- Acids and bases suppress water's ionisation; most hydrolysing salts promote it.
## pH calculations for simple cases
- Strong acid: [H⁺] = c × number of H. 0.005 mol/L H₂SO₄ gives [H⁺] = 0.01 mol/L, pH = 2.
- Strong base: find [OH⁻], then pOH, then pH = 14 − pOH. 0.05 mol/L Ba(OH)₂ gives [OH⁻] = 0.1 mol/L, pOH 1, pH 13.
- Dilution of a strong acid or base by 10ⁿ shifts pH by n towards 7, but never past 7: pH 5 HCl diluted 1000 times is close to 7, not 8.
- Mixing an acid and a base: subtract moles of H⁺ and OH⁻, divide the excess by the total volume.
> Example: 100 mL of 0.3 mol/L HCl is mixed with 100 mL of 0.1 mol/L NaOH. Find the pH.
> n(H⁺) = 0.03 mol, n(OH⁻) = 0.01 mol. Excess H⁺ = 0.02 mol in 0.2 L, so [H⁺] = 0.1 mol/L, pH = 1.
> Example: Equal volumes of pH = 2 HCl and pH = 12 NaOH are mixed. Find the pH.
> [H⁺] = 0.01 and [OH⁻] = 0.01 mol/L, equal volumes, so they neutralise exactly: pH = 7.
> Example: In 0.01 mol/L NaOH at 25 °C, what is the concentration of H⁺ from water?
> [H⁺] = Kw / [OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ / 10⁻² = 10⁻¹² mol/L. All the H⁺ comes from water, and water's OH⁻ is also 10⁻¹² mol/L.
! Trap: pH 2 acetic acid mixed with equal volume pH 12 NaOH gives an acidic solution, because most of the acetic acid was still un-ionised and reacts later.
## Neutralisation
- Acid + base → salt + water; ionic form for strong acid and base: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
- At the equivalence point, moles of H⁺ supplied = moles of OH⁻ supplied. For an acid with a H atoms and a base with b OH: a × c(acid) × V(acid) = b × c(base) × V(base).
- The salt formed decides the pH at the equivalence point: strong acid + strong base → pH 7; weak acid + strong base → basic; strong acid + weak base → acidic.
> Example: What volume of 0.1 mol/L NaOH neutralises 20 mL of 0.05 mol/L H₂SO₄?
## Hydrolysis of salts
- Ions of weak acids or weak bases react with water and shift its balance. "Whoever is weak hydrolyses; whoever is strong decides the nature."
- Strong acid + weak base salts are acidic: NH₄Cl, CuSO₄, FeCl₃, AlCl₃. NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃·H₂O + H⁺.
- Weak acid + strong base salts are basic: CH₃COONa, Na₂CO₃, NaHCO₃, NaClO. CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ (the first step dominates; write steps separately and use ⇌, no ↑ or ↓).
- Strong acid + strong base salts do not hydrolyse: NaCl, KNO₃, Na₂SO₄ (neutral). NaHSO₄ is acidic because it ionises fully to give H⁺.
- The weaker the parent acid, the stronger the hydrolysis: at equal concentration, pH of Na₂CO₃ > NaHCO₃ and NaClO > CH₃COONa.
- Hydrolysis is endothermic, so heating increases it (hot soda solution cleans grease better). Dilution also increases the extent of hydrolysis.

- Applications: FeCl₃ solutions are prepared in dilute HCl to suppress hydrolysis; heating AlCl₃ or FeCl₃ solution to dryness gives Al(OH)₃ or Fe(OH)₃ (then oxides on strong heating) because HCl escapes; alum and FeCl₃ purify water through hydroxide colloids; NH₄Cl solution removes rust.
> Example: Rank the pH of 0.1 mol/L solutions of NaCl, NH₄Cl, Na₂CO₃ and NaOH.
> NaOH (strong base) > Na₂CO₃ (hydrolysis, basic) > NaCl (neutral, 7) > NH₄Cl (hydrolysis, acidic).
## Conservation rules in salt solutions
- Charge balance: in Na₂CO₃ solution, c(Na⁺) + c(H⁺) = 2c(CO₃²⁻) + c(HCO₃⁻) + c(OH⁻).
- Material balance: c(Na⁺) = 2[c(CO₃²⁻) + c(HCO₃⁻) + c(H₂CO₃)].
- In CH₃COONa solution: c(Na⁺) > c(CH₃COO⁻) > c(OH⁻) > c(H⁺).
! Trap: the coefficient 2 in the charge balance comes from the charge of CO₃²⁻, not from the formula Na₂CO₃. Students often put the 2 in the wrong place.
## Buffers (qualitative)
- A buffer resists pH change when a little acid or base is added, or on dilution. It is a weak acid with its salt (CH₃COOH / CH₃COONa) or a weak base with its salt (NH₃·H₂O / NH₄Cl).
- Added H⁺ is taken up by the conjugate base (CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH); added OH⁻ is taken up by the weak acid (CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O).
- Blood is buffered mainly by H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻, keeping pH near 7.4. A buffer fails if too much acid or base is added.
## Titration basics

- Apparatus: burette (reads to 0.01 mL, zero at the top), pipette, conical flask, white tile. Rinse the burette with the solution it will hold; never rinse the conical flask with the solution being titrated.

- Indicators: phenolphthalein colourless below about pH 8.2, red above about 10; methyl orange red below 3.1, yellow above 4.4. Use phenolphthalein for weak acid with strong base; methyl orange for strong acid with weak base. Litmus is not used (colour change too gradual).
- End point: one drop changes the colour and it stays for 30 seconds.

- Error analysis: think about how the error changes V(standard). Burette not rinsed with standard solution → standard diluted → V larger → result high. Bubble in the burette tip that disappears → V reads larger → high. Reading the final volume looking down from above → V reads smaller → low. Water already in the conical flask → no effect.
> Example: 25.00 mL of NaOH needs 20.00 mL of 0.1000 mol/L HCl. Find c(NaOH).

title: Analytic Geometry: Lines, Circles and Conics
lines: Analytic geometry turns pictures into equations. Learn the standard forms and the few distance formulas below; then most questions are a short substitution. Always sketch a quick picture to catch sign mistakes.
## Slope and inclination
- The inclination α of a line is the angle from the positive x-axis, 0 ≤ α < π.
- Slope k = tan α (undefined for a vertical line, α = π/2).
- Through (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂): k = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), x₁ ≠ x₂.
> Example: Find the inclination of the line √3x + 3y − 1 = 0.
! Trap: when the slope is negative, the inclination is obtuse. Do not answer −π/6.
## Equations of lines
- Point-slope: y − y₀ = k(x − x₀). Slope-intercept: y = kx + b.
- Intercept form: x/a + y/b = 1 (a, b ≠ 0). General form: Ax + By + C = 0, slope −A/B.
- A line through the origin has no intercept form; remember it when a question says "equal intercepts".
> Example: Find the lines through (2, 3) with equal x- and y-intercepts.
> Through the origin: y = (3/2)x. Otherwise x/a + y/a = 1 with 2 + 3 = a, so x + y − 5 = 0. Two answers.
## Parallel and perpendicular
- With slopes: parallel ⇔ k₁ = k₂ (and different intercepts); perpendicular ⇔ k₁k₂ = −1.
- With general forms A₁x + B₁y + C₁ = 0 and A₂x + B₂y + C₂ = 0: perpendicular ⇔ A₁A₂ + B₁B₂ = 0; parallel ⇔ A₁B₂ = A₂B₁ and the lines are not identical.
> Example: ax + 2y + 1 = 0 is perpendicular to x − y + 3 = 0. Find a.
> Example: ax + 2y + 1 = 0 is parallel to x + (a − 1)y + 2 = 0. Find a.
> a(a − 1) = 2 gives a = 2 or a = −1. a = 2: 2x + 2y + 1 = 0 and x + y + 2 = 0, parallel ✓. a = −1: −x + 2y + 1 = 0 and x − 2y + 2 = 0, parallel ✓ (not identical). So a = 2 or −1.
! Trap: for the parallel condition, always check that the two lines do not coincide.
## Distances
- Between points: |AB| = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). Midpoint ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
- Point (x₀, y₀) to line Ax + By + C = 0: d = |Ax₀ + By₀ + C| / √(A² + B²).
- Between parallel lines Ax + By + C₁ = 0 and Ax + By + C₂ = 0: d = |C₁ − C₂| / √(A² + B²).
> Example: Distance from (1, 2) to 3x + 4y − 1 = 0.
> Example: Distance between 3x + 4y − 2 = 0 and 6x + 8y + 1 = 0.
> Rewrite the first as 6x + 8y − 4 = 0. d = |−4 − 1|/10 = 1/2.
! Trap: the parallel-line formula needs identical A and B. Scale one equation first.
## Circles
- Standard form: (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r², centre (a, b), radius r.
- General form: x² + y² + Dx + Ey + F = 0, centre (−D/2, −E/2), radius ½√(D² + E² − 4F); it is a circle only if D² + E² − 4F > 0.
> Example: Find the centre and radius of x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 3 = 0.
## Line and circle; circle and circle
- Let d be the distance from the centre to the line. d < r: two intersection points; d = r: tangent; d > r: no common point.
- Chord length: L = 2√(r² − d²).
- Tangent at a point P on the circle is perpendicular to the radius to P.

- Two circles with radii R, r and centre distance d: d > R + r separate; d = R + r externally tangent; |R − r| < d < R + r intersecting; d = |R − r| internally tangent; d < |R − r| one inside the other.
- Subtracting the equations of two intersecting circles gives the equation of their common chord.
> Example: Find the chord cut from x² + y² = 25 by the line 3x + 4y − 15 = 0.
> Example: The line y = x + m is tangent to x² + y² = 2. Find m.
> Example: Position of circles x² + y² = 4 and (x − 3)² + (y − 4)² = 9.
> d = 5 = 2 + 3, so they are externally tangent.
! Trick: for chords and tangents of circles, use the distance d from the centre. It is much faster than substituting and using the discriminant.
## Ellipse
- Definition: the sum of distances to two foci is a constant 2a (2a > the focal distance 2c).
- Foci on the x-axis: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, a > b > 0, c² = a² − b². Foci (±c, 0), vertices (±a, 0), (0, ±b).
- Eccentricity e = c/a, with 0 < e < 1. The closer e is to 1, the flatter the ellipse.
- Whichever denominator is larger tells you the axis of the foci.
> Example: Ellipse x²/25 + y²/16 = 1. Find c, e and the perimeter of triangle PF₁F₂ for any point P on it.
> c² = 25 − 16 = 9, c = 3, e = 3/5. |PF₁| + |PF₂| = 2a = 10 and |F₁F₂| = 6, so the perimeter is 16.
> Example: x²/m + y²/4 = 1 is an ellipse with foci on the y-axis. Find the range of m.
> Need 4 > m > 0, so 0 < m < 4.
! Trap: for the ellipse, a is the largest: a² = b² + c². For the hyperbola, c is the largest: c² = a² + b². Mixing these is the most common error.
## Hyperbola
- Definition: the absolute difference of distances to the foci is a constant 2a (2a < 2c).
- Foci on the x-axis: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, c² = a² + b², foci (±c, 0), vertices (±a, 0).
- Asymptotes: y = ±(b/a)x. For y²/a² − x²/b² = 1 they are y = ±(a/b)x.
- Eccentricity e = c/a > 1. Also e² = 1 + b²/a², so the asymptote slope b/a = √(e² − 1).
- The axis of the foci follows the positive term, not the bigger denominator.
> Example: x²/9 − y²/16 = 1. Find the foci, the eccentricity and the asymptotes.
> Example: A hyperbola has asymptotes y = ±2x and foci on the x-axis. Find e.
> Example: Find a hyperbola with asymptotes y = ±(1/2)x passing through (4, 1).
> Write x²/4 − y² = λ. At (4, 1): 4 − 1 = 3 = λ. So x²/12 − y²/3 = 1.
! Trick: hyperbolas sharing asymptotes y = ±(b/a)x all have the form x²/a² − y²/b² = λ (λ ≠ 0). This avoids guessing which axis the foci lie on.
! Trap: on the hyperbola ||PF₁| − |PF₂|| = 2a. If |PF₁| = 7 and a = 3, then |PF₂| = 1 or 13; reject any value smaller than c − a.
## Parabola
- Definition: the set of points equally distant from a focus F and a directrix line.
- y² = 2px (p > 0): focus (p/2, 0), directrix x = −p/2, opens right. Similarly x² = 2py opens up with focus (0, p/2), directrix y = −p/2.
- Focal distance: for P(x₀, y₀) on y² = 2px, |PF| = x₀ + p/2. This is the most used parabola fact.
- Eccentricity e = 1.
> Example: Find the focus and directrix of y = 4x².
> Rewrite as x² = y/4, so 2p = 1/4, p = 1/8. Focus (0, 1/16), directrix y = −1/16.
> Example: P on y² = 8x is at distance 6 from the focus. Find the x-coordinate of P.
! Trap: y = ax² is a parabola opening up or down; put it into x² = (1/a)y before reading off the focus. Many students wrongly answer (a/4, 0).
## Simple chord problems
- Substitute the line into the conic to get a quadratic in x. Use Vieta: x₁ + x₂ and x₁x₂.
- Chord length: |AB| = √(1 + k²)·|x₁ − x₂| = √(1 + k²)·√((x₁ + x₂)² − 4x₁x₂).
- Midpoint of chord: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
- Focal chord of y² = 2px: |AB| = x₁ + x₂ + p.
> Example: A line through the focus of y² = 4x meets the parabola at A and B with x₁ + x₂ = 6. Find |AB|.
> Example: Line y = x − 1 meets y² = 4x at A and B. Find |AB|.
> (x − 1)² = 4x ⇒ x² − 6x + 1 = 0. x₁ + x₂ = 6, and the line passes through the focus (1, 0), so |AB| = 6 + 2 = 8. (Check: √2·√(36 − 4) = √2·4√2 = 8.)
> Example: The chord of x²/4 + y²/2 = 1 has midpoint (1, 1). Find its slope.
> Subtract the curve equations for the two endpoints: (x₁² − x₂²)/4 + (y₁² − y₂²)/2 = 0. So k = −(x₁ + x₂)/(2(y₁ + y₂)) = −2/(2·2) = −1/2.
! Midpoint trick (point-difference method): for x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 with chord midpoint (x₀, y₀), slope k = −b²x₀/(a²y₀). For the hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, k = b²x₀/(a²y₀).

title: Derivatives and Their Applications
lines: Derivative questions follow a few fixed patterns: differentiate, find a tangent, find where f′ changes sign, then compare values. Fast, accurate differentiation is the whole game.
## Definition and meaning
- Average rate of change from x₀ to x₀ + Δx: Δy/Δx = (f(x₀ + Δx) − f(x₀))/Δx.
- Derivative: f′(x₀) = lim as Δx → 0 of (f(x₀ + Δx) − f(x₀))/Δx.
- Geometric meaning: f′(x₀) is the slope of the tangent to y = f(x) at (x₀, f(x₀)).
- Physical meaning: if s(t) is position, s′(t) is instantaneous velocity and s″(t) is acceleration.
> Example: f′(2) = 3. Find the limit as h → 0 of (f(2 + 2h) − f(2))/h.
> Write it as 2 · (f(2 + 2h) − f(2))/(2h). The fraction tends to f′(2), so the limit is 2 · 3 = 6.
! Trap: (f(x₀ + h) − f(x₀ − h))/h tends to 2f′(x₀), not f′(x₀). Match the denominator to the change inside f.
> Example: s(t) = t³ − 2t (metres, seconds). Find the velocity at t = 2.
## Derivatives of basic functions
- (c)′ = 0; (xⁿ)′ = nxⁿ⁻¹ for any real n.
- (sin x)′ = cos x; (cos x)′ = −sin x.
- (eˣ)′ = eˣ; (aˣ)′ = aˣ ln a.
- (ln x)′ = 1/x; (logₐ x)′ = 1/(x ln a).
! Trap: (cos x)′ has a minus sign; (sin x)′ does not. Also (ln 2)′ = 0 because ln 2 is a constant.
## Rules: sum, product, quotient, chain
- Product: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′.
- Quotient: (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v².
- Chain (simple form): (f(ax + b))′ = a·f′(ax + b). More generally (f(g(x)))′ = f′(g(x))·g′(x).
> Example: y = x² sin x. Find y′.
> y′ = 2x sin x + x² cos x.
> Example: y = ln x / x. Find y′.
> Example: y = e^(2x − 1) + cos 3x. Find y′.
> Example: y = ln(x² + 1). Find y′(1).
! Trick: before using the quotient rule, simplify. (x² + 1)/x = x + 1/x, whose derivative 1 − 1/x² is quicker.
## Tangent lines
- Tangent at the point (x₀, f(x₀)): y − f(x₀) = f′(x₀)(x − x₀).
- Normal line is perpendicular: slope −1/f′(x₀) (when f′(x₀) ≠ 0).
- "Tangent at a point" means the point is on the curve. "Tangent through a point" may mean the point is off the curve: then call the touching point (t, f(t)) and solve for t.
> Example: Find the tangent to y = x³ − 2x at x = 1.
> Example: Find the tangent to y = eˣ that passes through the origin.
> Touching point (t, eᵗ), slope eᵗ. Tangent: y − eᵗ = eᵗ(x − t). Through (0, 0): −eᵗ = −teᵗ, so t = 1. Tangent: y = ex.
> Example: The line y = 2x + b touches y = x² − 2x + 3. Find b.
> Slope: 2x − 2 = 2 gives x = 2, so the touching point is (2, 3). Then 3 = 4 + b, b = −1.
! Trap: if the question says "through" a point, first check whether that point lies on the curve. If it does not, you must use the touching-point method.
## Increasing and decreasing intervals
- On an interval: f′(x) > 0 ⇒ f increasing; f′(x) < 0 ⇒ f decreasing.
- Steps: find the domain, compute f′, solve f′(x) = 0, make a sign chart.
- If "f is increasing on an interval" is given, the condition is f′(x) ≥ 0 on that interval (f′ may touch 0 at isolated points).
> Example: Find the intervals of monotonicity of f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 1.
> f′(x) = 3x² − 6x = 3x(x − 2). f′ > 0 for x < 0 or x > 2; f′ < 0 for 0 < x < 2. Increasing on (−∞, 0) and (2, ∞), decreasing on (0, 2).
> Example: f(x) = x − ln x. Find its decreasing interval.
> Domain x > 0. f′(x) = 1 − 1/x = (x − 1)/x < 0 for 0 < x < 1. Decreasing on (0, 1).
> Example: f(x) = x³ + ax is increasing on R. Find the range of a.
> f′(x) = 3x² + a ≥ 0 for all x needs a ≥ 0.
! Trap: forgetting the domain. For ln x, √x or 1/x terms, intervals outside the domain must not appear in your answer.
! Trap: two increasing intervals are written separately, joined by "and", not with ∪, because f need not be increasing across the gap.
## Extrema
- A local maximum at x₀: f′ changes from + to −. A local minimum: f′ changes from − to +.
- f′(x₀) = 0 alone is not enough: f(x) = x³ has f′(0) = 0 but no extremum (f′ does not change sign).
- If a question says f has an extremum at x₀ (and f is differentiable), use f′(x₀) = 0, then check the sign change.
> Example: Find the local extrema of f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 1.
> From the sign chart above: local maximum f(0) = 1; local minimum f(2) = 8 − 12 + 1 = −3.
> Example: f(x) = x³ + ax² + 3x is said to have an extremum at x = 1. Find a.
> f′(1) = 3 + 2a + 3 = 0, so a = −3. Check: f′(x) = 3x² − 6x + 3 = 3(x − 1)² ≥ 0, no sign change. So there is no such a. Always check!
! This is a real exam trap: solving f′(x₀) = 0 gives a candidate; the sign check decides.
> Example: f(x) = x³ − ax has a local minimum at x = 2. Find a and the local maximum.
## Maximum and minimum on a closed interval
- Compare the values at the critical points inside [a, b] and at both endpoints. The largest is the maximum, the smallest is the minimum.
> Example: Find the maximum and minimum of f(x) = x³ − 3x on [−2, 3].
! Trap: a local maximum is not necessarily the largest value. Here the local maximum 2 is beaten by the endpoint value 18.
- Inequality problems: "f(x) ≥ k for all x in D" means the minimum of f on D is ≥ k.
> Example: x − ln x ≥ m for all x > 0. Find the largest m.
> f(x) = x − ln x has minimum f(1) = 1 (decreasing on (0, 1), increasing after). So m ≤ 1; the largest m is 1.
## Simple optimisation
- Steps: choose a variable, write the quantity as a function, state the domain, differentiate, check the critical point, answer the question asked (with units).
> Example: A square sheet of side 6 has equal squares of side x cut from each corner, and the sides are folded up to make an open box. Find the largest volume.
> V = x(6 − 2x)², 0 < x < 3. V′ = (6 − 2x)² − 4x(6 − 2x) = (6 − 2x)(6 − 6x). Inside (0, 3), V′ = 0 at x = 1. V′ > 0 before 1 and < 0 after, so V(1) = 1 · 16 = 16 is the maximum.
> Example: A rectangle has perimeter 20. Find its largest area.
> Sides x and 10 − x: A = 10x − x², A′ = 10 − 2x = 0 at x = 5. Largest area 25 (a square).
## Quick checklist
- Write the domain first.
- Factor f′ fully before making the sign chart.
- After f′(x₀) = 0, check the sign change.
- On a closed interval, always include the endpoints.

title: Functions, Exponents and Logarithms
lines: Functions are the largest maths topic on the paper. Most questions test one law at a time: a domain, a log rule, a shift of a graph or a count of zeros. Learn the laws exactly and check domains every time.
## Function, domain and range
- A function assigns exactly one output f(x) to each input x in its domain.
- Domain rules: a denominator ≠ 0; an even root needs its inside ≥ 0; a logarithm needs its argument > 0 (and base > 0, base ≠ 1); x⁰ needs x ≠ 0.
- Two functions are equal only if they have the same domain and the same rule.
> Example: Find the domain of f(x) = √(x + 1) + 1/(x − 2) + lg(3 − x).
- Range of a quadratic: complete the square. Range of a fraction like (2x + 1)/(x − 1): write it as 2 + 3/(x − 1), so y ≠ 2.
> Example: Range of y = x² − 4x + 1 on [0, 3].
> y = (x − 2)² − 3. Vertex x = 2 is inside: minimum −3. Endpoints: y(0) = 1, y(3) = −2. Range [−3, 1].
! Trap: f(x) = x and g(x) = x²/x are not the same function, because g is undefined at 0.
## Composition and inverse functions
- (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)): apply g first. The domain of f(g(x)) is the set of x for which g(x) lies in the domain of f.
- To find an inverse: write y = f(x), solve for x, swap x and y. The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f.
- The graphs of f and f⁻¹ are reflections in the line y = x. Only one-to-one functions have inverses.
- The inverse of y = aˣ is y = logₐ x.
> Example: f(x) = 2x + 3, g(x) = x². Find f(g(−1)) and g(f(−1)).
> g(−1) = 1, f(1) = 5. f(−1) = 1, g(1) = 1. So 5 and 1: composition is not commutative.
> Example: Inverse of f(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 2).
! Trick: if f⁻¹(a) = b, then f(b) = a. You never need the inverse formula to answer that.
## Monotonicity, odd/even, periodicity
- f is increasing on an interval if x₁ < x₂ implies f(x₁) < f(x₂).
- Even: f(−x) = f(x), graph symmetric about the y-axis. Odd: f(−x) = −f(x), symmetric about the origin.
- The domain must be symmetric about 0, otherwise f is neither odd nor even.
- If an odd function is defined at 0 then f(0) = 0.
- Odd × odd = even, odd × even = odd, even × even = even.
- Period T: f(x + T) = f(x). If f(x + a) = −f(x) then the period is 2a.
> Example: f is odd and for x > 0, f(x) = x² − 2x. Find f(−1).
> Example: f has period 4 and f(x) = 2ˣ on [0, 4). Find f(9).
! Trap: an even function is increasing on one side and decreasing on the other. If f is even and increasing on [0, ∞), then f(a) < f(b) ⇔ |a| < |b|.
## Graph transformations
- y = f(x − h) + k: shift right by h, up by k. "Inside" changes act opposite to what they look like.
- y = −f(x): reflect in the x-axis. y = f(−x): reflect in the y-axis.
- y = af(x): vertical stretch by a. y = f(bx): horizontal compression by factor b.
- y = |f(x)|: reflect the parts below the x-axis upwards. y = f(|x|): keep the right half and mirror it to the left.
> Example: y = 2ˣ is shifted 3 units left and 1 unit down. New equation?
## Linear and quadratic functions
- y = kx + b: slope k, y-intercept b; increasing if k > 0.
- y = ax² + bx + c: axis x = −b/(2a); vertex value c − b²/(4a); opens up if a > 0.
- Vieta: x₁ + x₂ = −b/a, x₁x₂ = c/a.
- On a closed interval, the extreme values occur at the vertex (if inside) or at the endpoints.
> Example: f(x) = x² − 2ax + 3 is decreasing on (−∞, 2]. Find the range of a.
> The axis is x = a, and f decreases left of the axis. Need 2 ≤ a, so a ≥ 2.
! Trap: when the axis contains a parameter, split into cases: axis left of, inside, or right of the interval.
## Power and exponential functions
- Power function y = x^α. On (0, ∞) it is increasing if α > 0 and decreasing if α < 0. Every power function passes through (1, 1).
- Exponent laws: aᵐ·aⁿ = a^(m+n), aᵐ/aⁿ = a^(m−n), (aᵐ)ⁿ = a^(mn), a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, a^(m/n) = ⁿ√(aᵐ), a⁰ = 1.
- y = aˣ (a > 0, a ≠ 1): domain R, range (0, ∞), passes through (0, 1). Increasing if a > 1, decreasing if 0 < a < 1.
! Comparing powers: write both with the same base (use monotonicity) or the same exponent. For mixed cases compare with 0 and 1.
## Logarithms
- logₐ N = b ⇔ aᵇ = N (a > 0, a ≠ 1, N > 0).
- logₐ 1 = 0, logₐ a = 1, a^(logₐ N) = N.
- logₐ(MN) = logₐ M + logₐ N; logₐ(M/N) = logₐ M − logₐ N; logₐ(Mⁿ) = n logₐ M.
- Change of base: logₐ b = log_c b / log_c a. So logₐ b · log_b a = 1, and log_(aᵐ)(bⁿ) = (n/m) logₐ b.
- lg means log₁₀; ln means logₑ.
- y = logₐ x: domain (0, ∞), passes through (1, 0); increasing if a > 1, decreasing if 0 < a < 1.
> Example: Evaluate lg 4 + 2 lg 5 − log₂ 3 · log₃ 8.
> lg 4 + lg 25 = lg 100 = 2. log₂ 3 · log₃ 8 = log₂ 8 = 3. Total 2 − 3 = −1.
> Example: Order a = log₂ 3, b = log₃ 2, c = log_(1/2) 3.
> a > log₂ 2 = 1. 0 = log₃ 1 < b < log₃ 3 = 1. c < log_(1/2) 1 = 0 because the base is below 1. So a > b > c.
! Trap: log(M + N) is not log M + log N, and (log M)² is not 2 log M.
## Exponential and logarithmic equations
- Same base: a^f(x) = a^g(x) ⇒ f(x) = g(x). logₐ f(x) = logₐ g(x) ⇒ f(x) = g(x) with both > 0.
- Substitution: equations like 4ˣ − 3·2ˣ + 2 = 0 become quadratics in t = 2ˣ (t > 0).
> Example: Solve 4ˣ − 6·2ˣ + 8 = 0.
> t = 2ˣ: t² − 6t + 8 = 0, t = 2 or 4. So x = 1 or x = 2.
> Example: Solve log₂(x − 1) + log₂(x + 1) = 3.
> log₂(x² − 1) = 3 ⇒ x² = 9 ⇒ x = ±3. Need x − 1 > 0, so x = 3 only.
! Trap: always check log solutions in the original equation. Combining logs can create false roots.
## Piecewise functions
- Evaluate by first deciding which piece the input belongs to; work from the inside out for f(f(a)).
- For "f(a) = k", solve in each piece and keep only answers inside that piece's interval.
> Example: f(x) = 2ˣ for x ≤ 0, and log₂ x for x > 0. Find f(f(1/4)).
! For a piecewise function to be increasing on R, each piece must increase and the left piece's value at the joint must not exceed the right piece's value.
## Zeros of functions
- A zero of f is a real x with f(x) = 0: an x-intercept, not a point.
- Existence theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b] and f(a)·f(b) < 0, then f has a zero in (a, b).
- The number of solutions of f(x) = g(x) equals the number of intersection points of the two graphs.
> Example: In which interval is the zero of f(x) = 2ˣ + x − 4?
> f is increasing. f(1) = −1 < 0, f(2) = 2 > 0. So the only zero lies in (1, 2).
> Example: How many solutions does 2ˣ = x² have?
> Graphs meet at x = 2 and x = 4, and once more for some negative x (between −1 and 0: at x = −1, 2ˣ = 0.5 < 1 = x²; at x = 0, 1 > 0). So 3 solutions.
! Trap: f(a)f(b) > 0 does not mean there is no zero in between (x² − 1 on [−2, 2] has two). The sign test only guarantees existence.

title: Probability and Statistics
lines: This topic needs little theory but careful counting. Decide first whether order matters, then count the favourable and total cases the same way. Statistics questions are mostly short calculations from a list or a table.
## Counting principles
- Addition principle: if a task can be done in one of several separate ways (choose one route), add the numbers of ways.
- Multiplication principle: if a task has several steps done one after another, multiply the numbers of ways for each step.
> Example: A meal is one of 3 starters, one of 4 mains and one of 2 drinks. How many different meals?
> Example: How many 3-digit numbers can be made from the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 with no repeated digit?
> Hundreds digit: 4 choices (not 0). Then 4 and 3 choices. 4 × 4 × 3 = 48.
! Trap: a number cannot start with 0. Fill the restricted position first.
## Permutations and combinations
- Permutation (order matters): A(n, r) = n!/(n − r)! = n(n − 1)…(n − r + 1). Arranging all n objects: n!.
- Combination (order does not matter): C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n − r)!).
> Example: Choose a team of 3 from 5 boys and 4 girls with at least one girl.
> All teams: C(9, 3) = 84. All-boy teams: C(5, 3) = 10. Answer 84 − 10 = 74.
> Example: 5 people stand in a row and A and B must be next to each other.
> Glue A and B into one block: 4! arrangements of 4 units, times 2 orders inside the block: 48.
> Example: 5 people stand in a row and A and B must not be next to each other.
> Arrange the other 3: 3! = 6. There are 4 gaps around them; put A and B into 2 different gaps in order: A(4, 2) = 12. Total 72. (Check: 120 − 48 = 72.)
! Bundling for "together", gaps for "not together". "At least one" is usually easiest as total minus none.
! Trap: choosing 3 students for 3 different jobs is a permutation; choosing 3 students for a committee is a combination.
## Classical probability
- If all outcomes are equally likely: P(A) = (number of outcomes in A)/(total number of outcomes).
- 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1. A sure event has probability 1, an impossible event 0.
> Example: Two fair dice are rolled. Find the probability that the sum is 7.
> Example: A bag has 3 red and 2 white balls. Two are drawn together. Find P(both red).
! Trap: with two dice, (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different outcomes. Treat the dice as distinguishable so that all 36 outcomes are equally likely.
## Complementary, mutually exclusive and independent events
- Complement: P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
- Mutually exclusive (cannot happen together): P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).
- General: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
- Independent (one does not affect the other): P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B).
- Mutually exclusive is not the same as independent. Two exclusive events with positive probabilities are never independent.
> Example: Ali hits a target with probability 0.8 and Mei with probability 0.5, independently. Find the probability that the target is hit at least once.
> P(both miss) = 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.1. P(at least one hit) = 1 − 0.1 = 0.9.
> Example: In the same situation, find the probability that exactly one of them hits.
> Example: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. Find P(at least one head).
- Repeated independent trials: the probability of exactly k successes in n trials, each with success probability p, is C(n, k)pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ.
> Example: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. Find P(exactly 2 heads).
! Trap: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) only for independent events. For draws without replacement, the events are not independent.
## Averages: mean, median, mode
- Mean x̄ = (x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ)/n.
- Median: sort the data; the middle value (n odd) or the mean of the two middle values (n even).
- Mode: the most frequent value; there can be more than one.
- If every value is changed to ax + b, the new mean is a·x̄ + b.
> Example: Data 3, 7, 4, 9, 7, 6. Find the mean, median and mode.
> Sum 36, mean 6. Sorted: 3, 4, 6, 7, 7, 9; median (6 + 7)/2 = 6.5. Mode 7.
! Trap: always sort before finding the median.
## Variance and standard deviation
- Variance s² = [(x₁ − x̄)² + … + (xₙ − x̄)²]/n. Standard deviation s = √(s²).
- Shortcut: s² = (mean of the squares) − (square of the mean).
- If every value becomes ax + b, the new variance is a²s² and the new standard deviation is |a|s. Adding b does not change the spread.
- Smaller variance means the data are more concentrated (more stable).
> Example: Find the variance of 2, 4, 6, 8.
> Mean 5. Squared deviations 9, 1, 1, 9, sum 20. s² = 20/4 = 5.
> Example: Data x₁, …, xₙ have mean 3 and variance 2. Find the mean and variance of 2x₁ + 1, …, 2xₙ + 1.
> Mean 2·3 + 1 = 7. Variance 2²·2 = 8.
! Trap: adding a constant changes the mean but not the variance; multiplying by a multiplies the variance by a², not by a.
## Frequency tables and histograms
- From a frequency table: x̄ = Σ(xᵢfᵢ)/Σfᵢ. With grouped data, use the midpoint of each class.
- In a frequency histogram, the height is frequency/class width, so the area of each bar is the frequency (or relative frequency), and the total area of relative-frequency bars is 1.
- The mode of grouped data is estimated by the midpoint of the tallest bar; the median is where the area to the left is 0.5.
> Example: Scores 60, 70, 80, 90 occur with frequencies 2, 3, 4, 1. Find the mean.

> Example: A relative-frequency histogram has classes of width 10 with heights 0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.03 for [50, 60), [60, 70), [70, 80), [80, 90). Find the relative frequency of [70, 80) and the median.
> Relative frequencies: 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.3 (they add to 1). The first two give 0.3, so the median lies in [70, 80): 70 + (0.5 − 0.3)/0.04 = 70 + 5 = 75.
! Trap: in a histogram the bar height is not the frequency. Multiply by the class width.
## Normal distribution basics
- X ~ N(μ, σ²): bell-shaped curve, symmetric about x = μ, highest at x = μ. The total area under the curve is 1.
- Larger σ: flatter and wider. Smaller σ: taller and narrower. μ only shifts the curve left or right.
- Approximate rules: P(μ − σ < X < μ + σ) ≈ 0.683; P(μ − 2σ < X < μ + 2σ) ≈ 0.954; P(μ − 3σ < X < μ + 3σ) ≈ 0.997.
- Symmetry: P(X < μ − a) = P(X > μ + a), and P(X < μ) = 0.5.
> Example: X ~ N(2, σ²) and P(X < 4) = 0.8. Find P(0 < X < 2).
> P(X > 4) = 0.2, so P(X < 0) = 0.2 by symmetry. P(0 < X < 4) = 0.6, and half of it is P(0 < X < 2) = 0.3.
> Example: X ~ N(1, σ²). If P(X < a) = P(X > 5), find a.
> The two points are symmetric about μ = 1: (a + 5)/2 = 1, so a = −3.
! Trap: N(μ, σ²) writes the variance, not the standard deviation. N(3, 4) has σ = 2.

title: Sequences
lines: Sequence questions are mostly arithmetic and geometric sequences plus a few standard summing tricks. The key skill is turning the given facts into equations in a₁ and d (or a₁ and q) and solving them quickly.
## General term and recursion
- A sequence is a list a₁, a₂, a₃, … ; aₙ is the general (nth) term.
- Sₙ = a₁ + a₂ + … + aₙ is the sum of the first n terms.
- From the sum to the term: a₁ = S₁, and aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ for n ≥ 2.
- A recursive definition gives a first term and a rule such as aₙ₊₁ = 2aₙ + 1.
> Example: Sₙ = n² + 2n. Find aₙ.
> a₁ = S₁ = 3. For n ≥ 2, aₙ = (n² + 2n) − ((n − 1)² + 2(n − 1)) = 2n + 1. Since 2·1 + 1 = 3 matches a₁, aₙ = 2n + 1 for all n.
> Example: Sₙ = n² + 1. Find aₙ.
> a₁ = 2. For n ≥ 2, aₙ = 2n − 1, which would give 1 at n = 1. So aₙ = 2 for n = 1 and 2n − 1 for n ≥ 2.
! Trap: always check n = 1 separately. If Sₙ has a constant term, the formula for n ≥ 2 usually fails at n = 1.
> Example: a₁ = 1, aₙ₊₁ = aₙ/(1 + aₙ). Find a₄.
> a₂ = 1/2, a₃ = (1/2)/(3/2) = 1/3, a₄ = 1/4. (Taking reciprocals, 1/aₙ₊₁ = 1/aₙ + 1, so 1/aₙ = n.)
! Trick: for a recursion question with a far term like a₂₀₂₆, write the first five or six terms. They often repeat (periodic) or follow an obvious pattern.
## Arithmetic sequences
- Each term adds a constant difference d: aₙ₊₁ − aₙ = d.
- nth term: aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d, and aₙ = aₘ + (n − m)d.
- Sum: Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2 = na₁ + n(n − 1)d/2.
- Arithmetic mean: if a, b, c are in arithmetic sequence then 2b = a + c.
- If m + n = p + q then aₘ + aₙ = aₚ + a_q. In particular a₁ + aₙ = a₂ + aₙ₋₁ = …
- For odd n, Sₙ = n · (middle term). For example S₉ = 9a₅.
- Sₙ, S₂ₙ − Sₙ, S₃ₙ − S₂ₙ also form an arithmetic sequence (common difference n²d).
- Sₙ has the form An² + Bn (no constant term). aₙ has the form pn + q.
> Example: a₃ = 7 and a₇ = 19. Find a₁₀ and S₁₀.
> Example: a₂ + a₈ = 10. Find S₉.
> Example: a₁ = 25, d = −4. For which n is Sₙ largest?
> aₙ = 29 − 4n > 0 for n ≤ 7 (a₇ = 1, a₈ = −3). Sₙ is largest when all positive terms are included: n = 7, S₇ = 7(25 + 1)/2 = 91.
! Trick for maximum Sₙ: find where aₙ changes sign. If some term equals exactly 0, two consecutive n give the same maximum.
## Geometric sequences
- Each term multiplies by a constant ratio q ≠ 0: aₙ₊₁/aₙ = q. No term can be 0.
- nth term: aₙ = a₁qⁿ⁻¹, and aₙ = aₘqⁿ⁻ᵐ.
- Sum: if q ≠ 1, Sₙ = a₁(1 − qⁿ)/(1 − q) = (a₁ − aₙq)/(1 − q). If q = 1, Sₙ = na₁.
- Geometric mean: if a, b, c are in geometric sequence then b² = ac (and b ≠ 0).
- If m + n = p + q then aₘaₙ = aₚa_q.
- Sₙ, S₂ₙ − Sₙ, S₃ₙ − S₂ₙ form a geometric sequence (ratio qⁿ), provided none of them is 0.
> Example: a₂ = 6 and a₅ = 48. Find q and S₅.
> Example: In a positive geometric sequence a₃a₇ = 64. Find a₅.
> a₅² = a₃a₇ = 64 and a₅ > 0, so a₅ = 8.
> Example: The geometric mean of 2 and 8 is…
> b² = 16, so b = 4 or b = −4. Both are correct unless the question says the terms are positive.
! Trap: when the ratio is unknown, do not use the q ≠ 1 sum formula without checking whether q = 1 is possible.

! Trap: in a geometric sequence, terms with indices of the same parity have the same sign (a₁, a₃, a₅ … all share the sign of a₁), because q² > 0. So if a₃a₇ = 64, a₅ = ±8 in general, but a₅ has the same sign as a₃.
## Infinite geometric series
- If |q| < 1, the sum of all terms is S = a₁/(1 − q). If |q| ≥ 1 the infinite sum does not exist (except the trivial zero case).
> Example: Find 6 + 2 + 2/3 + 2/9 + …
> Example: Write 0.4545… (repeating 45) as a fraction.
> Example: An infinite geometric series has sum 4 and first term 3. Find q.
## Mixed and special sums
- Grouping: split a sum into an arithmetic part and a geometric part. For example the sum of (2k + 2ᵏ) for k = 1 to n is n(n + 1) + 2ⁿ⁺¹ − 2.
- Pairing: alternating sums like 1 − 2 + 3 − 4 + … are easiest by grouping in pairs.
> 50 pairs, each equal to −1. Sum = −50.
## Telescoping (splitting fractions)
- After splitting, most terms cancel and only the first and last few remain.
> Example: Find the sum of 1/((2k − 1)(2k + 1)) for k = 1 to n.
> Each term is √(k + 1) − √k. Sum = √9 − √1 = 2.
! Trap: with 1/(n(n + 2)) type fractions, two terms survive at each end. Write out the first three and last three before cancelling.
## Arithmetic-geometric sums (shift and subtract)
- For a sum like Σ k·2ᵏ, write Tₙ, then 2Tₙ shifted one place, and subtract: the middle becomes a geometric sum.
> Example: Tₙ = 1·2 + 2·2² + … + n·2ⁿ.
> 2Tₙ = 1·2² + … + (n − 1)·2ⁿ + n·2ⁿ⁺¹. Subtract: Tₙ − 2Tₙ = 2 + 2² + … + 2ⁿ − n·2ⁿ⁺¹ = 2ⁿ⁺¹ − 2 − n·2ⁿ⁺¹. So Tₙ = (n − 1)2ⁿ⁺¹ + 2.
! Exam trick: check any formula for Sₙ by plugging in n = 1 and n = 2. In a multiple-choice question this often eliminates three options at once.
## Common recursion types
- aₙ₊₁ = aₙ + f(n): add up (aₙ = a₁ + sum of f(1) … f(n − 1)).
- aₙ₊₁ = aₙ · f(n): multiply up.
- aₙ₊₁ = paₙ + r (p ≠ 1): add a constant c to both sides so that aₙ₊₁ + c = p(aₙ + c), with c = r/(p − 1). Then aₙ + c is geometric.
> Example: a₁ = 1, aₙ₊₁ = 2aₙ + 1. Find aₙ.
> aₙ₊₁ + 1 = 2(aₙ + 1), and a₁ + 1 = 2. So aₙ + 1 = 2ⁿ and aₙ = 2ⁿ − 1.

title: Sets and Inequalities
lines: This topic gives quick, reliable marks if you are careful with endpoints and signs. Most questions combine a set with an inequality: solve the inequality, then intersect or unite the answer sets.
## Sets and notation
- A set is a collection of distinct objects called elements. a ∈ A means a belongs to A; a ∉ A means it does not.
- Common number sets: N (natural numbers, in China N includes 0), N* or N⁺ (positive integers), Z (integers), Q (rationals), R (reals).
- Describe a set by listing, {1, 2, 3}, or by a rule, {x | x² < 4} = {x | −2 < x < 2}.
- The empty set ∅ has no elements and is a subset of every set.
- A ⊆ B means every element of A is in B. A ⊊ B (proper subset) means A ⊆ B and A ≠ B.
- A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets and 2ⁿ − 1 proper subsets.
> Example: How many proper subsets does {x ∈ N | x < 3} have?
> The set is {0, 1, 2}, so n = 3. Proper subsets: 2³ − 1 = 7.
! Trap: in Chinese papers N contains 0. If the question writes N* or N⁺, 0 is excluded.
## Union, intersection and complement
- A ∩ B: elements in both. A ∪ B: elements in at least one.
- Complement of A in the universal set U: ∁U A = {x ∈ U | x ∉ A}.
- De Morgan: ∁(A ∪ B) = ∁A ∩ ∁B and ∁(A ∩ B) = ∁A ∪ ∁B.
- A ∩ B = A is the same statement as A ⊆ B; A ∪ B = B is also the same as A ⊆ B.
- For interval sets, draw a number line and shade. Watch open (<) and closed (≤) ends.
> Example: U = R, A = {x | x ≥ 1}, B = {x | −1 < x < 3}. Find A ∩ (∁U B).
> ∁U B = {x | x ≤ −1 or x ≥ 3}. Intersect with x ≥ 1: the answer is {x | x ≥ 3}.
! Trap: if a question says A ⊆ B with A depending on a parameter, always test the case A = ∅ first. It is easy to forget and often gives extra parameter values.
## Venn diagrams and counting
- For three sets: |A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A| + |B| + |C| − |A∩B| − |B∩C| − |A∩C| + |A∩B∩C|.
> Example: In a class of 40, 25 study French, 18 study Arabic and 7 study neither. How many study both?
## Conditions and quantifiers
- "p ⇒ q" means: if p is true then q must be true. Then p is a sufficient condition for q, and q is a necessary condition for p.
- If p ⇒ q and q ⇒ p, then p is a necessary and sufficient condition (p ⇔ q).
- Set view: if p corresponds to set P and q to set Q, then p is sufficient for q exactly when P ⊆ Q. The smaller set is the sufficient one.
- Universal statement: "for all x, p(x)". Its negation: "there exists x such that not p(x)".
- Existential statement: "there exists x, p(x)". Its negation: "for all x, not p(x)".
> Example: Is "x > 2" sufficient, necessary, both or neither for "x² > 4"?
> x > 2 gives x² > 4, so it is sufficient. But x = −3 gives x² > 4 without x > 2, so it is not necessary. Answer: sufficient but not necessary.
> Example: Negate "for every real x, x² + 1 > 0".
> "There exists a real x such that x² + 1 ≤ 0." The quantifier changes and > becomes ≤.
! Trap: when negating, change the quantifier and negate the conclusion, but leave the condition on x unchanged. Do not negate "x ∈ R" itself.
## Properties of inequalities
- If a > b then a + c > b + c for any c.
- If a > b and c > 0 then ac > bc; if c < 0 then ac < bc (the sign flips).
- If a > b > 0 then aⁿ > bⁿ and 1/a < 1/b.
- You may add inequalities in the same direction, but you may not subtract them.
- If a > b > 0 and c > d > 0 then ac > bd.
> Example: Which must be true if a < b < 0? (i) a² > b² (ii) 1/a < 1/b (iii) ab > b².
> Take a = −2, b = −1. (i) 4 > 1 true. (ii) −1/2 < −1 false. (iii) 2 > 1 true. So (i) and (iii).
! Quick trick: test a statement with small concrete numbers that satisfy the conditions. One counterexample kills a choice.
## Linear and quadratic inequalities
- Linear: ax > b. Divide by a, and flip the sign if a < 0.
- Quadratic ax² + bx + c > 0 with a > 0 and roots x₁ < x₂: the solution is x < x₁ or x > x₂ ("outside the roots").
- ax² + bx + c < 0 with a > 0: x₁ < x < x₂ ("between the roots").
- If the discriminant Δ = b² − 4ac < 0 and a > 0, the quadratic is positive for every real x.
- If a < 0, multiply by −1 first so the leading coefficient is positive.
> Example: Solve −x² + x + 6 ≥ 0.
> Multiply by −1: x² − x − 6 ≤ 0, i.e. (x − 3)(x + 2) ≤ 0. Between the roots: −2 ≤ x ≤ 3.
> Example: For which k is x² + kx + 4 > 0 for all real x?
> Need Δ = k² − 16 < 0, so −4 < k < 4.
! Link: the solution set of ax² + bx + c > 0 tells you the roots. If the solution is −1 < x < 2, then a < 0 and the roots are −1 and 2 (Vieta: −b/a = 1, c/a = −2).
## Rational (fractional) inequalities
- Move everything to one side and combine into a single fraction f(x)/g(x) > 0.
- f/g > 0 is equivalent to f·g > 0. f/g ≥ 0 is equivalent to f·g ≥ 0 together with g ≠ 0.
- Never multiply both sides by an expression whose sign you do not know.
> Example: Solve (x − 1)/(x + 2) ≤ 0.
> Equivalent to (x − 1)(x + 2) ≤ 0 with x ≠ −2. So −2 < x ≤ 1.
> Example: Solve 1/x < 1.
! Trap: the denominator's zero is always an open endpoint, even when the inequality is ≤ or ≥.

! Sign-chart trick: mark all zeros of numerator and denominator on a line. Start at the far right with the sign of the leading term (positive if all factors look like x − a) and alternate at each simple root.
## Absolute-value inequalities
- |x| > a (a > 0) ⇔ x < −a or x > a.
- |x − m| is the distance from x to m on the number line.
- For |x − a| + |x − b|, the minimum value is |a − b|, reached for x between a and b.
> Example: Solve |2x − 3| ≤ 5.
> Example: What is the minimum of |x + 1| + |x − 4|?
> Distance to −1 plus distance to 4 is smallest between them: 4 − (−1) = 5.
! Trap: |x| < a with a ≤ 0 has no solution, and |x| > a with a < 0 holds for all real x.
## AM-GM for maxima and minima
- For a, b > 0: (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab), with equality only when a = b.
- Fixed product ab = P: the sum a + b is at least 2√P. Fixed sum a + b = S: the product ab is at most S²/4.
- Three conditions must hold: both terms positive, the sum or product is constant, and equality can actually happen.
> Example: For x > 0, find the minimum of x + 9/x.
> x + 9/x ≥ 2√(x · 9/x) = 2·3 = 6, with equality when x = 9/x, i.e. x = 3. Minimum 6.
> Example: x > 0, y > 0 and x + 2y = 8. Find the maximum of xy.
> x · 2y ≤ ((x + 2y)/2)² = 16, so xy ≤ 8, with equality at x = 2y = 4 (x = 4, y = 2). Maximum 8.
> Example: x > 1. Find the minimum of x + 1/(x − 1).
> Write it as (x − 1) + 1/(x − 1) + 1 ≥ 2 + 1 = 3, with equality at x − 1 = 1, x = 2. Minimum 3.
! Trap: x + 1/x ≥ 2 only for x > 0. For x < 0, x + 1/x ≤ −2.

! Trap: if equality needs a value outside the allowed domain (for example x + 4/x on x ≥ 3), AM-GM gives a bound that is never reached. Then use monotonicity instead: x + 4/x is increasing for x ≥ 2, so the minimum on x ≥ 3 is 3 + 4/3 = 13/3.
## Quick checklist
- Shade intervals on a number line before combining sets.
- Check endpoints one by one: included, excluded, or a denominator zero.
- Flip the inequality sign whenever you multiply or divide by a negative.
- For "for all x" quadratic conditions, check both the leading coefficient and Δ, and the case a = 0 if the leading coefficient contains a parameter.

title: Solid Geometry
lines: Solid geometry on the CSCA is mostly formula work (areas and volumes), a few true-or-false statements about lines and planes, and coordinate calculations in 3-D. Draw a quick sketch and label every length you know.
## Prisms and pyramids
- Prism: two congruent parallel bases joined by parallelogram faces. Volume V = Sh (S = base area, h = height).
- Cuboid a × b × c: V = abc, surface area 2(ab + bc + ca), space diagonal √(a² + b² + c²). Cube of edge a: diagonal a√3.
- Pyramid: V = ⅓Sh. A regular pyramid has a regular-polygon base and its apex above the base's centre.
- Frustum (cut pyramid or cone): V = ⅓h(S + √(SS′) + S′), with S, S′ the two base areas.
- Surface area = sum of the areas of all faces.
> Example: A regular square pyramid has base edge 6 and height 4. Find its volume and lateral surface area.
> V = ⅓ · 36 · 4 = 48. Slant height of a face (apex to midpoint of a base edge) = √(4² + 3²) = 5. Each triangular face has area ½ · 6 · 5 = 15, so the lateral area is 60.
> Example: A cube has edge 2. Find the length of its space diagonal.
! Trap: the slant height of a face is not the height of the pyramid, and not the lateral edge. In the example the lateral edge is √(4² + (3√2)²) = √34.
! Trap: a pyramid's volume has the factor ⅓. A prism with the same base and height has three times the volume.
## Cylinders, cones and spheres
- Cylinder (radius r, height h): V = πr²h; lateral area 2πrh; total area 2πr² + 2πrh.
- Cone (radius r, height h, slant height l = √(r² + h²)): V = ⅓πr²h; lateral area πrl; total area πr² + πrl.
- Unrolled cone: a sector with radius l and arc length 2πr. Its central angle is 2πr/l (radians).
- Sphere (radius R): V = (4/3)πR³; surface area 4πR².
- Cross-section of a sphere at distance d from the centre: a circle of radius √(R² − d²).
> Example: A cone has radius 3 and height 4. Find its volume and lateral area.
> l = 5. V = ⅓π · 9 · 4 = 12π. Lateral area π · 3 · 5 = 15π.
> Example: The lateral surface of a cone unrolls into a semicircle of radius 4. Find the cone's base radius.
> Arc length = half of 2π·4 = 4π = 2πr, so r = 2.
> Example: A sphere's surface area is 36π. Find its volume.
> Example: A plane at distance 1 from the centre of a sphere of radius 2 cuts it. Find the area of the cross-section.
> r² = 4 − 1 = 3, area 3π.
! Scaling rule: if all lengths are multiplied by k, areas are multiplied by k² and volumes by k³. Doubling a sphere's radius multiplies its volume by 8.
## Inscribed and circumscribed spheres
- A cuboid's vertices lie on a sphere whose diameter is the space diagonal: 2R = √(a² + b² + c²).
- For a cube of edge a: circumscribed sphere R = (√3/2)a; inscribed sphere r = a/2; sphere touching all edges r = (√2/2)a.
- For a regular tetrahedron of edge a: height (√6/3)a, volume (√2/12)a³.
> Example: A cuboid 1 × 2 × 2 has all vertices on a sphere. Find the sphere's surface area.
! Trick: if three edges at one vertex are mutually perpendicular (for example PA, PB, PC in a "corner" tetrahedron), complete the cuboid. Its circumscribed sphere is the same.
## Lines and planes in space
- Two lines in space are parallel, intersecting, or skew (not parallel and not meeting, so not in one plane).
- Line parallel to plane: if a line outside a plane is parallel to some line in the plane, it is parallel to the plane.
- Plane parallel to plane: if two intersecting lines in one plane are each parallel to the other plane, the planes are parallel.
- If a plane meets two parallel planes, the two lines of intersection are parallel.
- Line perpendicular to plane: a line perpendicular to two intersecting lines in a plane is perpendicular to the plane. Then it is perpendicular to every line in that plane.
- Two lines perpendicular to the same plane are parallel.
- Planes perpendicular: if a plane contains a line perpendicular to another plane, the two planes are perpendicular.
- Three-perpendiculars idea: if PO ⊥ plane α and a line in α is perpendicular to the projection OA, it is perpendicular to PA as well.

> Example: Which is true? (i) Two lines parallel to the same plane are parallel. (ii) Two lines perpendicular to the same plane are parallel. (iii) Two planes perpendicular to the same plane are parallel.
> (i) false: they may intersect or be skew. (ii) true. (iii) false: two walls of a room are both perpendicular to the floor but meet in a corner. Answer: (ii) only.
! Trick: test space statements in a classroom or a cube. Floor, walls, edges and diagonals give counterexamples quickly.
! Trap: "perpendicular to two lines in the plane" is not enough if the two lines are parallel; they must intersect.
## 3-D rectangular coordinates
- A point is P(x, y, z). Points on the x-axis look like (a, 0, 0); points in the xOy plane look like (a, b, 0).
- Distance: |AB| = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²).
- Midpoint: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2, (z₁ + z₂)/2).
- Symmetric points of (x, y, z): about the origin (−x, −y, −z); about the xOy plane (x, y, −z); about the z-axis (−x, −y, z).
- Vectors in space work like plane vectors with a third coordinate: a·b = x₁x₂ + y₁y₂ + z₁z₂.
> Example: A(1, 2, −1) and B(3, 0, 1). Find |AB| and the midpoint.
> Example: Find the point symmetric to (2, −3, 4) about the xOy plane.
! Trap: reflecting about an axis keeps that axis's coordinate and changes the other two; reflecting about a plane changes only the coordinate not in the plane.
## Simple angles in solids
- Angle between skew lines: move one line parallel until they meet; the angle is in (0, π/2]. With vectors: cos θ = |a·b|/(|a||b|).
- Angle between a line and a plane: the angle between the line and its projection on the plane, in [0, π/2].
- Dihedral angle: the angle between two lines, one in each plane, both perpendicular to the common edge at the same point.
> Example: In the unit cube ABCD-A₁B₁C₁D₁ (A₁ above A, and so on), find the angle between the skew lines A₁B and AD₁.
> Example: In the same unit cube, find the angle between the diagonal AC₁ and the base ABCD.
> The projection of AC₁ on the base is AC = √2, and CC₁ = 1. tan θ = 1/√2 = √2/2, so sin θ = 1/√3 = √3/3.
! Trap: the angle between two lines is never obtuse. If the dot product is negative, take the absolute value.
! Trick: in a cube, the face diagonals A₁B, BC₁ and A₁C₁ form an equilateral triangle, so any two of them meet at 60°.

title: Trigonometry
lines: Trigonometry questions reward memory: if you know the special values, the identities and the shape of y = A sin(ωx + φ), most items take under a minute.
## Radians and arc length
- Arc length l = rθ and sector area S = ½r²θ = ½lr (θ in radians).
> Example: A sector has radius 4 and central angle 3π/4. Find its arc length and area.
! Trap: arc and sector formulas only work with θ in radians. Convert degrees first.
## Unit-circle definitions and signs
- For the point P(x, y) where the terminal side of angle α meets the unit circle: sin α = y, cos α = x, tan α = y/x (x ≠ 0).
- For any point (x, y) on the terminal side at distance r = √(x² + y²): sin α = y/r, cos α = x/r, tan α = y/x.
- Signs: Quadrant I all positive; II sin positive; III tan positive; IV cos positive.
> Example: The terminal side of α passes through (−3, 4). Find sin α and cos α.
## Special angle values
- cos runs the same list backwards: cos 0 = 1, cos π/6 = √3/2, cos π/4 = √2/2, cos π/3 = 1/2, cos π/2 = 0.
- tan π/6 = √3/3, tan π/4 = 1, tan π/3 = √3; tan π/2 is undefined.
## Basic identities
- sin²α + cos²α = 1 and tan α = sin α / cos α.
- 1 + tan²α = 1/cos²α.
> Example: sin α = 3/5 and α is in Quadrant II. Find cos α and tan α.
> cos²α = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25. In Quadrant II cos is negative: cos α = −4/5. tan α = −3/4.
> Example: tan α = 2. Find (sin α + cos α)/(sin α − cos α).
> Divide top and bottom by cos α: (tan α + 1)/(tan α − 1) = 3/1 = 3.
! Trick: for expressions homogeneous in sin and cos, divide by cos α (or by cos²α, using sin²α + cos²α as the denominator for things like sin α cos α).
> Example: tan α = 2. Find sin α cos α.
> sin α cos α / (sin²α + cos²α) = tan α / (tan²α + 1) = 2/5.
## Reduction (induction) formulas
- For angles kπ ± α: the function name stays the same. For π/2 ± α or 3π/2 ± α: sin and cos swap.
- The sign is the sign of the original function in the quadrant where the angle would lie if α were acute.
- Key ones: sin(π − α) = sin α, cos(π − α) = −cos α, sin(π + α) = −sin α, cos(π + α) = −cos α, sin(−α) = −sin α, cos(−α) = cos α, sin(π/2 − α) = cos α, cos(π/2 + α) = −sin α.
> Example: Evaluate sin(7π/6) and cos(−2π/3).
> Example: Evaluate tan(5π/4) + sin(13π/6).
> tan(π + π/4) = tan π/4 = 1. sin(13π/6) = sin(2π + π/6) = 1/2. Total 3/2.
## Sum, difference and double angle
- sin(α ± β) = sin α cos β ± cos α sin β.
- cos(α ± β) = cos α cos β ∓ sin α sin β (note the opposite sign).
- tan(α ± β) = (tan α ± tan β)/(1 ∓ tan α tan β).
- sin 2α = 2 sin α cos α.
- cos 2α = cos²α − sin²α = 2cos²α − 1 = 1 − 2sin²α.
- tan 2α = 2 tan α / (1 − tan²α).
- Power reduction: cos²α = (1 + cos 2α)/2, sin²α = (1 − cos 2α)/2.
- Auxiliary angle: a sin x + b cos x = √(a² + b²) sin(x + φ), where tan φ = b/a; the maximum is √(a² + b²).
> Example: Evaluate sin 75°.
> Example: Evaluate cos 15° cos 45° + sin 15° sin 45°.
> Example: tan α = 1/2, tan β = 1/3, both acute. Find α + β.
> Example: sin α = 1/3. Find cos 2α.
> Example: Maximum of y = sin x + √3 cos x.
> √(1 + 3) = 2, so y = 2 sin(x + π/3) and the maximum is 2.
! Trap: sin 2α is not 2 sin α. And when a question gives sin α only, the sign of cos α depends on the quadrant; read the range of α.
## Graphs of sin, cos and tan
- y = sin x: period 2π, range [−1, 1], odd, maxima at x = π/2 + 2kπ.
- y = cos x: period 2π, range [−1, 1], even, maxima at x = 2kπ.
- y = tan x: period π, range R, odd, undefined at x = π/2 + kπ, increasing on each interval (−π/2 + kπ, π/2 + kπ).
- sin x increases on [−π/2 + 2kπ, π/2 + 2kπ]; cos x decreases on [2kπ, π + 2kπ].
## y = A sin(ωx + φ) + B
- Amplitude |A|; period T = 2π/|ω|; phase shift −φ/ω; vertical shift B; maximum B + |A|, minimum B − |A|.
- For y = A tan(ωx + φ) the period is π/|ω|.
- Symmetry axes are where ωx + φ = π/2 + kπ; symmetry centres are where ωx + φ = kπ.
- To get y = sin(2x + π/3) from y = sin 2x, shift left by π/6 (not π/3), because sin(2x + π/3) = sin 2(x + π/6).
> Example: y = 3 sin(2x − π/6) + 1. Find the period, the maximum and an x where it occurs.
> T = 2π/2 = π. Maximum 3 + 1 = 4 when 2x − π/6 = π/2, i.e. x = π/3.
> Example: Find an increasing interval of y = sin(2x + π/4).
> Example: The graph of y = 2 sin(ωx + φ) (ω > 0, |φ| < π/2) has neighbouring maximum and minimum at x = π/12 and x = 7π/12. Find ω and φ.
> Half a period is 7π/12 − π/12 = π/2, so T = π and ω = 2. At the maximum: 2 · π/12 + φ = π/2, so φ = π/3.
! Trap: when A or ω is negative, the increasing and decreasing intervals swap. Rewrite with positive ω first.
## Solving triangles
- Angle sum: A + B + C = π. Larger side faces larger angle.
- Sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = 2R (R is the circumradius).
- Cosine rule: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, so cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc).
- Area S = ½ab sin C = ½bc sin A = ½ca sin B.
- Use the sine rule for two angles and a side, or two sides and an opposite angle; use the cosine rule for three sides or two sides and the included angle.
> Example: In triangle ABC, a = √3, b = 1, A = π/3. Find B.
> sin B = b sin A / a = (1 · √3/2)/√3 = 1/2. Since b < a, B < A, so B = π/6 (not 5π/6).
> Example: b = 3, c = 5, A = 2π/3. Find a and the area.
> Example: The sides are 3, 5, 7. Find the largest angle.
! Trap (ambiguous case): sin B = k has two solutions in (0, π), B and π − B. Keep π − B only if the angle sum stays below π and the larger side still faces the larger angle.
! Trick: if a question says a cos B = b cos A or similar, use the sine rule to turn sides into sines: sin A cos B − cos A sin B = 0 gives sin(A − B) = 0, so A = B (isosceles).
## Quick checklist
- Read the range of α before taking a square root.
- Convert degrees to radians when a formula needs it.
- For shifts, factor out ω: the shift is the amount added to x, not to ωx.

title: Vectors and Complex Numbers
lines: These two short topics usually give easy marks. Vectors are about coordinates and the dot product; complex numbers are about arithmetic with i and the picture in the complex plane.
## Vectors: basics and addition
- A vector has size and direction; a and AB (written with an arrow in print) are vectors. The zero vector 0 has length 0 and any direction.
- Triangle rule: AB + BC = AC. Parallelogram rule: if ABCD is a parallelogram, AB + AD = AC.
- Subtraction: AB = OB − OA (end minus start).
- Equal vectors have the same length and direction; opposite vectors have the same length and opposite directions.
> Example: In triangle ABC, D is the midpoint of BC. Write AD in terms of AB and AC.
> AD = ½(AB + AC).
> Example: Simplify AB − AC + BD − CD.
> AB − AC = CB, and BD − CD = BD + DC = BC. Sum: CB + BC = 0.
! Trick: turn every subtraction into addition of the reverse vector, then chain heads to tails.
## Scalar multiples and collinearity
- λa has length |λ||a|; same direction if λ > 0, opposite if λ < 0.
- a ∥ b (b ≠ 0) ⇔ a = λb for some real λ.
- Three points A, B, C are collinear ⇔ AB ∥ AC.
- If OP = xOA + yOB with A, B, P collinear, then x + y = 1.
> Example: P divides AB with AP = 2PB. Express OP.
> OP = OA + (2/3)AB = OA + (2/3)(OB − OA) = (1/3)OA + (2/3)OB. Coefficients add to 1 ✓.
## Coordinates
- For a = (x₁, y₁), b = (x₂, y₂): a ± b = (x₁ ± x₂, y₁ ± y₂); λa = (λx₁, λy₁).
- AB = (x_B − x_A, y_B − y_A).
- Length: |a| = √(x₁² + y₁²).
- Parallel: a ∥ b ⇔ x₁y₂ − x₂y₁ = 0.
- Perpendicular: a ⊥ b ⇔ x₁x₂ + y₁y₂ = 0.
> Example: a = (1, 2), b = (x, −4). Find x if a ∥ b, and if a ⊥ b.
> Parallel: 1·(−4) − 2x = 0, x = −2. Perpendicular: x − 8 = 0, x = 8.
! Trap: the parallel test is a cross product (x₁y₂ − x₂y₁); the perpendicular test is a dot product (x₁x₂ + y₁y₂). Swapping them is the most common error.
## Dot product, angle and length
- a·b = |a||b|cos θ, where θ ∈ [0, π] is the angle between them.
- In coordinates a·b = x₁x₂ + y₁y₂.
- cos θ = a·b / (|a||b|).
- Projection (scalar) of a onto b: |a|cos θ = a·b / |b|.
- a·b > 0 means θ is acute or 0; a·b < 0 means θ is obtuse or π.
> Example: a = (1, 1), b = (0, 2). Find the angle between a and b.
> Example: |a| = 2, |b| = 3, the angle between them is π/3. Find |a − b|.
> Example: |a| = 1, |b| = 2 and (a + b) ⊥ a. Find the angle between a and b.
> Example: In an equilateral triangle ABC with side 2, find AB·BC.
> The angle between AB and BC (placed tail to tail) is π − π/3 = 2π/3. AB·BC = 2·2·(−½) = −2.
! Trap: the angle between two vectors is measured with both starting at the same point. For AB and BC in a triangle it is π − B, not B.
! Trap: "the angle is acute" needs a·b > 0 and the vectors not in the same direction (exclude the parallel case).
> Example: a = (1, 2), b = (1, λ). For which λ is the angle between them acute?
> a·b = 1 + 2λ > 0 gives λ > −1/2. Same direction when λ = 2. So λ > −1/2 and λ ≠ 2.
## Complex numbers: i and algebraic form
- i² = −1. Powers repeat with period 4: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1.
- z = a + bi (a, b real): a is the real part, b is the imaginary part (b, not bi).
- z is real if b = 0; purely imaginary if a = 0 and b ≠ 0.
- a + bi = c + di ⇔ a = c and b = d.
> Example: Find i²⁰²⁶ and i + i² + i³ + i⁴.
> 2026 = 4·506 + 2, so i²⁰²⁶ = i² = −1. The four consecutive powers sum to i − 1 − i + 1 = 0.
> Example: (m² − m) + (m − 1)i is purely imaginary. Find m.
> m² − m = 0 gives m = 0 or 1, and m − 1 ≠ 0 rules out m = 1. So m = 0.
! Trap: for "purely imaginary", do not forget the condition that the imaginary part is non-zero.
## Arithmetic
- Add and subtract part by part. Multiply like brackets and replace i² with −1.
- Divide by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator: (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b².
> Example: Compute (2 + i)(1 − 3i).
> Example: Compute (3 + i)/(1 − i).
> Example: z(1 + i) = 2i. Find z.
> Example: Compute (1 + i)⁸.
## Conjugate and modulus
- The conjugate of z = a + bi is z̄ = a − bi (reflection in the real axis).
- z + z̄ = 2a and z·z̄ = a² + b² = |z|².
- |z| = √(a² + b²). Also |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂| and |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂|.
> Example: z = (1 + 2i)/i. Find z̄ and |z|.
> Example: Find |(3 − 4i)/(1 + i)|.
! Trick: for a modulus, never simplify the fraction first. Use |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂|.
## The complex plane
- z = a + bi is the point Z(a, b), or the vector OZ. The x-axis is the real axis; the y-axis is the imaginary axis (the origin is real, not imaginary).
- |z| is the distance from O to Z; |z₁ − z₂| is the distance between the points z₁ and z₂.
- |z − z₀| = r describes a circle with centre z₀ and radius r.
- Adding complex numbers matches adding vectors.
> Example: In which quadrant is the point for z = i(2 − i)?
> z = 2i − i² = 1 + 2i, the point (1, 2): first quadrant.
> Example: |z − 1| = 1. Find the maximum of |z − 4i|.
> z lies on the circle centre (1, 0), radius 1. The distance from (1, 0) to (0, 4) is √17. Maximum √17 + 1.
> Example: z₁ = 1 + 2i, z₂ = 3 − i. Find the distance between their points.
! Trap: the imaginary part of 3 − 4i is −4, not −4i, and not 4.

title: DC Circuits
lines: Circuit questions are mostly arithmetic with resistors, so practise combining resistances quickly and always ask whether the battery has internal resistance. A neat redrawn circuit solves half the problem.
## Current
- Current I = q/t, the charge passing a cross-section per second. Unit: ampere (1 A = 1 C/s).

- Conventional current flows from + to − outside the source; in metals the electrons actually drift the other way. The drift speed of electrons is very slow (fractions of a mm per second); the field that pushes them sets up almost instantly.
- Microscopic form: I = nqSv (n = carriers per m³, S = cross-section area, v = drift speed).
> Example: A current of 2 A flows for 5 s. How much charge passes, and how many electrons?
> q = It = 10 C. Number = 10/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.25 × 10¹⁹ electrons.
## Resistance, resistivity and Ohm's law
- Resistance R = U/I, unit ohm (Ω). Ohm's law: for a metal at constant temperature, I is proportional to U.
- On an I-U graph a straight line through the origin is ohmic; its gradient is 1/R. A filament lamp's graph bends towards the U axis because its resistance rises as it heats up.
- Resistivity: R = ρL/S. ρ (Ω·m) depends on the material and temperature, not on the shape. For metals ρ rises with temperature.
> Example: A wire of resistance 4 Ω is stretched uniformly to twice its length. Find its new resistance.
> The volume is unchanged, so doubling L halves S. R = ρL/S becomes 2 × 2 = 4 times larger: 16 Ω.
! Trap: cutting a wire in half and putting the halves side by side gives one quarter of the resistance, not one half.
## Series and parallel
- Series: same current; R = R₁ + R₂ + ...; voltages divide in proportion to resistance: U₁ : U₂ = R₁ : R₂.
- Parallel: same voltage; 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...; for two resistors R = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂); currents divide in inverse proportion: I₁ : I₂ = R₂ : R₁.
- n equal resistors R in parallel give R/n. The parallel total is always smaller than the smallest branch.
> Example: A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor are in parallel, and this pair is in series with a 4 Ω resistor across an ideal 12 V supply. Find the current in each resistor.
> Parallel pair = 18/9 = 2 Ω; total = 6 Ω; main current = 12/6 = 2 A, which flows through the 4 Ω resistor. Voltage across the pair = 2 × 2 = 4 V, so 4/6 = 2/3 A in the 6 Ω and 4/3 A in the 3 Ω.
! Trick: points joined by a plain wire (or an ideal ammeter) are at the same potential; merge them when redrawing. An ideal voltmeter can be removed from the circuit for the current calculation.
## EMF and internal resistance
- The EMF E of a source is the energy it supplies per coulomb (V). A real source has internal resistance r.
- Closed-circuit law: I = E/(R + r). Terminal voltage U = E − Ir. With the circuit open, U = E. Short circuit: I = E/r (dangerous, large).
- The U-I graph of a source is a straight line falling to the right: the U-intercept is E, and the size of the gradient is r.
- Power delivered to the external resistor is greatest when R = r, and then P(max) = E²/(4r). The efficiency at that point is only 50 %.
> Example: A battery with E = 6 V and r = 1 Ω is connected to a 5 Ω resistor. Find the current, terminal voltage and short-circuit current.
> Example: Which external resistance takes the most power from this battery, and how much?
! Trap: a larger external resistance gives a larger terminal voltage but a smaller current. More resistance outside means less "lost volts" Ir inside.
## Electrical power and energy
- Power P = UI. For a pure resistor (heater, lamp), P = I²R = U²/R too. Energy W = UIt; heat Q = I²Rt (Joule's law).
- A rating such as "220 V, 100 W" lets you find R = U²/P = 48400/100 = 484 Ω. At a different voltage, keep R fixed and use P = U²/R.
- A motor is not a pure resistor: input power UI, heating I²R (coil resistance), mechanical output UI − I²R. Ohm's law U = IR does not apply to a running motor.
> Example: A "220 V, 100 W" lamp is connected to 110 V. Find its power (assume R constant).
> Half the voltage gives a quarter of the power: 25 W.
> Example: A motor runs on 12 V and draws 2 A; its coil resistance is 1 Ω. Find the heat and mechanical power.
> Input = 24 W. Heat = 2² × 1 = 4 W. Mechanical = 24 − 4 = 20 W.
! Trap: if the motor is jammed (not turning), it becomes a pure resistor: the current jumps to 12/1 = 12 A and the coil may burn out.
## Meters
- An ammeter goes in series and should have very small resistance. A voltmeter goes in parallel and should have very large resistance.
- A sensitive meter (galvanometer) with full-scale current I(g) and resistance R(g) becomes a voltmeter with a large resistor in series, and an ammeter with a small resistor (shunt) in parallel.
- Voltmeter of range U: series resistor = U/I(g) − R(g). Ammeter of range I: shunt = I(g)R(g)/(I − I(g)).
> Example: A meter with I(g) = 1 mA and R(g) = 100 Ω is to read up to 3 V. Find the series resistor.
> Total resistance = 3/0.001 = 3000 Ω, so add 3000 − 100 = 2900 Ω in series.
> Example: A meter with I(g) = 1 mA and R(g) = 99 Ω is to read up to 0.1 A. Find the shunt.
> The shunt carries 0.099 A at the same voltage 0.001 × 99 = 0.099 V, so the shunt is 0.099/0.099 = 1 Ω.
! Trap: a real voltmeter draws some current, so it reads slightly less than the true voltage across a large resistor.
## Changing circuits (dynamic analysis)
- If any one resistor increases, the total external resistance increases, so the main current falls and the terminal voltage rises (with r ≠ 0).
- Quick rule: a component in series with the changed resistor changes in the opposite sense; a component in parallel with it changes in the same sense (its current, voltage and power all follow).

> Example: A battery with internal resistance supplies lamp A in series with a parallel pair: lamp B and a variable resistor. The variable resistance is increased. What happens to the brightness of A and B?
> Total resistance rises, main current falls, so lamp A (in series) dims. The voltage across the parallel part rises, so lamp B (in parallel) brightens.
## Exam checklist
- Redraw the circuit; merge points at equal potential.
- Use I = E/(R + r) whenever r is given; terminal voltage is not E.
- Check whether a device is a pure resistor before using I²R = UI.

title: Circular Motion and Gravitation
lines: Circular motion needs one idea: something must supply a net force towards the centre. Gravitation then becomes a special case where gravity is that force. Take g = 10 m/s² unless a question says otherwise.
## Describing circular motion
- Period T: time for one revolution (s). Frequency f = 1/T (Hz); also given as revolutions per second (r/s) or per minute (rpm).
- Angular velocity ω = Δθ/Δt = 2π/T = 2πf, in rad/s. Linear (tangential) speed v = ωr = 2πr/T.
- In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the velocity is not, because its direction keeps changing. So there is always an acceleration.
- Linked wheels: points on a belt or on touching gear rims share the same linear speed v. Points on the same rigid wheel or axle share the same ω.
> Example: A wheel of radius 0.5 m turns at 2 revolutions per second. Find ω and the rim speed.
> ω = 2πf = 4π rad/s. v = ωr = 4π × 0.5 = 2π m/s (about 6.3 m/s).
> Example: A belt joins pulley A (radius 10 cm) and pulley B (radius 20 cm). Compare their angular velocities.
> Same rim speed, so ω(A) × 10 = ω(B) × 20, giving ω(A) : ω(B) = 2 : 1. The smaller pulley turns faster.
## Centripetal acceleration and force
- Centripetal acceleration a = v²/r = ω²r = 4π²r/T², directed towards the centre.
- Centripetal force F = mv²/r = mω²r. It is not a new kind of force. It is the resultant of real forces (tension, friction, gravity, normal force) along the radius.
- Never draw "centripetal force" as an extra arrow in a free-body diagram.
> Example: A 0.2 kg puck on a smooth table moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m at 3 m/s, held by a string to a fixed pin. Find the tension.
> Example: A coin sits 0.25 m from the centre of a turntable with μ = 0.4. Find the largest ω at which it does not slip.
> Static friction supplies the force: μmg = mω²r, so ω² = μg/r = 4/0.25 = 16 and ω = 4 rad/s. The mass cancels.
! Trap: on a turntable, a coin further out slips first, because the required force mω²r grows with r.
## Vertical circles
- Speed changes around a vertical circle; use energy between points: v(bottom)² = v(top)² + 4gr.
- At the top, with a string (or the inside of a track): T + mg = mv²/r. The string stays tight only if v ≥ √(gr). At this minimum speed gravity alone gives the centripetal force.
- At the bottom: T − mg = mv²/r, so the tension is greatest at the bottom.
- With a rigid rod or a body inside a closed tube, the minimum speed at the top is 0, because the rod can push as well as pull.
> Example: A 0.1 kg ball on a 0.4 m string moves in a vertical circle, just keeping the string tight at the top. Find the speed at the top, and the tension at the bottom.
> Top: v² = gr = 4, v = 2 m/s. Bottom: v² = 4 + 4 × 10 × 0.4 = 20 m²/s². T = mg + mv²/r = 1 + 0.1 × 20/0.4 = 1 + 5 = 6 N, which is 6mg.
- Car over a hump-backed bridge of radius r: mg − N = mv²/r, so N < mg. The car leaves the road when v = √(gr). In a dip, N = mg + mv²/r > mg.
> Example: A car crosses a hump of radius 40 m at 10 m/s. What fraction of its weight is the road's support force?
> N = m(g − v²/r) = m(10 − 2.5) = 7.5m, which is 3/4 of mg.
## Banked curves
- On a smooth bank at angle θ, the normal force alone provides the centripetal force at the design speed: N sin θ = mv²/r and N cos θ = mg, so tan θ = v²/(gr).
- Faster than the design speed, friction acts down the slope; slower, up the slope.
- A conical pendulum works the same way: tan θ = v²/(gr), with θ the angle of the string from the vertical.
> Example: A bend of radius 120 m is banked at 37° (tan 37° = 0.75). Find the speed needed so that no sideways friction is needed.
! Trap: on a flat curve the centripetal force comes only from friction, giving v(max) = √(μgr). On a bank, the normal force helps.
## Newton's law of gravitation
- F = GMm/r², with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² and r the distance between the centres.
- At the Earth's surface, mg = GMm/R², so GM = gR². This substitution ("golden substitution") removes G and M from many questions.
- At a height h above the surface, g' = GM/(R + h)² = g × R²/(R + h)².
> Example: What is the gravitational acceleration at a height equal to the Earth's radius?
> r = 2R, so g' = g/4 = 2.5 m/s². A 600 N astronaut would weigh 150 N there.
! Trap: r is measured from the centre of the planet. Height h above the surface means r = R + h.
## Satellites and orbits
- For a circular orbit, gravity is the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r = mω²r = m4π²r/T².
- Results: v = √(GM/r), ω = √(GM/r³), T = 2π√(r³/GM), a = GM/r².
- Rule: the higher the orbit, the smaller v, ω and a, and the larger T. Only T increases. The satellite's own mass cancels.

- First cosmic velocity (orbit just above the surface): v = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s, the largest orbital speed and the smallest launch speed for orbit. Second cosmic velocity (escape from Earth) ≈ 11.2 km/s.
- A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator with T = 24 h, so its height and speed are fixed.
- Everything inside an orbiting spacecraft is weightless: gravity still acts but is fully used as the centripetal force.
- Finding a planet's mass: if a moon has radius r and period T, M = 4π²r³/(GT²). For an orbit close to the surface, density ρ = 3π/(GT²).
> Example: A satellite orbits at r = 4R. Compare its speed and period with those of a satellite just above the surface.
> v ∝ 1/√r, so v is halved (about 3.95 km/s). T ∝ r^(3/2) = 4^(3/2) = 8, so the period is 8 times longer.
! Trap: to move to a higher orbit a satellite must speed up (fire its engine forward), yet once settled in the higher orbit it moves more slowly.
## Kepler's third law
- For all bodies orbiting the same central body, T²/r³ is the same (for ellipses, use the semi-major axis instead of r).
- Kepler's second law: a planet moves fastest when nearest the Sun.
> Example: A planet's orbit radius is 4 times the Earth's. Find its orbital period.
> T² ∝ r³: T²/1² = 4³ = 64, so T = 8 years.
! Trap: the constant in T²/r³ depends on the central mass. You cannot compare a moon of Jupiter with a moon of the Earth this way.
## Exam checklist
- Find which real forces point along the radius; set their resultant equal to mv²/r.
- In vertical circles, combine energy (between points) with Newton's second law (at a point).
- In gravitation, use GM = gR² and ratios instead of big numbers.

title: Electrostatics
lines: Electrostatics deals with charges at rest and the fields they create. Two quantities run through everything: field strength E (a vector, about force) and potential φ (a scalar, about energy). Keep them separate and most questions become routine. Use k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
## Charge
- Two kinds of charge: like charges repel, unlike charges attract. Unit: coulomb (C).
- Charge is conserved: it can move from one body to another but is never created or destroyed in total.
- Charge is quantised: every charge is a whole-number multiple of the elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
- Charging methods: friction (electrons move from one material to the other), contact (charge is shared), induction (a nearby charge separates the charges in a conductor without touching).
- Two identical conducting spheres that touch end up sharing the total charge equally.
> Example: Identical metal spheres carry +6q and −2q. They touch and are separated. Find each charge.
> Total = +4q, shared equally: each sphere carries +2q.
## Coulomb's law
- F = kq₁q₂/r² between two point charges, along the line joining them. Unit check: N.
- Doubling the distance quarters the force; doubling one charge doubles the force.
> Example: Two charges of 1 × 10⁻⁶ C each are 0.3 m apart. Find the force between them.
> Example: For the spheres above (+6q and −2q at distance r), how does the force change after they touch and are put back at the same distance?
> Before: F = 12kq²/r², attractive. After: (+2q)(+2q) gives 4kq²/r², repulsive. The size is one third of the original.
! Trap: three free charges on a line in equilibrium follow "two like charges outside, the opposite charge in the middle, closer to the smaller outer charge".
## Electric field
