- Field strength E = F/q, the force per unit positive test charge. Unit: N/C, which equals V/m. Its direction is the direction of force on a positive charge.
- The field does not depend on the test charge: put in double the charge and the force doubles, E stays the same.
- Field of a point charge Q: E = kQ/r², pointing away from a positive Q and towards a negative Q.
- Fields add as vectors (superposition). Midway between two equal like charges E = 0; midway between equal unlike charges E is twice that of one charge, pointing towards the negative charge.
> Example: Find the field strength 0.3 m from a point charge of 2 × 10⁻⁸ C.
> E = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁸ / 0.09 = 180/0.09 = 2000 N/C, directed away from the charge.

- Field lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges (or at infinity). They never cross. Closer lines mean a stronger field. Between two parallel oppositely charged plates the lines are parallel and evenly spaced: a uniform field.
- At the surface of a conductor in equilibrium, field lines are perpendicular to the surface; inside the conductor the field is zero.
! Trap: a field line is not the path of a charge in general. A charge released from rest follows a field line only if the line is straight.
## Potential, potential difference and work
- Potential energy of a charge q at a point: E(p) = qφ, where φ is the potential (unit volt, 1 V = 1 J/C). Potential depends on the reference point (usually infinity or the earth).
- Potential difference (voltage) U(AB) = φA − φB. Work done by the field from A to B: W(AB) = qU(AB) = −ΔE(p).
- Potential falls along the direction of the field lines.
- A positive charge moving along the field loses potential energy (the field does positive work). A negative charge moving along the field gains potential energy.
- Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines; moving a charge along one needs no work. Closer equipotentials mean a stronger field.
- In a uniform field: U = Ed, where d is measured along the field direction.
- Energy unit: 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, the energy gained by an electron crossing 1 V.
> Example: A charge of +2 × 10⁻⁶ C moves from A to B with U(AB) = 50 V. Find the work done by the field and the change in potential energy.
> W = qU = 2 × 10⁻⁶ × 50 = 1 × 10⁻⁴ J (positive), so the potential energy decreases by 1 × 10⁻⁴ J.
> Example: Two parallel plates 2 cm apart have 100 V across them. Find E.
! Trap: keep the signs in W = qU. For an electron, q is negative, so moving to a higher potential means the field does positive work on it.
! Trap: zero field does not mean zero potential, and zero potential does not mean zero field.
## Capacitors
- Capacitance C = Q/U, unit farad (F); 1 μF = 10⁻⁶ F. Q is the charge on one plate.
- Parallel-plate capacitor: C is proportional to εᵣS/d (plate area S, separation d, dielectric constant εᵣ). C = εᵣS/(4πkd).
- Two key cases. Still connected to the battery: U stays fixed. Disconnected (isolated): Q stays fixed.
- Field between the plates: E = U/d. With Q fixed, E depends only on Q/S, so changing d does not change E.
- Energy stored: ½QU = ½CU².
> Example: A 2 μF capacitor is connected to a 10 V battery. Find the charge.
> Example: A charged capacitor is disconnected, then its plates are pulled to twice the separation. What happens to C, U and E?
> C halves. Q is fixed, so U = Q/C doubles. E = U/d stays the same. (If it had stayed connected, U would stay fixed, Q would halve and E would halve.)
## Charges moving in uniform fields
- Balance: a charged drop is held at rest when qE = mg.
- Acceleration from rest through a voltage U: qU = ½mv². An electron accelerated through 100 V gains 100 eV of kinetic energy.

- Deflection between plates: a charge entering at speed v₀ parallel to plates of length L and separation d, with voltage U, moves like a projectile. Along the plates: constant speed, t = L/v₀. Across the plates: a = qU/(md), deflection y = ½at² = qUL²/(2mdv₀²).
- A particle accelerated by U₁ and then deflected by U₂ has y = U₂L²/(4dU₁). It does not depend on q or m, so different ions starting from rest follow the same path.
> Example: An oil drop of mass 8 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held still between horizontal plates 2 cm apart with 100 V across them. Find its charge.
> Example: Electrons are accelerated by U₁ = 1000 V, then enter plates of length 8 cm and separation 2 cm with U₂ = 100 V. Find the deflection at the exit.
> y = U₂L²/(4dU₁) = 100 × 0.0064/(4 × 0.02 × 1000) = 0.64/80 = 0.008 m = 8 mm. This is less than half the gap (10 mm), so the electrons get out.
! Trap: for electrons, protons and ions, gravity is negligible next to electric forces. For drops, dust and small balls, include mg.
## Exam checklist
- Force and field: vectors, add with directions. Potential and energy: scalars, add with signs.
- For capacitors, first ask: connected (U fixed) or isolated (Q fixed)?
- For moving charges, energy for speeds, projectile method for deflections.

title: Work, Energy and Power
lines: Energy methods skip the details of the motion and compare only the start and the end. When a question asks for a speed, height or distance and does not ask for time, try energy first. Take g = 10 m/s².
## Work
- Work done by a constant force: W = Fs cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Unit: joule (1 J = 1 N·m). Work is a scalar but can be negative.
- θ < 90°: positive work (the force helps the motion). θ = 90°: zero work. θ > 90°: negative work (the force resists).
- The normal force on a body sliding on a fixed surface and the tension in a pendulum string do no work, because they are perpendicular to the motion. A centripetal force never does work.
- Kinetic friction on a body sliding over a fixed surface always does negative work: W = −fs.
- For a varying force, work is the area under the F-x graph. For a spring stretched from 0 to x, W = ½kx².
- The net work is the sum of the works of all forces, or the work of the resultant force.
> Example: A box is dragged 5 m along a floor by a rope pulling with 20 N at 60° above the horizontal. Find the work done by the rope.
! Trap: work by gravity depends only on the change in height, W = mg(h₁ − h₂), not on the path taken.
## Power
- Average power P = W/t; unit watt (1 W = 1 J/s). Instantaneous power P = Fv cos θ, or P = Fv when force and velocity are in line.
- A vehicle with a fixed engine power P has its maximum speed when the driving force equals the resistance: v(max) = P/f.
- At a lower speed v, the driving force is P/v, larger than f, so the vehicle still accelerates: a = (P/v − f)/m.
> Example: A 1000 kg car has engine power 60 kW and faces a constant resistance of 2000 N. Find its top speed and its acceleration at 20 m/s.
! Trap: a car starting at constant power has decreasing acceleration. A car starting at constant acceleration has increasing power until it reaches the rated power; after that its acceleration falls.
## Kinetic energy and the work-energy theorem
- Kinetic energy Eₖ = ½mv², a scalar, never negative. Doubling the speed multiplies Eₖ by 4.
- Work-energy theorem: the total work done by all forces equals the change in kinetic energy, W(net) = ½mv² − ½mu².
- It works for curved paths and varying forces, and is the fastest route for stopping distances.
> Example: A 2 kg block sliding at 6 m/s on a floor with μ = 0.3 comes to rest. How far does it slide?
> Friction = 0.3 × 20 = 6 N. 6 × s = ½ × 2 × 36 = 36, so s = 6 m. Note the mass cancels: s = v²/(2μg) = 36/6 = 6 m.
! Trick: stopping distance under a constant braking force grows with v². Twice the speed means four times the distance.
## Potential energy
- Gravitational potential energy E(p) = mgh, where h is measured from a chosen reference level. The value depends on the reference level; the change does not.
- Gravity's work equals minus the change in potential energy: W(gravity) = −ΔE(p). Going up, gravity does negative work and E(p) increases.
- Elastic potential energy of a spring: E(p) = ½kx², the same for stretch x and compression x.
> Example: A spring with k = 400 N/m is compressed by 0.1 m and launches a 1 kg block across a smooth floor. Find the block's speed.
! Trap: a body below the reference level has negative potential energy. That is allowed; only differences have physical meaning.
## Conservation of mechanical energy
- If only gravity and spring forces do work (no friction, no air resistance, no other driving force), then Eₖ + E(p) is constant: ½mv₁² + mgh₁ = ½mv₂² + mgh₂.
- Normal forces from fixed smooth surfaces and string tensions do no work, so they do not break conservation.
- Speed at the bottom of a smooth slope or curve from height h: v = √(2gh), whatever the shape and whatever the mass.
- For a system (for example two blocks linked over a pulley) use the total energy of the system: the loss of one body's potential energy is shared out as kinetic energy of both.
> Example: A pendulum bob on a 0.8 m string is released from rest with the string horizontal. Find its speed at the lowest point.
> Example: A 3 kg block on a smooth table is joined by a string over the edge pulley to a 1 kg hanging mass. From rest, the hanging mass falls 0.8 m. Find the speed.
> Energy lost by the hanging mass = 1 × 10 × 0.8 = 8 J = ½ × (3 + 1) × v², so v² = 4 and v = 2 m/s.
! Trap: for a single block, mechanical energy is not conserved if the string is doing work on it. Choose the whole system.
## Energy with friction
- With friction, mechanical energy decreases. Work-energy: initial mechanical energy − energy lost to friction = final mechanical energy.
- The heat produced by sliding friction is Q = f × (relative sliding distance between the two surfaces), not the distance either body moves relative to the ground.
> Example: A 2 kg block slides from rest down a rough curved ramp of height 5 m and reaches the bottom at 8 m/s. Find the work done against friction.
> mgh = 100 J, Eₖ at the bottom = ½ × 2 × 64 = 64 J, so 36 J was turned into heat.
> Example: A 1 kg block is placed on a long board. Sliding friction between them is 4 N and the block slides 1.5 m relative to the board before they move together. Find the heat produced.
> Q = f × relative distance = 4 × 1.5 = 6 J, whatever distances the block and board each move over the ground.
## Efficiency
- Efficiency η = useful output energy ÷ total input energy = useful power ÷ input power, always less than 100 % in real machines.
> Example: A motor with an input power of 500 W lifts a 50 kg load by 6 m at constant speed in 10 s. Find its efficiency.
! Trap: lifting "at constant speed" means the lifting force equals mg, so useful work is just mgh, with no kinetic energy term.
## Exam checklist
- No time asked? Use energy. A collision in the middle? Use momentum there, energy elsewhere.
- List which forces do work; decide whether mechanical energy is conserved.
- Keep signs: friction and resistance do negative work.

title: Forces and Newton's Laws
lines: Forces questions reward one habit above all: draw the body alone, mark every force on it, and only then write equations. Take g = 10 m/s². Force is measured in newtons (1 N = 1 kg·m/s²).
## The common forces
- Gravity (weight): G = mg, acting vertically downward from the centre of gravity. Mass (kg) never changes; weight depends on g.
- Normal (support) force N: pushes perpendicular to the contact surface, away from the surface. It is not always equal to mg; it adjusts to whatever the situation needs.
- Tension T: pulls along a string, away from the body. An ideal light string has the same tension all along, and an ideal pulley only changes the direction of the tension.
- Spring force (Hooke's law): F = kx, where x is the extension or compression from natural length and k is the stiffness in N/m.
- Two identical springs (k each) in series behave like one spring of k/2; side by side (parallel) they behave like 2k.
> Example: A 4 kg mass hangs at rest from a spring with k = 200 N/m. Find the extension.
> kx = mg gives x = 40/200 = 0.2 m = 20 cm.
! Trap: a spring balance pulled by 20 N at each end reads 20 N, not 40 N and not 0.
## Friction
- Kinetic (sliding) friction: f = μN, opposite to the motion of the surface relative to the other surface. μ has no unit.
- Static friction: whatever size is needed to stop slipping, from 0 up to a maximum f(max) = μₛN (usually taken equal to μN if only one μ is given).
- Friction opposes relative motion, not motion itself. The friction on the rear wheel of a bicycle and on your shoe when you walk points forwards.
> Example: A 5 kg box on a floor has μₛ = 0.4 and μₖ = 0.3. Find the friction when it is pushed horizontally with 15 N, and with 30 N.
> N = 50 N, maximum static friction = 0.4 × 50 = 20 N. With 15 N the box stays still and the static friction is 15 N. With 30 N it slides: f = 0.3 × 50 = 15 N and a = (30 − 15)/5 = 3 m/s².
! Trap: never write f = μN for a body that is not sliding. Static friction equals the applied force until the limit is reached.
## Resolving forces and equilibrium
- Any force F can be split into perpendicular components F cos θ and F sin θ, where θ is the angle measured from the first direction.
- Equilibrium (at rest or moving at constant velocity) means the resultant force is zero: ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0.
- Three forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle when drawn head to tail; their lines of action meet at one point.
- Two forces F₁ and F₂ have a resultant between |F₁ − F₂| and F₁ + F₂.
> Example: A 30 N lamp hangs from two ropes, each making 30° with the horizontal ceiling. Find the tension in each rope.
> Vertical balance: 2T sin 30° = 30, so T = 30 N. Each rope carries the full weight even though there are two ropes.
! Trap: the flatter the ropes (smaller angle with the horizontal), the larger the tension. A completely horizontal rope cannot hold up a weight.

! Trick: in a dynamic-equilibrium question where one force keeps its direction and another changes, draw the force triangle and rotate the changing side; the shortest side is perpendicular to the fixed-direction side.
## Newton's three laws
- First law: a body stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless a resultant force acts. Mass is the measure of inertia; speed does not change inertia.
- Second law: F(net) = ma, with a in the direction of the resultant force. The acceleration appears and changes at the same instant as the force.

- Third law: when A pushes B, B pushes A with a force equal in size, opposite in direction, of the same type, acting on a different body. Action-reaction pairs never cancel because they act on different bodies.
> Example: A 2 kg block on a smooth floor is pulled by a horizontal 10 N force. Find its acceleration and its speed after 3 s from rest.
! Trap: weight and the normal force on a book on a table are equal and opposite but are NOT a third-law pair. They act on the same body. The pair of the book's weight is the book's pull on the Earth.
## Inclines
- On a slope of angle θ, resolve along and perpendicular to the slope: the weight gives mg sin θ down the slope and mg cos θ into the slope, so N = mg cos θ (no other perpendicular forces).
- Smooth slope: a = g sin θ, independent of mass.
- Rough slope, sliding down: a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ). Sliding up (projected up): a = g(sin θ + μ cos θ) directed down the slope.
- If μ = tan θ, a block already sliding down keeps a constant speed. A block placed at rest stays at rest whenever μ ≥ tan θ.
> Example: A block slides down a 37° slope with μ = 0.5 (sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8). Find its acceleration.
! Trick: the 37°/53° angles with sin = 0.6 and 0.8 appear constantly. A 3-4-5 triangle gives the same numbers.
## Connected bodies and pulleys
- Whole-system method: if bodies move together, treat them as one mass to find a, then isolate one body to find the internal force (tension or contact force).
- Atwood machine (masses m₁ > m₂ over a light pulley): a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) and T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).
- Block on a smooth table connected to a hanging mass m: a = mg/(M + m). The tension is less than mg while the system accelerates.
> Example: Blocks A (3 kg) and B (2 kg) touch on a smooth floor. A horizontal 10 N force pushes A, which pushes B. Find the force between them.
> Whole system: a = 10/5 = 2 m/s². B alone: contact force = 2 × 2 = 4 N.
> Example: Masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang on either side of a light, smooth pulley. Find a and T.
> a = (3 − 2) × 10/5 = 2 m/s². For the 2 kg mass: T − 20 = 2 × 2, so T = 24 N. Check with the 3 kg mass: 30 − 24 = 3 × 2. Correct.
> Example: A 4 kg block on a smooth table is tied over the edge pulley to a hanging 1 kg mass. Find a and T.
> a = 1 × 10/(4 + 1) = 2 m/s². For the block: T = 4 × 2 = 8 N, less than the 10 N weight of the hanging mass.
! Trap: the internal force depends on which body is pushed. Push B with 10 N instead and the contact force becomes 3 × 2 = 6 N.
## Apparent weight in lifts
- A scale reads the normal force N, not mg. With upward acceleration a: N = m(g + a) (overweight). With downward acceleration a: N = m(g − a) (underweight). In free fall N = 0 (weightless).
- Only the direction of acceleration matters, not the direction of motion. A lift moving up while slowing down has downward acceleration, so the reading is low.
> Example: A 60 kg student stands on a scale in a lift that accelerates upward at 2 m/s². Find the reading. Then repeat for a downward acceleration of 2 m/s².
! Trap: overweight does not mean the gravitational force increased. The weight mg is unchanged; only the support force changes.
## Exam checklist
- Choose the body, draw the free-body diagram, choose axes along the acceleration.
- Static or kinetic friction? Check the maximum before using μN.
- For systems, use whole-body for a and one-body for internal forces.

title: Electromagnetic Induction and AC
lines: Electromagnetic induction is about one cause, a changing magnetic flux, and one result, an induced EMF. Faraday's law gives the size, Lenz's law gives the direction. Alternating current and transformers are applications of the same idea. Take g = 10 m/s².
## Magnetic flux

- Flux through a flat area S in a uniform field B: Φ = BS when B is perpendicular to the area; in general Φ = BS cos θ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal to the area. Unit: weber (1 Wb = 1 T·m²).
- Flux can change because B changes, because the area inside the field changes, or because the angle changes (rotation).
- Flux has a sign depending on which face the field enters. Turning a coil over by 180° in a field changes the flux by 2BS, not 0.
- The number of turns does not affect the flux through the coil; it multiplies the EMF.
> Example: A 0.5 m² loop sits in a 0.2 T field whose direction makes 60° with the normal to the loop. Find the flux.
## Faraday's law
- Induced EMF: E = nΔΦ/Δt, the rate of change of flux linkage. An EMF appears whenever the flux changes, even in an open circuit; a current flows only if the circuit is closed.
- On a Φ-t (or B-t) graph, the EMF is proportional to the gradient, not to the value. Where Φ is largest the EMF may be zero, and where Φ is zero the EMF may be largest.
- Charge passing through a circuit of total resistance R during a flux change: q = nΔΦ/R, independent of how fast the change happens.
> Example: A coil of 100 turns has its flux increased from 0.02 Wb to 0.08 Wb in 0.2 s. Find the average EMF. If the coil's circuit has total resistance 10 Ω, how much charge flows?
! Trap: large flux does not mean large EMF. Only a fast change of flux gives a large EMF.
## Lenz's law

- The induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change of flux that causes it. If the flux increases, the induced field points against the original field; if it decreases, the induced field points the same way.
- Equivalent forms: "come close, get pushed; move away, get pulled"; a loop tends to shrink when the flux through it increases; induced currents oppose relative motion.
- Lenz's law is energy conservation: work must be done against the opposing force to produce the electrical energy.
> Example: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards one face of a coil. Which pole forms on that face, and which way does the current flow as seen from the magnet?
> The coil opposes the approach, so the near face becomes a north pole. By the right-hand grip rule, a north face seen from outside has anticlockwise current.
! Trap: "oppose" does not mean "prevent". The flux still changes, just less steeply than without the induced current.
## Motional EMF
- A straight conductor of length L moving at speed v perpendicular to B: E = BLv. If v makes angle θ with B, use the perpendicular component: E = BLv sin θ.

- Direction: right-hand rule. Field lines enter the palm, the thumb points along the velocity, the fingers give the current direction inside the rod. The end the current flows towards inside the rod is the positive terminal.

- With a closed circuit, current I = BLv/R flows and the rod feels a retarding force F = BIL = B²L²v/R. Pushing at constant speed needs a force equal to this, and the mechanical power Fv equals the electrical power EI.
- A rod falling or sliding under a constant driving force reaches a terminal speed when the magnetic force balances it.
- A rod of length L rotating about one end at angular speed ω: E = ½BωL² (use the average speed of the rod, ωL/2).
> Example: A 0.5 m rod slides at 4 m/s along rails in a 0.2 T field, in a circuit of total resistance 0.4 Ω. Find the EMF, the current, the retarding force and the power needed.
> Example: A horizontal rod of mass 0.01 kg and length 0.2 m falls along vertical smooth rails in a horizontal 0.5 T field; the circuit resistance is 0.1 Ω. Find the terminal speed.
## Self-induction

- A current changing in a coil changes its own flux, so the coil induces an EMF in itself that opposes the change in current: E = LΔI/Δt, where L is the inductance in henry (H). An iron core and more turns give a larger L.
- Switching on: a lamp in series with a large inductor lights up gradually.

- Switching off: a lamp connected in parallel with the coil may flash brighter before going out, but only if the coil's steady current was larger than the lamp's. The coil keeps its current flowing briefly through the lamp, in the reverse direction for the lamp.
> Example: The current in a 0.5 H coil falls from 2 A to 0 in 0.01 s. Find the average self-induced EMF.
> E = 0.5 × 2/0.01 = 100 V, much bigger than a typical supply voltage. This is why switches can spark.
## Alternating current

- A coil of n turns and area S rotating at ω in a uniform field B produces a sinusoidal EMF. Starting from the position where the coil plane is perpendicular to B (the neutral plane): e = E(m) sin ωt, with peak E(m) = nBSω.
- At the neutral plane, flux is greatest but the EMF is zero and the current changes direction (twice per turn). With the coil plane parallel to B, flux is zero and the EMF is greatest.
- Period T = 2π/ω, frequency f = 1/T. Mains in China: 220 V, 50 Hz, so the current reverses direction 100 times per second.

- The rms (effective) value is the steady DC value that gives the same heating in a resistor. For sine waves only: U(rms) = U(m)/√2 and I(rms) = I(m)/√2. Meter readings, ratings and power calculations use rms values.
- The peak of 220 V mains is 220√2 ≈ 311 V; capacitor and insulation ratings must survive the peak.
> Example: A coil with n = 100, B = 0.1 T, S = 0.02 m² rotates at ω = 100 rad/s. Find the peak and rms EMF. If it drives a 10 Ω resistor (ignore coil resistance), find the power.
! Trap: the average EMF over a quarter turn is not the rms value. Use E = nΔΦ/Δt for averages and charge, and rms for heat and power.
## Ideal transformers
- For an ideal transformer: U₁/U₂ = n₁/n₂, I₁/I₂ = n₂/n₁, and input power equals output power, P₁ = P₂.
- The output decides the input: if no load is connected the primary current is (ideally) zero; adding loads increases the primary current.
- A transformer does not work with steady DC, because the flux would not change. It does not change the frequency.
- Power transmission: line loss P(loss) = I²R(line). For a fixed power sent, raising the transmission voltage by a factor of k cuts the current by k and the loss by k².
> Example: A transformer steps 220 V mains down to 11 V for a 22 W lamp. Find the turns ratio and the primary current.
> n₁ : n₂ = 220 : 11 = 20 : 1. Input power = 22 W, so I₁ = 22/220 = 0.1 A (the lamp current is 22/11 = 2 A).
> Example: Power is sent along a line first at 10 kV, then at 100 kV, with the same power delivered. How does the line loss change?
> The current falls to 1/10, so the loss falls to 1/100.
! Trap: if you write the line loss as U²/R(line), U must be the voltage drop along the line itself, not the transmission voltage. Using the transmission voltage gives an absurdly large loss.
## Exam checklist
- Size from E = nΔΦ/Δt or BLv; direction from Lenz or the right-hand rule.
- Energy: work against magnetic forces becomes electrical energy and heat.
- AC: peak for insulation, rms for heating and meters, average for charge.

title: Kinematics
lines: Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. Almost every mechanics question uses these ideas, so learn the five equations of uniform acceleration until you can choose the right one in seconds. Take g = 10 m/s² throughout.
## Displacement, velocity and acceleration
- Distance is the total path length (a scalar). Displacement is the straight-line change in position from start to finish, with a direction (a vector). Unit: metre (m).
- Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. Average velocity = displacement ÷ time. They differ whenever the path bends or reverses.
- Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at one moment; its size is the instantaneous speed.
- Acceleration a = Δv/Δt, unit m/s². It measures how fast velocity changes, not how big velocity is. A body can have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration (top of a vertical throw).
- Sign convention: choose one direction as positive and keep it. A negative acceleration only means "opposite to the chosen positive direction"; it does not always mean slowing down.
> Example: A student walks 3 m east and then 4 m north in 5 s. Find the distance, the displacement and the average velocity.
> Distance = 3 + 4 = 7 m. Displacement = √(3² + 4²) = 5 m, directed north of east. Average velocity = 5/5 = 1 m/s; average speed = 7/5 = 1.4 m/s.
! Trap: a runner who completes one full lap of a track has displacement zero and average velocity zero, but a non-zero average speed.
## Uniform motion and uniformly accelerated motion
- Uniform motion: constant velocity, x = vt.
- Uniformly accelerated (constant a) motion, starting speed v₀:
- v = v₀ + at
- x = v₀t + ½at²
- v² − v₀² = 2ax
- x = (v₀ + v)t/2, so the average velocity equals (v₀ + v)/2 and also equals the velocity at the middle moment of the interval.
- Each equation leaves out one quantity. Pick the one that leaves out what you neither know nor need.
> Example: A car moving at 4 m/s accelerates at 2 m/s² for 3 s. Find its final speed and the distance covered.

! Trap (braking): a car at 20 m/s brakes at 5 m/s². How far does it go in 6 s? It stops after 20/5 = 4 s, so the answer is v²/(2a) = 400/10 = 40 m. Putting t = 6 s into x = v₀t − ½at² gives 30 m, which is wrong because the car does not reverse.
## Useful results for constant acceleration
- In consecutive equal time intervals T, the displacements differ by a constant: Δx = aT². This finds a from tape or photo data quickly.
- Starting from rest, the distances in the 1st, 2nd, 3rd ... equal intervals are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : ...; the total distances after 1, 2, 3 intervals are in the ratio 1 : 4 : 9.
- Velocity at the midpoint of a displacement: √((v₀² + v²)/2). It is always larger than the velocity at the middle moment.
> Example: A trolley covers 2 m in one second and 6 m in the next second. Find its acceleration.
> Δx = aT² gives 6 − 2 = a × 1², so a = 4 m/s².
! Trick: a body that decelerates uniformly to rest can be treated in reverse as starting from rest with the same size of acceleration. Then the 1 : 3 : 5 pattern applies backwards.
## Free fall and vertical throws
- Free fall: released from rest, only gravity acts, a = g downward. v = gt, h = ½gt², v² = 2gh.
- Values to memorise with g = 10: after 1, 2, 3 s the speed is 10, 20, 30 m/s and the fall is 5, 20, 45 m.

- Vertical throw upward at speed v₀: the motion is symmetric. Time to the top = v₀/g, maximum height = v₀²/(2g), total time to return to the launch point = 2v₀/g, and the ball returns with the same speed v₀.
- Throughout the flight the acceleration is g downward, including at the highest point, where only the velocity is zero.
> Example: A stone is dropped from a height of 45 m. Find the time to reach the ground and the landing speed.
> 45 = ½ × 10 × t², so t² = 9 and t = 3 s. v = gt = 30 m/s.
> Example: A ball is thrown straight up at 10 m/s from the top of a 15 m tower. When does it hit the ground?
> Take up as positive: −15 = 10t − 5t², so t² − 2t − 3 = 0, (t − 3)(t + 1) = 0 and t = 3 s.
! Trap: with a sign convention, the whole up-and-down motion is a single equation. Do not split it unless asked about the top point.
## Motion graphs

- x-t graph: the gradient is the velocity. A straight line means uniform motion; a curve means changing velocity. A horizontal line means at rest. Where two lines cross, the bodies are at the same place at the same time (they meet).
- v-t graph: the gradient is the acceleration and the area between the line and the time axis is the displacement. Area below the axis counts as negative displacement.
- On a v-t graph, crossing the time axis means the body reverses direction. A change from rising to falling (a peak) only means the acceleration changed sign; the direction of motion stays the same.
- An x-t graph is not the path of the body. Both graphs describe straight-line motion only.
> Example: A v-t graph is a straight line from 0 at t = 0 to 12 m/s at t = 4 s, then horizontal at 12 m/s up to t = 6 s. Find the acceleration in the first stage and the total displacement.
> a = 12/4 = 3 m/s². Displacement = triangle + rectangle = ½ × 4 × 12 + 2 × 12 = 24 + 24 = 48 m.
! Trap: in a v-t graph where two lines cross, the bodies have the same velocity at that moment, not the same position. Very often that moment is when the gap between them is largest or smallest.
## Projectile motion
- Split the motion into two independent parts. Horizontal: no force, so constant velocity vₓ. Vertical: acceleration g downward.
- Horizontal launch from height h with speed v₀: time t = √(2h/g) depends only on h. Range x = v₀t. At landing the vertical velocity is gt and the speed is √(v₀² + (gt)²).
- Launch at speed v at angle θ above the horizontal on level ground: vₓ = v cos θ, vy = v sin θ. Time of flight = 2v sin θ/g, maximum height = v² sin²θ/(2g), range = v² sin 2θ/g.
- The range is greatest at θ = 45°. Two complementary angles, for example 30° and 60°, give the same range.
- At the highest point the velocity is horizontal (vₓ, not zero) and the acceleration is still g.
> Example: A ball is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from the top of a cliff 20 m high. Find the time, the range and the landing speed.
> t = √(2 × 20/10) = 2 s. Range = 15 × 2 = 30 m. Vertical speed = 10 × 2 = 20 m/s, so the landing speed = √(15² + 20²) = 25 m/s.
> Example: A ball is launched at 20 m/s at 30° above level ground. Find the time of flight, the maximum height and the range.
! Trick: two objects released at the same moment from the same height, one dropped and one thrown horizontally, land together. Horizontal speed never changes the falling time.
! Trap: the angle of the velocity is not the angle of the displacement. For a horizontal launch, tan(velocity angle) = 2 × tan(displacement angle).
## Relative motion basics
- The velocity of A relative to B is v(A rel B) = v(A) − v(B) (vector subtraction). Along one line: same direction, subtract speeds; opposite directions, add speeds.
- A meeting or chase problem becomes easy in the frame of one body: it stands still and the other moves at the relative speed.
- River crossing: the boat's velocity relative to the ground is the vector sum of its velocity relative to the water and the water's velocity.
- Shortest time: point the boat straight across; time = width ÷ boat speed, whatever the current.
- Shortest path (only if boat speed > current speed): point upstream so the resultant is straight across.
> Example: Two trains 1000 m apart move towards each other at 20 m/s and 30 m/s. When do they meet?
> Relative speed = 20 + 30 = 50 m/s, so t = 1000/50 = 20 s.
> Example: A river is 60 m wide and flows at 3 m/s. A boat moves at 5 m/s relative to the water. Find the shortest crossing time, and the time for the shortest path.
> Shortest time: head straight across, t = 60/5 = 12 s (it drifts 3 × 12 = 36 m downstream). Shortest path: the resultant across is √(5² − 3²) = 4 m/s, so t = 60/4 = 15 s.
! Trap: for the shortest time, the current does not change the crossing time; it only changes where the boat lands.
## Exam checklist
- Draw a quick line diagram, mark the positive direction and list v₀, v, a, t, x before choosing an equation.
- Check stopping times in braking questions before using t.
- Learn the patterns: 1 : 3 : 5, 5-20-45 m for free fall, and the 3-4-5 triangle for speeds.

title: Magnetic Fields
lines: Magnetic-field questions test two skills: finding directions with the hand rules, and using F = BIL or F = qvB to get sizes. Practise the hand rules until they are automatic; a wrong direction costs the whole question.
## Magnetic field and field lines

- A magnetic field exists around magnets and around moving charges (currents). Its strength is the magnetic flux density B, unit tesla (T). Its direction at a point is the direction a compass needle's north pole points.
- Field lines: outside a bar magnet they run from N to S, inside the magnet from S to N, so every line is a closed loop. They never cross; closer lines mean a stronger field.
- A uniform field is shown by parallel, equally spaced lines. Inside a long solenoid the field is nearly uniform.
- The Earth behaves like a large bar magnet whose south pole is near the geographic north. Its horizontal component points roughly north.
- Notation for diagrams described in words: "into the page" is drawn as crosses, "out of the page" as dots.
! Trap: magnetic field lines never start or end, unlike electric field lines, which begin on positive and end on negative charges.
## Fields of currents (right-hand grip rule)
- Straight wire: grip the wire with the right thumb along the current; the curled fingers show the direction of the circular field lines. The field gets weaker further from the wire.
- Circular loop or solenoid: curl the right-hand fingers along the current; the thumb points to the north pole end (the direction of the field inside).
- Two parallel wires with currents in the same direction attract; opposite directions repel.
> Example: A long straight wire runs north to south on a table with current flowing north. What is the field direction just above the wire?
> Thumb north, fingers curl: above the wire the field points east (and below the wire, west). So a compass needle held just above the wire swings towards the east.
! Trap: "like currents attract" is the opposite of "like charges repel". Do not mix them up.
## Force on a current-carrying wire
- F = BIL when the wire is perpendicular to B. If the wire makes angle θ with B, F = BIL sin θ. A wire parallel to the field feels no force.

- Direction: the left-hand rule. Stretch the left hand so the field lines enter the palm, the four fingers point along the current, and the thumb gives the force. The force is perpendicular to both B and I.
- A rectangular coil carrying current in a field feels a turning effect; this is how an electric motor works and how a moving-coil meter deflects.
> Example: A 0.5 m wire carrying 2 A lies at right angles to a 0.4 T field. Find the force. What if the wire is turned to lie along the field?
> F = 0.4 × 2 × 0.5 = 0.4 N. Along the field the force is zero.
> Example: A 0.5 m metal rod of mass 0.04 kg hangs horizontally from two light springs in a horizontal 0.4 T field perpendicular to the rod. What current makes the springs carry no load?
> The magnetic force must balance the weight: BIL = mg, so I = 0.4/(0.4 × 0.5) = 2 A, flowing in the direction that gives an upward force.
! Trap: for a bent wire, the effective length is the straight-line distance between its two ends (measured perpendicular to B).
## Lorentz force on moving charges
- A charge q moving at velocity v perpendicular to B feels F = qvB. At angle θ to B: F = qvB sin θ. A charge at rest or moving along B feels no magnetic force.
- Direction: left-hand rule with the four fingers along the velocity of a positive charge. For a negative charge (an electron), the fingers point opposite to its velocity.
- The Lorentz force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it never does work. It changes direction, never speed or kinetic energy.
> Example: A proton (q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 1 × 10⁶ m/s at right angles to a 0.5 T field. Find the force.
## Circular motion in a magnetic field
- A charge entering a uniform field perpendicular to B moves in a circle: qvB = mv²/r.
- Radius r = mv/(qB). Period T = 2πm/(qB), which does not depend on the speed or the radius. Faster particles make bigger circles in the same time.
- Using kinetic energy: r = √(2mEₖ)/(qB). Using an accelerating voltage U: r = (1/B)√(2mU/q).
- Time spent in the field = (θ/360°) × T, where θ is the angle turned through, which equals the angle by which the velocity direction changes.

- Geometry tips: the centre lies on the line perpendicular to the velocity at entry (and at exit). Entering a straight boundary at some angle, the particle leaves at the same angle on the other side of the normal.
> Example: A particle with q/m = 1 × 10⁸ C/kg enters a 0.1 T field at right angles with speed 2 × 10⁶ m/s. Find the radius and period.
> Example: A proton and an alpha particle (mass 4 units, charge 2 units) enter the same field with the same speed. Compare their radii. Then compare them with the same kinetic energy.
> Same speed: r ∝ m/q, proton 1/1, alpha 4/2, so the alpha's radius is twice as large. Same kinetic energy: r ∝ √m/q, proton 1, alpha 2/2 = 1, so the radii are equal.
! Trap: a particle entering perpendicular to a straight boundary and turning through a half circle exits a distance 2r from where it entered, after half a period.
## Combined fields
- Velocity selector: crossed E and B fields let through undeflected only particles with qE = qvB, that is v = E/B, whatever their charge or mass.
- Mass spectrometer: after a velocity selector, ions enter a field B' and land at a distance 2r = 2mv/(qB'), so heavier ions land further away.

- Cyclotron: the particle's period in B does not depend on speed, so a fixed-frequency alternating voltage can accelerate it each half turn. The maximum kinetic energy depends on B and the radius of the device, not on the voltage.
> Example: A selector has E = 2 × 10⁴ V/m and B = 0.1 T. Which speed passes straight through?
! Trap: a particle faster than E/B is pushed towards the magnetic force side; a slower one towards the electric force side.
## Exam checklist
- Right hand for the field a current makes; left hand for the force on a current or a moving charge.
- Electrons: reverse the finger direction.
- In circle problems: find the centre, then the radius from geometry, then use r = mv/(qB).

title: Modern Physics
lines: Modern physics questions are usually short and factual, with simple arithmetic in electronvolts or powers of ten. Learn the key experiments, what each one proved, and the conservation rules for nuclear equations. Use h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
## Photons and photon energy
- Light energy comes in packets called photons. Energy of one photon: E = hf = hc/λ. Higher frequency (shorter wavelength) means more energetic photons.
- Handy shortcut: hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm, so E(in eV) ≈ 1240/λ(in nm). Red light (about 620 nm) has photons of about 2 eV; violet (about 400 nm) about 3.1 eV.
- The brightness (intensity) of light depends on how many photons arrive per second, not on the energy of each.
> Example: Find the energy of a photon of wavelength 6.6 × 10⁻⁷ m, in joules and in eV.
## The photoelectric effect
- Light shining on a metal can eject electrons. Each electron absorbs exactly one photon.
- Einstein's equation: E(k,max) = hf − W₀, where W₀ is the work function of the metal (the minimum energy to free an electron).
- Threshold frequency f₀ = W₀/h. Below f₀ no electrons come out, however bright the light. Above f₀ electrons are emitted almost instantly, even with dim light.
- Brighter light (same frequency) releases more electrons per second (larger saturation current), but does not raise their maximum kinetic energy.
- Stopping voltage U(c): the reverse voltage that just stops the fastest electrons, eU(c) = E(k,max).
- Graph of E(k,max) against f: a straight line with gradient h, crossing the f-axis at f₀. Every metal gives a line with the same gradient.
> Example: Photons of 4.0 eV fall on a metal with work function 2.3 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons and the stopping voltage.
! Trap: doubling the intensity doubles the photocurrent but leaves the stopping voltage unchanged. Only the frequency changes the stopping voltage.
## Wave-particle duality
- Light shows wave behaviour (interference, diffraction) and particle behaviour (photoelectric effect, Compton scattering). Neither picture alone explains everything.
- Matter also has a wave nature: a particle of momentum p has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p. Electron diffraction by crystals confirmed it.
- Photon momentum: p = h/λ.
- Everyday objects have huge momenta, so their wavelengths are far too small to notice.
> Example: An electron has momentum 6.6 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s. Find its de Broglie wavelength.
> λ = h/p = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ / 6.6 × 10⁻²⁴ = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, about the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is why electrons diffract.
! Trap: a faster electron has a shorter de Broglie wavelength, not a longer one.
## The Bohr model and energy levels
- Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment (most alphas pass straight through gold foil, a very few bounce back) showed that an atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
- Bohr's model of hydrogen: the electron can only occupy certain orbits with fixed energies, E(n) = −13.6/n² eV (n = 1, 2, 3 ...). n = 1 is the ground state. Orbit radius r(n) = n²r₁.

- An electron moving from a higher level m to a lower level n emits a photon with hf = E(m) − E(n). Absorbing a photon raises it, but only if the photon's energy exactly matches a gap (or exceeds the ionisation energy).
- Ionisation energy from the ground state is 13.6 eV.
- A collection of atoms in level n can emit n(n − 1)/2 different photon energies as they fall back to the ground state.
- In a higher orbit the electron's kinetic energy is smaller, its potential energy larger, and the total energy larger (less negative).
> Example: Find the photon energy when a hydrogen electron falls from n = 2 to n = 1, and from n = 3 to n = 2.
> E(2) = −3.4 eV, E(1) = −13.6 eV: photon 10.2 eV (ultraviolet). E(3) = −1.51 eV: 3 → 2 gives 3.4 − 1.51 = 1.89 eV (red visible light).
> Example: How many different spectral lines can hydrogen atoms in the n = 4 level emit?
! Trap: a 12 eV photon is not absorbed by ground-state hydrogen, because no gap equals 12 eV. A 12 eV electron, however, can give 10.2 eV to the atom and keep the rest.
## Spectra
- A continuous spectrum (all colours) comes from hot solids and dense hot gases.
- A line emission spectrum (bright lines) comes from hot thin gases. An absorption spectrum (dark lines on a continuous background) appears when white light passes through a cooler gas.
- The lines are at the same wavelengths for emission and absorption of a given element, so spectra identify elements, for example in the Sun and stars.
## Nuclear structure
- A nucleus contains Z protons and N neutrons; the mass number A = Z + N. Notation: element symbol with A at top left and Z at bottom left, written here as ²³⁸₉₂U.
- Isotopes have the same Z (same element, same chemistry) but different N.
- The strong nuclear force holds nucleons together. It is very strong but acts only over about 10⁻¹⁵ m.
## Radioactivity
- Alpha (α): a helium nucleus ⁴₂He, charge +2e. Strongly ionising, stopped by a sheet of paper or a few cm of air. Alpha decay: A decreases by 4, Z by 2.
- Beta (β): a fast electron created when a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton. Stopped by a few mm of aluminium. Beta decay: A unchanged, Z increases by 1.
- Gamma (γ): high-energy electromagnetic radiation, emitted after α or β decay as the nucleus settles. Weakly ionising, very penetrating (thick lead or concrete). A and Z unchanged.
- In electric or magnetic fields α and β bend in opposite directions; γ is not deflected.
> Example: ²³⁸₉₂U decays to ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb. How many α and β decays occur?
> A falls by 32, so there are 32/4 = 8 alpha decays, which lower Z by 16. Z actually falls by 10, so 6 beta decays raised it by 6.
! Trick: count alphas first from the mass number (only alphas change A), then fix Z with betas.
## Half-life
- Half-life T: the time for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. Remaining amount N = N₀(½)^(t/T).
- Half-life is not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical combination. It is a statistical rule for large numbers of nuclei; for a few nuclei it predicts nothing.
> Example: A sample contains 16 g of an isotope with half-life 5 days. How much is left after 15 days?
> 15 days is 3 half-lives: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 g.
! Trap: after two half-lives, one quarter remains, not zero. Three quarters have decayed.
## Nuclear equations
- In every nuclear reaction both the mass number (sum of top numbers) and the charge number (sum of bottom numbers) are conserved.
- Useful particles: proton ¹₁H, neutron ¹₀n, electron ⁰₋₁e, alpha ⁴₂He.
> Example: Balance ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + X. Identify X.
> Top: 14 + 4 = 17 + A, so A = 1. Bottom: 7 + 2 = 8 + Z, so Z = 1. X is a proton, ¹₁H (the reaction in which Rutherford found the proton).
! Trap: mass number is conserved but mass is not. A small mass defect becomes released energy.
## Mass-energy, fission and fusion
- E = mc²; energy released in a reaction ΔE = Δm c². In atomic units, 1 u corresponds to about 931.5 MeV.

- Binding energy is the energy needed to split a nucleus into separate nucleons. Binding energy per nucleon is largest for medium nuclei near iron, so splitting heavy nuclei (fission) and joining light nuclei (fusion) both release energy.

- Fission: a slow neutron splits uranium-235, for example ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n. The released neutrons can cause a chain reaction if the mass exceeds the critical mass. In a reactor, control rods absorb neutrons and a moderator slows them.
- Fusion: for example ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n. It needs extremely high temperatures to overcome the repulsion between nuclei. It powers the Sun and gives more energy per kilogram of fuel than fission.
> Example: A reaction has a mass defect of 1 × 10⁻³⁰ kg. Find the energy released.
> Example: Check the fission equation above.
## Exam checklist
- Photoelectric: frequency decides energy, intensity decides number.
- Energy levels: photon energy must equal a gap exactly.
- Nuclear equations: balance A and Z; count alphas first.

title: Momentum and Impulse
lines: Momentum is the tool for short, violent events: collisions, explosions, recoil and impacts, where forces are large and hard to measure but act for a short time. Always set a positive direction first; most mistakes in this topic are sign mistakes. Take g = 10 m/s².
## Momentum
- Momentum p = mv, a vector in the direction of the velocity. Unit: kg·m/s (the same as N·s).
- Change in momentum Δp = mv − mu is a vector subtraction. For a body that reverses along a line, the sizes add.
- Kinetic energy and momentum are linked: Eₖ = p²/(2m), so p = √(2mEₖ). Two bodies with equal momentum: the lighter one has more kinetic energy.
> Example: A 0.5 kg ball moving at 10 m/s to the right hits a wall and bounces back at 6 m/s. Find the change in momentum.
> Take right as positive: Δp = 0.5 × (−6) − 0.5 × 10 = −8 kg·m/s, that is 8 kg·m/s directed to the left.
! Trap: answering 0.5 × (10 − 6) = 2 kg·m/s forgets that the direction reversed.
## Impulse and the impulse-momentum theorem
- Impulse of a constant force: I = FΔt, unit N·s, in the direction of the force.
- For a varying force, the impulse is the area under the F-t graph.
- Impulse-momentum theorem: the impulse of the resultant force equals the change in momentum, F(net)Δt = Δp.
- For the same change in momentum, a longer contact time means a smaller average force. This is why helmets, airbags, sand pits and bending your knees on landing protect you.
- Gravity's impulse over time t is mgt even when the body is at rest; impulse is not zero just because nothing moves.
> Example: For the ball above, contact with the wall lasts 0.1 s. Find the average force of the wall on the ball.
> F = Δp/Δt = 8/0.1 = 80 N, directed away from the wall.
> Example: A 2 kg ball falls from rest for 3 s. Find the impulse of gravity and its final momentum.
> I = mgt = 2 × 10 × 3 = 60 N·s downward, so p = 60 kg·m/s downward (v = 30 m/s).
! Trap: in a landing problem, the ground's force must also support the weight. If a person's momentum changes by Δp in time Δt during landing, the ground pushes with Δp/Δt + mg, not just Δp/Δt.
## Conservation of momentum
- If the total external force on a system is zero, the total momentum stays constant: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.

- It also holds approximately when internal forces are much larger than external ones for a very short time (collisions, explosions), and along one direction if there is no external force in that direction.
- Friction between two bodies of the system is an internal force; it does not break conservation for the system. Friction from the ground is external.
> Example: A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they stick together. Find their common speed and the kinetic energy lost.
> 2 × 3 = 3v, so v = 2 m/s. Kinetic energy before = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J; after = ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 J; lost 3 J (to heat and sound).
## Elastic and inelastic collisions
- Momentum is conserved in every collision of an isolated system. Kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision.
- Perfectly inelastic: the bodies stick together, giving the largest possible loss of kinetic energy.
- Elastic collision of m₁ moving at v₀ with m₂ at rest:
- v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)v₀/(m₁ + m₂) and v₂ = 2m₁v₀/(m₁ + m₂).

- Equal masses exchange velocities. A light body bouncing off a very heavy one reverses with the same speed. A heavy body hitting a light one at rest keeps going almost unchanged, and the light one leaves at nearly 2v₀.
- In a head-on elastic collision the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach.
> Example: A 1 kg ball at 6 m/s makes an elastic head-on collision with a 2 kg ball at rest. Find both velocities afterwards.
> v₁ = (1 − 2) × 6/3 = −2 m/s (it bounces back). v₂ = 2 × 1 × 6/3 = 4 m/s. Check momentum: 6 = −2 + 8. Check energy: 18 J = 2 J + 16 J.

! Trick: to judge whether a proposed result is possible, test three things: momentum is conserved, total kinetic energy does not increase, and the rear body cannot pass through the front body (its velocity after must not exceed the front body's velocity if both keep moving forward).
## Recoil
- A system initially at rest has zero total momentum, so after firing or pushing apart: m₁v₁ = m₂v₂ in opposite directions. The lighter body moves faster.
- "Person on a boat" problems: since total momentum is zero at every moment, m₁x₁ = m₂x₂ for the distances moved relative to the ground, and x₁ + x₂ equals the length walked relative to the boat.
> Example: A 4 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet at 400 m/s. Find the recoil speed.
> 0.02 × 400 = 4v, so v = 2 m/s, opposite to the bullet.
> Example: A 60 kg person walks from one end to the other of a 3 m long, 120 kg boat at rest on still water. How far does the boat move?
> 60x₁ = 120x₂ and x₁ + x₂ = 3, so x₁ = 2 m and x₂ = 1 m. The boat moves 1 m the opposite way.
! Trap: always use ground-frame velocities in the conservation equation. If a speed is given "relative to the gun" or "relative to the boat", convert it first.
## Explosions
- An explosion conserves momentum but increases kinetic energy, released from chemical or stored energy.
- For a body at rest that splits in two, the pieces move in opposite directions with momenta of equal size.

> Example: A 2 kg shell moving horizontally at 10 m/s at the top of its path explodes into two 1 kg pieces. One piece falls straight down from rest. Find the velocity of the other piece and the energy released.
> Horizontal momentum: 2 × 10 = 1 × 0 + 1 × v, so v = 20 m/s forward. Kinetic energy before = ½ × 2 × 100 = 100 J; after = ½ × 1 × 400 = 200 J; released 100 J.
## Bullet-and-block problems
- Treat them in two stages. Stage 1, the very short impact: momentum conserved, mechanical energy NOT conserved. Stage 2, the swing or slide afterwards: use energy (with friction if any).
> Example: A 10 g bullet at 300 m/s embeds itself in a 990 g block hanging on a string. How high does the block rise?
! Trap: using ½mu² = (M + m)gh straight away ignores the large energy lost in the impact and gives a height far too big.
## Exam checklist
- Define the system and check that external forces are zero (or negligible, or zero in one direction).
- Write one momentum equation with signs; add an energy equation only if the collision is elastic.
- Split multi-stage problems at the collision.

title: Optics
lines: Optics has two halves. Geometrical optics treats light as rays that reflect and bend; wave optics explains interference, diffraction and polarisation. The exam mixes both, often in short concept questions. Use c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
## Reflection
- Law of reflection: the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane, and the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence (both measured from the normal).
- Plane mirror: the image is virtual, upright, the same size, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
- Turning a mirror by an angle θ turns the reflected ray by 2θ.
> Example: A ray strikes a plane mirror at 30° to the mirror surface. Find the angle between the incident and reflected rays.
> The angle with the normal is 60°, so the angle of reflection is 60° and the two rays are 120° apart.
! Trap: angles of incidence are measured from the normal, not from the surface. Many questions give the angle to the surface on purpose.
## Refraction and refractive index
- Light bends when it crosses a boundary because its speed changes. Going into a denser medium (larger n) it bends towards the normal.
- Refractive index (from air or vacuum into a medium): n = sin i / sin r. Also n = c/v, so n ≥ 1. Water is about 4/3, glass about 1.5.
- General Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.
- Frequency (and so colour) does not change on refraction. Speed and wavelength both fall by the factor n: λ(medium) = λ(vacuum)/n.
- Looking straight down into water, an object at real depth h appears at depth h/n.
> Example: Light in air hits glass at 60° to the normal and refracts at 30°. Find n and the speed of light in the glass.
> Example: A pool is 2 m deep (n = 4/3). How deep does it look from directly above?
## Total internal reflection
- Happens only when light goes from a denser to a less dense medium, and the angle of incidence is equal to or greater than the critical angle C.
- sin C = 1/n (for the boundary with air). n = 2 gives C = 30°; n = √2 gives C = 45°; glass with n = 1.5 gives C ≈ 42°.
- Uses: optical fibres (a core of higher index inside cladding of lower index), reflecting prisms, the sparkle of diamonds (very large n, small C).
> Example: Light enters one short face of a right-angled isosceles glass prism (n = 1.5) at right angles. Does it pass out through the long face?
> It goes straight in and meets the long face at 45°. sin 45° ≈ 0.71 is larger than 1/1.5 ≈ 0.67, so 45° exceeds the critical angle: total internal reflection, and the light turns through 90°.
! Trap: light going from air into glass can never be totally reflected, however large the angle.
## Lenses and mirrors (basic)
- A convex (converging) lens brings parallel rays to a real focus at focal length f. A concave (diverging) lens spreads them as if from a virtual focus.

- Three easy rays for a convex lens: a ray parallel to the axis passes through the far focus; a ray through the optical centre goes straight on; a ray through the near focus leaves parallel to the axis.

- Images in a convex lens with object distance u: u > 2f, real, inverted, smaller (camera). u = 2f, real, inverted, same size at 2f. f < u < 2f, real, inverted, larger (projector). u < f, virtual, upright, larger (magnifying glass). At u = f no image forms.
- Lens formula (real distances positive): 1/u + 1/v = 1/f; magnification = v/u.
- A concave lens always gives a virtual, upright, smaller image. A convex mirror does the same and gives a wide view (car wing mirrors). A concave mirror behaves like a convex lens.
> Example: An object stands 15 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the image.
> 1/v = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30, so v = 30 cm on the other side. Magnification = 30/15 = 2: real, inverted, twice the size.
! Trick: real images are always inverted and virtual images from a single lens are always upright.
## Dispersion
- The refractive index of glass is slightly different for each colour: largest for violet, smallest for red.
- So a prism splits white light into a spectrum, with violet bent most and red least. In glass, red light travels fastest and has the largest critical angle.
- In order of increasing frequency: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet. Wavelength runs the opposite way.
> Example: Red and violet light enter the same glass block at the same angle. Which bends more, and which goes faster inside?
> Violet has the larger n, so it bends more and travels more slowly; red bends less and travels faster.
## Interference
- Two coherent sources (same frequency, constant phase difference) are needed. In Young's double-slit experiment one source illuminates two narrow slits.
- Bright fringe where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, nλ; dark fringe where it is (n + ½)λ. The central fringe is bright.

- Fringe spacing Δx = Lλ/d (L = slit-to-screen distance, d = slit separation). The fringes are equally spaced. Red light gives wider fringes than blue. White light gives a white central fringe with coloured fringes either side.

- Thin films (soap bubbles, oil on water) show colours by interference between the reflections from the two surfaces. Anti-reflection coatings use a film one quarter of a wavelength thick (in the film).
> Example: Slits 0.2 mm apart are lit by 600 nm light and the screen is 1 m away. Find the fringe spacing.
! Trap: moving the slits closer together makes the fringes further apart. Δx is inversely proportional to d.
## Diffraction
- Light spreads into the region behind an obstacle or slit. It is obvious only when the slit or obstacle is about as small as the wavelength.

- Single-slit pattern: a wide, bright central band with narrower, dimmer bands on each side. A narrower slit gives a wider pattern. The bright spot at the centre of the shadow of a small disc (Poisson's spot) is a diffraction effect.
- How to tell them apart: double-slit fringes are equally wide and equally spaced; single-slit fringes have a central band about twice as wide as the others.
> Example: A single slit is made narrower. What happens to the central band?
> It becomes wider (and dimmer), because diffraction is stronger when the slit is narrower.
## Polarisation
- Polarisation shows that light is a transverse wave; longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.
- A polariser passes only the vibration along its transmission direction. Natural light through one polariser is reduced to half intensity, whatever the angle.
- Two polarisers with parallel directions pass the light; turning the second through 90° (crossed) makes the light disappear.
- Reflected light from water or glass is partly polarised, so polarising sunglasses and camera filters cut glare. 3D cinema glasses also use polarisation.
> Example: Light passes through two polarisers. The second is slowly turned through 180°. What does an observer see?
> The brightness falls from maximum to zero (at 90°) and rises back to maximum (at 180°).
## Exam checklist
- Measure all angles from the normal.
- Frequency never changes on refraction; speed and wavelength do.
- Total internal reflection: dense to less dense, and i ≥ C with sin C = 1/n.
- Interference fringes: equal spacing Δx = Lλ/d. Diffraction: wide central band.

title: Thermal Physics
lines: Thermal physics connects the invisible motion of molecules to things we can measure: temperature, pressure, volume and heat. Questions are usually short, so the marks go to students who know the definitions exactly and handle kelvin temperatures and signs correctly. Take g = 10 m/s².
## Molecular kinetic theory
- Matter is made of a huge number of molecules, about 10⁻¹⁰ m across. One mole contains N(A) = 6.0 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's constant).
- Molecules are in endless random (thermal) motion that becomes faster at higher temperature. Evidence: diffusion, and Brownian motion.

- Brownian motion is the random jiggling of small visible particles (pollen fragments, smoke grains) caused by uneven bombardment by liquid or gas molecules. It shows molecular motion indirectly; it is not itself the motion of molecules.

- Molecules attract and repel each other at the same time. At the equilibrium separation r₀ the two balance. Closer than r₀ repulsion wins; further than r₀ attraction wins; beyond about 10r₀ the forces are negligible.
- Molecular potential energy is smallest at r = r₀.
> Example: 18 g of water is 1 mol. Estimate the volume per molecule.
> 18 g of water occupies 18 cm³ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ m³. Volume per molecule = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ / (6.0 × 10²³) = 3 × 10⁻²⁹ m³, which matches a size of about 3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.
! Trap: at r₀ the net force is zero, but the attractive and repulsive forces are not individually zero.
## Temperature and internal energy
- Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules. Equal temperature means equal average molecular kinetic energy, even for different gases (lighter molecules then move faster).
- Kelvin scale: T(K) = t(°C) + 273. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K. Absolute zero (0 K) cannot be reached.
- Internal energy of a body = total molecular kinetic energy + total molecular potential energy. It depends on temperature, volume, amount of substance and state.
- For an ideal gas, molecular potential energy is ignored, so its internal energy depends only on temperature (for a fixed amount).
- Internal energy is changed by doing work or by heat transfer; the two are equivalent in effect.
> Example: Which has more internal energy, 1 kg of ice at 0 °C or 1 kg of water at 0 °C?
> The water. The temperature is the same, so the molecular kinetic energy is the same, but melting needed energy that went into molecular potential energy.
! Trap: a body moving fast does not have more internal energy. Internal energy has nothing to do with the motion of the body as a whole.
## Gas pressure and the gas laws
- Gas pressure comes from molecules hitting the walls. It increases with the number of molecules per unit volume and with their average kinetic energy (temperature).
- Ideal gas law: pV = nRT, with T in kelvin. For a fixed amount of gas: p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂.
- Constant T (Boyle): pV = constant. Constant V: p/T = constant. Constant p: V/T = constant.
- Pressure of a trapped gas under a piston of mass m and area S (vertical cylinder, piston on top): p = p₀ + mg/S.

- Graphs: an isotherm on a p-V graph is a hyperbola; a higher temperature gives a curve further from the axes. On a p-T graph a constant-volume line passes through the origin (0 K); a steeper line means a smaller volume.
> Example: A rigid container holds gas at 2 atm and 27 °C. It is heated to 177 °C. Find the new pressure.
> Example: 10 L of gas at 1 atm is slowly compressed at constant temperature to 2 L. Find the pressure.
> Example: A 10 kg piston of area 0.01 m² rests on gas in a vertical cylinder; p₀ = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Find the gas pressure.
! Trap: always convert to kelvin. Heating from 27 °C to 54 °C does not double the pressure; 300 K to 327 K raises it by only 9 %.
## Specific heat capacity and latent heat
- Heating without a change of state: Q = cmΔT. Water has c = 4.2 × 10³ J/(kg·K), which is large, so water warms and cools slowly.
- Change of state: Q = mL, where L is the specific latent heat (J/kg). During melting or boiling the temperature stays constant; the energy breaks molecular bonds and raises potential energy.
- Mixing (no losses): heat lost by the hot part = heat gained by the cold part.
> Example: How much heat warms 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 70 °C?
> Example: 1 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 3 kg of water at 20 °C. Find the final temperature.
## First law of thermodynamics

- ΔU = W + Q. Sign convention: W is positive when work is done ON the gas (compression); Q is positive when heat is absorbed by the gas; ΔU positive means internal energy (and for an ideal gas, temperature) rises.
- Work at constant pressure: |W| = pΔV. A gas that expands does work on the surroundings, so W is negative.

- Special cases for an ideal gas: isothermal, ΔU = 0, so Q = −W. Adiabatic (no heat exchange, for example a quick compression), Q = 0, so ΔU = W: compression heats the gas, expansion cools it. Constant volume, W = 0, so ΔU = Q.
- A gas expanding into a vacuum does no work.
> Example: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat while expanding at a constant 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa by 2 × 10⁻³ m³. Find the change in internal energy.
> Work done by the gas = pΔV = 10⁵ × 2 × 10⁻³ = 200 J, so W = −200 J. ΔU = −200 + 500 = +300 J; the gas gets hotter.
! Trap: a gas absorbing heat does not necessarily get hotter. If it does more work than the heat it absorbs, its internal energy falls.
## Second law of thermodynamics (qualitative)
- Heat flows spontaneously only from a hotter body to a colder body. A refrigerator moves heat the other way only because work is supplied.

- No heat engine can turn all the heat it absorbs into work; some heat must always be rejected to a colder place. Efficiency η = W/Q(in) < 100 %. A machine that would do this (a "perpetual motion machine of the second kind") is impossible even though it would not break energy conservation.
- Natural processes involving heat are irreversible; the disorder of an isolated system (its entropy) tends to increase.
> Example: An engine takes in 1000 J of heat per cycle and rejects 700 J. Find the work done per cycle and the efficiency.
! Trap: the first law forbids creating energy; the second law forbids complete conversion of heat into work. A statement can obey one and break the other.
## Exam checklist
- Temperatures in kelvin for every gas-law ratio.
- Write the signs of W and Q before using ΔU = W + Q.
- Ideal gas internal energy follows temperature only.

title: Oscillations and Waves
lines: This topic links two pictures: one particle vibrating back and forth (oscillation), and a whole pattern of vibration travelling through a medium (a wave). Many exam errors come from mixing up these two pictures, so keep asking which one a question is about. Take g = 10 m/s².
## Simple harmonic motion
- SHM: the restoring force is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and directed back towards it: F = −kx, so a = −(k/m)x.
- Amplitude A: largest displacement. Period T: time for one complete oscillation. Frequency f = 1/T. Angular frequency ω = 2π/T.
- Displacement can be written x = A sin(ωt + φ), where φ is the initial phase.
- At equilibrium (x = 0): speed is greatest, acceleration and restoring force are zero. At the extremes (x = ±A): speed is zero, acceleration is greatest.
- In one period a particle travels a distance 4A; in half a period, 2A, wherever it starts. In a quarter period it travels A only if it starts at equilibrium or at an extreme.
> Example: A particle in SHM has x = 0.05 sin(4πt) in metres. Find the amplitude, period and frequency.
> A = 0.05 m. ω = 4π rad/s, so T = 2π/4π = 0.5 s and f = 2 Hz.
! Trap: the acceleration points towards equilibrium, so it is opposite to the displacement, not opposite to the velocity.
## Spring and pendulum periods
- Mass on a spring: T = 2π√(m/k). It does not depend on the amplitude or on g (a vertical spring has the same period as a horizontal one).
- Simple pendulum (small angles, below about 5°): T = 2π√(L/g). It does not depend on the mass or the amplitude.
- With g ≈ π² m/s², a 1 m pendulum has T = 2π√(1/π²) = 2 s.
> Example: A pendulum's length is made 4 times longer. What happens to its period? And a spring-mass system whose mass is made 4 times larger?
> Pendulum: T ∝ √L, so T doubles. Spring: T ∝ √m, so T also doubles.
! Trap: a pendulum clock taken up a mountain (smaller g) has a longer period and runs slow. A spring-mass system would keep the same period.
## Energy in SHM
- Energy changes between kinetic and potential, but the total stays constant (no damping): E = ½kA² = ½mv(max)².
- So v(max) = Aω = A√(k/m). Doubling the amplitude multiplies the energy by 4 and doubles the maximum speed, but leaves the period unchanged.
- Damped oscillation: amplitude and energy decrease; the period stays almost the same.
- Forced oscillation: the system vibrates at the driving frequency. Resonance: the amplitude is greatest when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency.
> Example: A 1 kg block on a spring with k = 100 N/m oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. Find the total energy and the maximum speed.
## Mechanical waves
- A wave transfers energy and the vibration pattern; the particles of the medium only vibrate about their own positions and do not travel with the wave.

- Transverse wave: particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel (waves on a rope). Longitudinal wave: particles vibrate along the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions (sound in air).
- Mechanical waves need a medium. Every particle copies the motion of the source, with a delay.
- Wave equation: v = fλ = λ/T. In one period the wave moves forward one wavelength.
- Frequency is set by the source and stays the same when the wave enters a new medium. Speed is set by the medium. So the wavelength changes in proportion to the speed.
> Example: A sound of 680 Hz travels in air at 340 m/s and then enters water, where sound travels at 1360 m/s. Find the wavelength in each.
> Air: λ = 340/680 = 0.5 m. Water: the frequency stays 680 Hz, so λ = 1360/680 = 2 m.
## Reading wave graphs
- A wave graph (y against position x) is a snapshot of all particles at one instant. The distance between neighbouring crests is λ.
- A vibration graph (y against time t) follows one particle. The time between neighbouring crests is T.

- Direction rule for a wave graph: imagine walking along the graph in the direction the wave travels. A particle on an "uphill" part moves down; a particle on a "downhill" part moves up. Equivalently, each particle will next copy the particle just behind it (closer to the source).
- After a time t, the whole waveform shifts forward by vt. After a whole number of periods the picture looks the same.
> Example: A transverse wave travels in the +x direction with λ = 4 m and v = 2 m/s. Find T, and say how far the waveform shifts in 0.5 s.
> T = λ/v = 2 s. In 0.5 s (a quarter period) the waveform shifts 2 × 0.5 = 1 m, a quarter wavelength, in the +x direction.
> Example: On the same snapshot, a particle sits on a part of the curve rising from a trough to the next crest (moving in +x). Which way does it move now?
> Walking in +x, this part is uphill, so the particle is moving downward.
! Trap: the x-axis of a wave graph is position, not time. Read λ from a wave graph and T from a vibration graph; do not swap them.
## Reflection, superposition and interference
- Waves reflect at a boundary with the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence. Echoes are reflected sound.
- Superposition: where two waves meet, the displacements add; afterwards each wave continues unchanged.
- Two sources with the same frequency and a steady phase difference (coherent) produce a stable interference pattern.
- For sources in phase: path difference = nλ gives constructive interference (strong vibration); path difference = (n + ½)λ gives destructive interference (weak or no vibration).
- Diffraction (spreading around obstacles or through gaps) is noticeable when the gap or obstacle is about the same size as the wavelength or smaller.
> Example: Two in-phase sources emit waves with λ = 2 m. A point is 3 m from one source and 4 m from the other. Is it a point of strong or weak vibration?
> Path difference = 1 m = λ/2, so the waves cancel: weak (destructive) vibration.
! Trap: at a point of constructive interference the particle still oscillates; its displacement is not always at maximum, only its amplitude is.
## Standing waves
- Two identical waves travelling in opposite directions form a standing wave with fixed nodes (no vibration) and antinodes (largest vibration).
- Neighbouring nodes are λ/2 apart; a node and the nearest antinode are λ/4 apart. A standing wave carries no energy along the string.
- A string fixed at both ends has nodes at both ends: L = nλ/2, so f = nv/(2L), with n = 1 the fundamental.
> Example: A 0.6 m string carries waves at 120 m/s. Find the fundamental frequency.
> λ = 2L = 1.2 m, so f = 120/1.2 = 100 Hz. The next harmonics are 200 Hz and 300 Hz.
## Sound and the Doppler effect
- Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave; it cannot travel through a vacuum. It is faster in solids than in liquids, and faster in liquids than in gases. In air it is about 340 m/s.
- Pitch depends on frequency; loudness on amplitude. Humans hear about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz; above is ultrasound, below is infrasound.
- Doppler effect: when source and observer approach each other, the observed frequency is higher than the emitted one; when they separate, it is lower. The source's own frequency does not change.
> Example: A student shouts towards a cliff and hears the echo 2 s later. How far away is the cliff (sound at 340 m/s)?
> The sound travels there and back: 2d = 340 × 2, so d = 340 m.
! Trap: as an ambulance passes you, the pitch you hear drops suddenly. That does not mean its siren changed; only the received frequency changed.
## Exam checklist
- Pendulum: T depends on L and g only. Spring: T depends on m and k only.
- Frequency never changes across a boundary; speed and wavelength do.
- For direction questions, use the uphill-down, downhill-up rule in the direction of travel.
